World.title: “Aren’t We All PR People?”: Setting a new benchmark for communicators, By Yushau A. Shuaib
World.content:
For emerging communicators, this book will serve as a mentor. For educators, it will be a teaching companion. For practitioners, it will be a reminder of the discipline’s core values. And for the profession at large, it will be a contribution that strengthens the intellectual and practical foundation of PR in Nigeria.

Ahmed Balarabe Sa’id’s new book, Aren’t We All PR People?, is one of those rare works that immediately announce themselves as more than textbooks. It is a field guide, a mentor in print, and a career compass for anyone stepping into the demanding but rewarding world of Public Relations. After carefully reviewing the book, I am genuinely tempted — without any flattery — to call it the definitive PR career guide for emerging communicators. It is a standout resource that sets a new benchmark for the field.

Balarabe, a Mass Communication graduate of Bayero University Kano (BUK) more than two decades ago, is not merely a communication scholar, he is a true PR professional in every sense of the word — far beyond regulatory certification. Calling him a practitioner feels almost inadequate because he breathes, speaks, writes, and conducts himself with the instinctive discipline of someone who genuinely lives and promotes Public Relations through his relationships, engagements, and professional ethos.

What makes this book remarkable is not only its breadth but its narrative style. Balarabe writes with a clarity that demystifies PR practice and a warmth that draws readers into the profession’s human side. His storytelling approach, just like my recently released memoir, MNI Versus MNIPR in NIPSS, creates curiosity, making even foundational principles feel fresh and urgent. For budding communicators who often encounter PR as abstract theory, this book offers something different: a vivid, practical, and relatable journey into the craft.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Several chapters carry uniquely crafted titles that immediately spark curiosity and offer clear glimpses into their thematic direction. Chapter One, “From Ancient Rhetoric to Digital Dialogue,” sets the tone by tracing the evolution of communication from classical persuasion to today’s fast paced digital exchanges. Other standout chapters — “A Constellation of Concepts,” “Professionalising the Practice,” “That Good PR Practitioner,” “A Universe of Opportunities,” “Some of Your Mentors,” “Ethical Traps and Hidden Dangers,” “You and AI,” and “PR Shots” — present their subjects with clarity and creative framing. PR Shots, in particular, is an engaging compilation of short, sharp professional posts originally shared on social media, now curated into a chapter that reads like a pocket guide for daily practice. The final chapter, which foregrounds the emerging role of Public Relations in Nigeria’s national project, provides a thoughtful and forward looking conclusion — positioning PR not just as a profession but as a strategic pillar in nation building.

The book succeeds on multiple fronts. First, it bridges the gap between theory and practice. Many PR texts lean heavily on academic frameworks, leaving young practitioners unsure how to apply them in real world situations. Balarabe flips that script. He grounds every concept in lived experience — crisis moments, ethical dilemmas, communication landmines, and the subtle art of managing reputation. The result is a book that teaches not only what PR is but how PR is done.

Second, the book is structured to guide readers through the profession with increasing depth. From foundational ethics to the anatomy of a good practitioner, from crisis communication to the evolving role of AI, each chapter builds on the last with intentional clarity. The inclusion of real personalities — role models whose careers illuminate different pathways in the field — adds a human dimension that young readers will find both inspiring and instructive.

Third, Balarabe demonstrates a rare courage in addressing contemporary issues. His challenge to the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR) on the absence of AI regulation is bold and necessary. His exploration of digital crises, misinformation, and emerging technologies shows a practitioner who understands that PR is evolving rapidly — and that the next generation must be prepared for a landscape far more complex than what existed a decade ago.

The book also shines in its treatment of ethics. Balarabe does not present ethics as a checklist but as the backbone of professional credibility. His insistence that ethical grounding must precede technical skill is a message young communicators urgently need. In a world in which speed often competes with accuracy, and visibility competes with integrity, this emphasis is both timely and timeless.

One of the book’s strongest features is its use of narrative to teach principles. Balarabe’s stories — of practitioners, crises, institutions, and turning points — are not decorative. They are instructional. They show how PR works in real life, how reputations are built and broken, and how communicators must think, act, and adapt. This narrative approach makes the book accessible without sacrificing depth.

The book is also refreshingly honest. It does not romanticise the profession. It acknowledges the pressures, the politics, the ethical crossroads, and the emotional labour involved in communication work. Yet, it balances this realism with optimism, reminding readers that PR remains one of the most impactful careers for those who master its principles.

For emerging communicators, this book will serve as a mentor. For educators, it will be a teaching companion. For practitioners, it will be a reminder of the discipline’s core values. And for the profession at large, it will be a contribution that strengthens the intellectual and practical foundation of PR in Nigeria.

In my sincere assessment, this book is more than a guide. It is a benchmark. A resource that will inspire, instruct, and challenge. A book that emerging communicators will return to repeatedly as they navigate their careers.

And truly, Aren’t We All PR People is a book our profession has been waiting for.

Yushau A. Shuaib, an award-winning PR practitioner, is the author of MNI Versus MNIPR in NIPSS- Tackling Institutional Bullying. Email: [email protected]

World.title: AES criticises Tinubu’s comment on regional security
World.content:
The Alliance of Sahel States (AES) has criticised President Bola Tinubu for his comment, attributing Nigeria’s growing security crisis in part to insecurity in neighbouring states.

The AES — made of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso — considered Mr Tinubu’s remark “simplistic,” “hasty”, and trivialised the states’ efforts to address terrorist operations in the Sahel.

Burkina Faso’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Karamoko Traore, disclosed the AES’s stance on Thursday during a meeting with the Chargé d’Affaires of the Nigerian embassy in Burkina Faso.

President Tinubu made his comment last week while discussing the military operation that led to the rescue of pupils and teachers kidnapped in Oyo State. He linked the growing insecurity in the country and the resurgence of kidnapping to the security situation of its neighbours in the Sahel.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Some of them (the terrorists) are not Nigerian. You see, the problem of insecurity in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger only exacerbates our difficulties,” he said.

The three, in response to this, summoned the Nigerian Chargé d’Affaires for a meeting in Ouagadougou.

At the meeting, Mr Traore stated that Mr Tinubu’s “surprising” remark downplayed the sacrifice of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso in the fight to curb armed groups.

He also claimed the comment minimised the role played by the Nigerien army in the fight against Boko Haram.

He pointed out that Niamey was already facing the Boko Haram threat even before the emergence of large-scale terrorist insecurity in the other countries of the Alliance.

“Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, and Nigeria are facing the same enemy.

“We would have preferred a more accurate presentation of the security situation, rather than placing the blame for a complex situation on neighbouring countries, at the risk of fuelling misunderstandings and frustrations between peoples bound by history, geography, and fraternity,” the minister said.

Nigeria’s relations with Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso have been fraught since the 2023 military coup in Niger and the subsequent deterioration of relations between the AES and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the three countries officially exited ECOWAS in early 2025. This was after a year-long effort by the bloc to convince them to reconsider leaving.

The juntas in all three nations had accused ECOWAS of failing to support them in their fight against terrorism and of imposing sanctions that they claim harmed their populations.

Due to the strained relations, security cooperation also suffered, particularly along Nigeria’s borders with the three Sahelian countries.

The fragmentation of regional security arrangements has made intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border coordination more difficult.

However, the Nigerian government has been pushing for cooperation with the AES to counter cross-border criminal networks operating in the region.

Last week, Nigeria’s Minister of Defence, Christopher Musa, called for joint regional action between the AES and ECOWAS to combat insurgency in West Africa.

Mr Musa stated that confronting West Africa’s complex security landscape requires an inclusive, coordinated front.

World.title: The memoir on NIPSS, NIPR and an AI study that outlived institutional setbacks, By Kabir Abdulsalam
World.content:
The enduring strength of MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS lies not in its recounting of institutional disagreements but in its demonstration that resilience can transform disappointment into lasting contribution… The closing reflection captures this beautifully: “Institutions may grant opportunities, but they do not own ideas. Once knowledge becomes a mission, it acquires a life of its own. No withdrawal letter can take that away.”.. That single sentence summarises not only Chapter Nine but also the relationship between the memoir and its companion volume on artificial intelligence.

When I received copies of MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS: Tackling Institutional Bullying and AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria: Challenges and Prospects, both authored by Yushau A. Shuaib, managing director and chief executive officer of Image Merchants Promotion Limited (IMPR), I expected two very different books. One appeared to be a memoir of institutional conflict; the other, an academic work on emerging technology and crisis communication.

Having read both, I discovered they are, in many respects, companion volumes. Together, they tell the story of how personal adversity can become intellectual opportunity, and how an interrupted academic journey can ultimately produce work of lasting national and international significance.

As Associate Editor of Spokespersons Digest — the publication behind the National Spokespersons Awards — I was naturally drawn to Chapter Eight of the memoir, “The NIPR Betrayal” in MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS, spanning pages 139 to 161. Having covered the activities of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR) for several years, I approached the chapter with professional curiosity. What I found was an emotionally compelling account that raises broader questions about institutional relationships, professional loyalty, and the delicate balance between organisational discipline and support for members.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the memoir, shortly after his withdrawal from the Senior Executive Course (SEC) 47 at the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS), Kuru, Shuaib was invited to appear before the Ethics Panel of the NIPR Council over actions arising from the dispute.

For someone whose professional life had been closely intertwined with the Institute for more than three decades, the experience was understandably painful.

Shuaib traces his relationship with the NIPR back to his undergraduate days at Bayero University, Kano, where he specialised in Public Relations and, in 1992, became the first recipient of the NIPR President’s Prize for the Best Graduating Public Relations Student. Three years later, he was honoured as the Kano/Jigawa Chapter’s Public Relations Person of the Year.

His career subsequently expanded beyond Nigeria through advanced studies, including a Master’s degree in Public Relations from the University of Westminster, London, professional research in online public relations, and affiliations with international organisations such as the Chartered Institute of Public Relations (CIPR), the Public Relations Society of America (PRSA), and the International Public Relations Association (IPRA). Under his leadership, IMPR also earned multiple international recognitions, including the SABRE Awards Africa and IPRA Golden World Awards.

Against this backdrop, one seemingly minor incident in the memoir becomes symbolically significant. The invitation from NIPR reportedly addressed him as “ANIPR” rather than “MNIPR,” the professional designation he had used for many years and which, according to him, had previously appeared in official correspondence from the Institute.

At first glance, it appears trivial. Yet anyone familiar with public relations understands that titles, professional designations and institutional language often carry symbolic meaning. They communicate recognition, identity and belonging.

Shuaib writes that after drawing the Registrar’s attention to the issue, another invitation was issued, this time omitting any professional designation altogether.

Whether intentional or not, the incident deepened his perception that his decades of contribution were no longer receiving institutional acknowledgement.

Equally striking is the memoir’s account of the National Spokespersons Awards.

The book explains that the initiative was conceived in 2019 during the tenure of Mallam Mukhtar Sirajo as President of the NIPR. Its inaugural edition was independently organised by IMPR in 2021, with the Institute’s endorsement, before both organisations entered into a formal partnership through a Memorandum of Understanding in 2023.

The awards have since grown into one of Nigeria’s foremost platforms for recognising excellence in strategic communication; honouring spokespersons, public information managers, corporate affairs practitioners, military communicators and crisis communication professionals.

According to the memoir, however, the partnership was terminated before the expiration of the agreement by the Ike Neliaku-led NIPR.

What surprised me further was when the institute, following the termination, introduced another awards platform under a different name.

Reflecting on the episode, Shuaib writes: “Organisations can withdraw endorsements. Partnerships can be terminated. Titles can be withheld. But one’s name — carefully built over decades — must remain answerable first to conscience, history and truth.”

That statement captures the emotional centre of Chapter Eight.

If that chapter represents the wound, Chapter Nine — “A Blessed Disappointment” — represents the healing. In my view, it is the memoir’s most inspiring chapter.

Rather than dwelling on conflict, it chronicles how an interrupted academic journey became the catalyst for some of the author’s most significant professional achievements.

Shuaib begins by acknowledging the personal toll of the crisis. The combined effects of the NIPSS withdrawal, the NIPR investigation, and the ensuing legal battles, resulted in something he had never previously experienced — hypertension.

His opening reflection is both simple and profound: “As someone who had spent decades helping individuals and institutions navigate reputational crises, I suddenly found myself at the centre of one.”

Yet, the chapter is far from a catalogue of grievances. Instead, it documents how adversity redirected his energy towards new opportunities.

One source of encouragement came from his family, whose support inspired him to take a restorative vacation in Canada. Equally moving were the visits and messages from graduates of the Young Communication Fellowship, many of whom travelled long distances simply to encourage their mentor.

These moments reinforced one of the book’s enduring messages: “True success is not measured by certificates, titles or institutional recognition. It is measured by the positive impact one leaves in the lives of others.”

The memoir also recounts how the NIPSS experience unexpectedly strengthened his vision for expanding the Young Communication Fellowship.

Inspired by the residential model at NIPSS, he developed plans for hostel facilities at the PRNigeria Centres in Kano and Ilorin. During a visit to the Kano Centre, Professor Adamu Abubakar Gwarzo, President of MAAUN, asked whether similar facilities existed in Abuja.

When Shuaib explained that such a project was beyond his financial capacity, Professor Gwarzo donated a large building in Lugbe, Abuja, to serve as a training and residential centre for the Fellowship.

It is an extraordinary example of how one setback unexpectedly created room for another opportunity.

Perhaps the chapter’s most compelling narrative, however, concerns the research project that eventually became AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria: Challenges and Prospects.

Originally approved as a research proposal during SEC 47 at NIPSS, the study was titled “Artificial Intelligence and Crisis Communication in Nigeria’s Public Sector: An Assessment.”

Following his withdrawal from the programme, the institutional framework supporting the research disappeared. Many scholars would understandably have abandoned the project.

Shuaib chose otherwise. Driven by professional conviction and encouraged by colleagues at the Centre for Crisis Communication, he completed the study independently within three months.

The findings proved remarkably relevant. The research identified what he describes as Nigeria’s “awareness-adoption gap.” While many communication professionals are increasingly familiar with artificial intelligence, institutional use remains largely limited to drafting documents, monitoring media content, and generating reports.

More advanced applications — including predictive analytics, crisis forecasting, sentiment analysis and misinformation detection — remain significantly underutilised.

The study also highlights a “trust paradox.” Although AI improves speed and efficiency, communication professionals remain cautious about relying on it during crises because of concerns over deepfakes, misinformation, algorithmic bias, and the irreplaceable role of human empathy and judgment.

Its central conclusion is both balanced and timely: artificial intelligence should enhance human decision-making, not replace it.

Beyond diagnosis, the research identifies structural barriers to AI adoption, including inadequate digital infrastructure, inconsistent electricity supply, limited broadband penetration, shortages of specialised expertise, weak institutional coordination, and underdeveloped policy frameworks.

Importantly, the work did not remain confined to academia. It informed discussions at the Centre for Crisis Communication and the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), contributing to the National Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and Crisis Communication held at the National Defence College, Abuja, in November 2025.

One outcome of that symposium was the establishment of the Crisis Communication Hub (CCHub), a multi-stakeholder platform aimed at improving crisis management and combating misinformation in Nigeria.

The research subsequently evolved into the 200-page book AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria: Challenges and Prospects, endorsed by NITDA Director-General, Malam Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi; Major General Chris Olukolade (Rtd); Professor Abdalla Uba Adamu; and Professor Abiodun Adeniyi.

Its most remarkable achievement came when the book was shortlisted as a finalist for the 2026 International Public Relations Association (IPRA) Golden World Awards in Athens, Greece.

There is considerable irony in this outcome. A research project interrupted within one institution ultimately gained wider relevance beyond it.

Had it remained solely an academic exercise at NIPSS, it might have concluded as another research paper in an institutional archive.

Instead, it became a national symposium, a published book, a catalyst for policy conversations, and an internationally recognised work.

That is perhaps the memoir’s greatest lesson. Institutions undoubtedly create opportunities. They nurture ideas, shape careers, and provide platforms for scholarship. But ideas, once fully developed, often transcend the institutions that first gave them life.

The enduring strength of MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS lies not in its recounting of institutional disagreements but in its demonstration that resilience can transform disappointment into lasting contribution.

The closing reflection captures this beautifully: “Institutions may grant opportunities, but they do not own ideas. Once knowledge becomes a mission, it acquires a life of its own. No withdrawal letter can take that away.”

That single sentence summarises not only Chapter Nine but also the relationship between the memoir and its companion volume on artificial intelligence.

Together, they tell the story of an interrupted journey that ultimately reached destinations far beyond where it first began.

Kabir Abdulsalam is Associate Editor of Spokespersons Digest. He can be reached via [email protected].

World.title: ‘Jude caused our family’s problems’ — P-Square’s elder brother Henry alleges
World.content:
The long-running feud involving P-Square singers Peter and Paul Okoye and their elder brother and former manager, Jude Okoye, has taken another turn, with another member of the Okoye family publicly weighing in on the dispute.

Henry Okoye, who identified himself as the brother directly older than Jude and senior to Peter and Paul, has accused Jude of contributing to the family’s divisions and urged him to take responsibility for reconciling the estranged twins.

Henry’s intervention comes amid a fresh round of accusations between the brothers after Peter, popularly known as Mr P, began releasing a series of videos detailing his version of P-Square’s history, financial dealings and the circumstances surrounding the group’s repeated break-ups.

Peter and Paul formed P-Square and rose to become one of Africa’s biggest music groups before splitting in 2017. They reconciled in 2021 but separated again in 2024 following renewed disagreements over the group’s finances and management. The dispute subsequently led to an Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigation and an ongoing court case involving Jude, who has denied wrongdoing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Jude has also publicly responded to Peter’s recent allegations, disputing claims of financial impropriety and accusing his younger brother of manipulating the narrative surrounding P-Square’s finances and family disagreements.

Enter Henry Okoye

Henry, however, said his decision to speak was significant because he had never addressed the family’s problems publicly before. He said during his interview on “Nolly Serve,” posted on YouTube on Friday, that he had watched parts one to seven of Peter’s video series. Still, he stressed that he could not verify allegations about incidents he did not personally witness.

He said, “When Paul and Peter started running away from the family, we never knew that it was Jude causing the problem. Jude is not a good person. He’s my brother, but he’s very bad. I’m telling you the truth: Jude is very bad. I’m just telling the truth, he’s very bad. He’s not a nice person. Let me tell you, for almost a year to two years now, I haven’t talked to Jude, and he hasn’t talked to me. Even when I was sick in the hospital last year— I was admitted for two months, Jude knew.

“Peter used to call me. Paul used to call me. Jude never called me, not once. Jude doesn’t care about anybody. Look at my sister, she’s in Lagos, and she’s suffering there. Our last-born is also in Lagos, but nobody cares about her. Jude doesn’t care. I said nobody cares about her. Peter is trying, at least. But especially Jude, let me set Paul aside for now, because I don’t know if Jude used some voodoo on Paul. I don’t know; I can’t tell. If you come into the Okoye family, in our family, Paul is the nicest person.”

On set

Furthermore, Henry maintained that Jude was nowhere to be found when everything started.

According to him, he sacrificed his time, energy and resources for P-Square in its early days, serving as their bodyguard, among other roles.

“When they started this music, they were looking for sponsors. We couldn’t get one, so I started sponsoring them. Jude was not there at that time. Even when Baseline Ages came to Jos looking for artists, I took them to the stadium for the performance. They came first. We travelled from state to state for music. At one point, they even used my car to distribute flyers.

“When we travelled to Abuja, my sister, the one they call Lillian, was always the one collecting the gate fee. I served as a bodyguard for them, along with some of my friends. After everything was set up, before they started making real money, Jude suddenly came in, wanting to manage them”, he said.

According to Henry, their mother opposed Jude managing P-Square, as she was already aware of his character.

“My mother disagreed. It was our senior brother in P-Square who begged my mother to allow Jude to manage them. My mother said she knew the kind of person Jude was; she knew his character well.”

20 percent

Moreover, Henry revealed that before P-Square became known, there was an agreement that they would pay him a percentage of each song’s earnings as their sponsor.

Henry noted, “Before they started all this, they promised me 20 per cent of each song’s earnings. Nobody ever gave me that. After three or four years, I asked them about it, and I never received anything. I told them I hadn’t seen any of the 20 per cent they promised. Jude eventually cut in and said, “What do you mean, 20 per cent — for what?” He said something like: they’re the ones flying to different countries, and if their plane ever crashed, I’d just be sitting comfortably at home.

“When he said it, I responded, “Jude, were you there when we started this?” But he came in and tried to push everyone else away, and unfortunately, he succeeded. Tony is one of their dancers; he’s also P-Square’s senior brother, one of my own brothers, Tony Okoye. He’s in Lagos, but nobody hears from him, nobody at all. This is the first time I’m speaking out, the first time, ever, on social media, even though we share the same father and mother.”

World.title: “Deeply embarrassed” President Tinubu puts EFCC on a leash, By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
President Tinubu may have been “deeply embarrassed” by the EFCC’s timing. The greater embarrassment would be allowing Nigeria’s institutions to remain so politically vulnerable that every controversial decision is judged less by the law than by the politics surrounding it. That is a leash no serious democracy should ever place on its regulators.

It was a stunning public rebuke.

This week, the fragility of Nigeria’s democratic institutions came into sharp focus. The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) exercised its sweeping powers by freezing the Osun State Government’s accounts over alleged financial misconduct. There has been no judicial determination of wrongdoing. Within hours, however, President Bola Tinubu ordered the anti-corruption agency to reverse itself and unfreeze the accounts. His explanation was simple: he was “deeply embarrassed.”

The episode has reignited concerns about regulatory capture and what it means for Nigeria’s democracy. It is not a choice between the “white devil” and the “black devil.” Rather, it exposes a deeper problem: institutions that are either vulnerable to political influence or capable of exercising enormous powers without sufficient institutional safeguards.

The political context makes the incident impossible to ignore. Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke is seeking re-election amid an intense contest with the ruling party, which is determined to reclaim a state it lost nearly four years ago. Against that backdrop, the EFCC’s decision to freeze the state’s accounts just days before the election inevitably attracted suspicion.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

President Tinubu appeared to recognise exactly that. Explaining his intervention, he said, “I feel deeply embarrassed… by the timing of the agency’s action.”

Nigeria’s greatest governance challenge is not the absence of regulators. It is the gradual erosion of their independence and, at times, the abuse of the extensive powers that Parliament has entrusted to them. Agencies established to regulate markets, combat corruption or oversee public services increasingly operate under the shadow of the Executive, whether through direct influence or the public perception of it.

That is why the President’s justification deserves closer examination.

Tinubu argued that he intervened to preserve “public confidence and the integrity, credibility, and fairness of our democratic process.” Yet his public reversal of the EFCC has inadvertently reinforced another damaging perception: that regulatory decisions in Nigeria can ultimately be shaped by political calculations. For investors, businesses and citizens alike, institutional certainty matters as much as the law itself.

This is not to dismiss legitimate questions about the EFCC’s conduct. Freezing a state government’s accounts barely a week before a governorship election deserves careful scrutiny, particularly if there is any basis for believing that the Commission’s chairman, Ola Olukoyede, was acting in a manner that could benefit the ruling party. Whether or not that perception is justified, it now exists in the public domain.

The President himself acknowledged the danger.

“Osun State is only a few days away from its gubernatorial election. Therefore, nothing ought to be done to give an impression that the EFCC or indeed any other agency of the federal government is being used to interfere with the election.”

That statement should become more than an explanation for one intervention. It should become the starting point for institutional reform.

This is history repeating itself as tragedy. President Tinubu knows this playbook intimately; during his tenure as governor of Lagos State, he famously weathered the heavy hand of federal power weaponised against his administration. To watch his government now mirror those very tactics is like watching a former victim inherit the whip. Will Tinubu break that cycle rather than repeat it?

Nigeria’s Constitution devotes enormous attention to distributing political power among the Executive, Legislature and Judiciary, and between the federal and state governments. It pays considerably less attention to designing institutions capable of remaining independent, regardless of who occupies political office.

The real test of institutional strength lies not in constitutional theory but in governance structures: who appoints regulators, how they can be removed, how they are funded, and whether their governing boards possess genuine independence. Those questions affect anti-corruption agencies, financial regulators, electoral bodies and virtually every institution expected to operate above politics.

The EFCC itself illustrates the problem.

Today, Nigerians know the Commission’s chairman, but few know who sits on its Board. Section 2 of the EFCC Act 2004 provides for representatives from the Central Bank of Nigeria; the Ministries of Justice, Finance and Foreign Affairs; the SSS; NIA; Police; Customs; Immigration; NDLEA; CAC; SEC; NDIC; NAICOM; NIPOST; NCC; and only four eminent Nigerians from outside government.

Who are those independent members? What qualifications do they bring? How were they selected? Few Nigerians can answer those questions.

From a corporate governance perspective, effective boards are expected to include a substantial proportion of genuinely independent directors capable of exercising objective oversight. The EFCC board, however, is overwhelmingly populated by representatives of executive agencies. That composition risks creating an institution characterised more by inter-agency coordination than by independent governance.

Institutional decline rarely begins with operational failure. More often, it begins quietly, at the boardroom table, where oversight weakens long before the public notices the consequences.

Nigeria does not suffer from a shortage of anti-corruption laws. It has enacted modern legislation against financial crime, procurement abuse, money laundering and illicit enrichment. The country’s recurring challenge has never been the laws themselves. It has been building institutions strong enough to enforce them consistently, independently, and beyond the reach of politics.

President Tinubu may have been “deeply embarrassed” by the EFCC’s timing. The greater embarrassment would be allowing Nigeria’s institutions to remain so politically vulnerable that every controversial decision is judged less by the law than by the politics surrounding it. That is a leash no serious democracy should ever place on its regulators.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving businesses and African diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: A bond that must never be broken (6), By Femi Fani-Kayode
World.content:
The South African people, as hostile, violent, aggressive and annoying as some of them may be, are our African brothers and sisters, and given all they have been through they do not deserve our anger and hate but rather our compassion, sympathy, love, care, support, concern and pity… Regardless of all, we must offer them all these things, re-build the bridge and work closely with them for the sake of our collective future.

Permit me to once again share the words of the Sweden-based Nigerian writer, Prince Kio Jaja Amachree. He wrote the following on X:

“In 1990 when Mandela came to thank Nigeria for its support to the ANC and the Pan African Congress he was given 10 ten million USD by the Nigerian Government as our further contribution to the ANC when he was leaving. 61 billion dollars was the total figure that Nigeria donated to the ANC and the Pan African Congress by 1994. Adjusted for three decades of inflation, and with even a conservative rate of interest applied, as any court applies to any unpaid debt, the true present value of Nigeria’s sacrifice runs into the hundreds of billions of dollars.”

He went further by saying, “this was money that Nigeria, with its own crushing debt burden, collapsing infrastructure and 130 million of its own citizens living in multidimensional poverty, needs desperately at home.”

He was right.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He went on to ask the following question and immediately provided the answer.

“How the debt is being repaid? Here is how South Africa has serviced this account in the year 2026. Musa Yunana Joe and Charles Iroegbu, two Nigerian nationals, were killed on June 28, one allegedly at the hands of South African police officers, the other by attackers who remain conveniently unidentified. They died two days before an unofficial deadline set by anti migrant vigilantes for foreigners to leave the country. They were not the first this year. In April, Amaramiro Emmanuel was beaten to death, according to Nigeria’s consul general, by officers of the South African National Defence Force, soldiers of the very state Nigerian money helped bring into being. Ekpenyong Andrew was arrested in Pretoria and was next seen in a mortuary. The mobs of Operation Dudula and the March and March movement have marched through Johannesburg and Durban, some in warrior dress, carrying spears, whips and shields, telling African migrants to leave or, in the words circulated on their platforms, return in a coffin. By early July, nearly 600 Nigerians had been evacuated on emergency flights, with roughly 1000 registered to flee, abandoning shops, cars, homes and life savings built over decades. Across all nationalities, more than 13000 African migrants have been driven out in a matter of weeks. None of this is new. It is the fourth great wave. After 2008, when more than 60 people were butchered. After 2015. After 2019. Each time, Pretoria issues its regrets. Each time, no meaningful prosecutions follow. Each time, the machetes return. This is how South Africa repays the country that paid for its freedom.”

Amachree’s analysis is factual and unassailable.

He concluded with the following.

“History matters! Those who say Nigerians should stop talking about South Africa and face Nigeria’s own problems have it exactly backwards. This is Nigeria’s problem. It is 61 billion dollars of Nigeria’s problem. Money taken from the salaries of Nigerian clerks and the pockets of Nigerian students and the treasury of a struggling young republic, invested in the freedom of a people whose government now cannot summon the will to stop mobs from hunting Nigerians in the streets. Nelson Mandela knew what Nigeria had done. He said so, in Lagos, on camera, in 1990. The tragedy is that the nation he founded has chosen amnesia. Nigeria and 220 million Nigerians have not forgotten. The dead, Musa, Charles, Amaramiro, Ekpenyong, and the scores before them, will have justice. Through courts, through commissions, through commerce, and through the unyielding memory of history. Not today, perhaps. But the ledger is open, the arithmetic is documented, and history, as it always does, will collect.”

Can anyone dispute what he has said?

Now consider the following words which came from one Phakel Umthakaki Ndanbandaba, who is one of leaders of March on March and who was recently hosted by President Cyril Ramaphosa.

In front of a massive and unruly crowd of supporters a few days ago he said, “I don’t sleep because I am so scared that PEOPLE FROM NIGERIA who are feeding our kids drugs are here in this country. They are all very dangerous people. And as a man, I took it upon myself to say, you know, let me choose death than to look at what is going on like this. Let me protect our kids. Let me protect our law enforcement officers. Let me protect even our government.”

I am not given to responding to those whose words are fuelled by ignorance, racism, Afrophobia and hate but in this case I will make an exception.

Someone should remind this Zulu Phakel that innocent Nigerians don’t sleep easily in South Africa anymore because they are being targeted, beaten, persecuted and killed like chickens in the streets by murderous, homicidal mobs that walk around half-naked, wielding axes and spears, and that are led by thugs like him.

It is the job of law enforcement to catch drug dealers and we support them in doing so wherever those dealers are from, but it is not the job of angry mobs who always lump the innocent and kill them with the guilty to do so.

What this man is doing is called race-baiting and incitement against Nigerians and he is endangering our lives.

He is also being supported, encouraged and bankrolled by a hidden foreign hand, to do all this because he is not capable of doing it on his own.

Yet the question must be asked, has it not occurred to this Zulu Phakel that Nigerians are not the only ones selling drugs in his country?

Some do, just as South Africans smuggle in and sell drugs to Nigerians in Nigeria and South Africa too, but we cannot possibly demonise all South Africans and call them all drug dealers.

There are evil men that are involved in this evil trade from both sides and the answer is for the good men and women on both sides to join forces and resist them.

The answer is NOT to criminalise and demonise all Nigerians and label us as drug dealers.

This has to stop.

One of the leaders of the South African opposition by the name of Herman Mashaba, who we have been reliably informed is one of those bankrolling the madness and egging thugs like Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma and Phakel Umkathaki Ndanbandaba on, said the following on X:

“South Africa is not going to be blackmailed by anyone or country to accept illegality because they claim to have assisted during apartheid.”

Mashaba would do well to take heed of the following words.

Outside of that, one thing is clear: those that carry out these barbaric hate crimes and acts of Afrophobia in South Africa deserve more of our pity than our anger… I say this because when you see a black South African attacking or threatening a foreign African national and telling him to “go back home,” it is like a person pouring petrol all over his own body, setting a match to it and burning himself alive.

Nigeria will not sit by silently as our nationals are being targeted and killed.

Deny it as much as you like, but the truth is that if not for us you would still be in chains.

No one is asking South Africa to accept illegality.

If you choose to be ungrateful and repay our good with evil, that is your call and we leave you to God.

Needless to say, had it not been for our efforts during your struggle, you would still be bondage and abject poverty today and probably be speaking Afrikaans as your national language.

Do as you please but what we insist on is that you operate according to due process and within the law and stop vilifying, demonising, targetting and killing our nationals.

Is this too much to ask?

If you insist on taking the course you have chosen, know that nothing is off the table and there will be consequences which will come at a time and place of our own choosing.

Nigerian lives are precious. For each one that your thugs take, there will be a heavy price to pay.

Know this and know peace. A word is enough for the wise.

Permit me to add the following.

Many in our country are boiling with anger today about what is happening to our compatriots in South Africa and this is understandable.

The situation is unacceptable and has, rightly, resulted in outrage, not just in Nigeria but throughout the entire African continent and indeed the civilised world.

As I approach the end of this contribution, I appeal for restraint, understanding, patience and calm from our people, despite the smears, violence, and mindless and inexplicable provocations for, as the Bible says, “this too shall pass.”

Outside of that, one thing is clear: those that carry out these barbaric hate crimes and acts of Afrophobia in South Africa deserve more of our pity than our anger.

I say this because when you see a black South African attacking or threatening a foreign African national and telling him to “go back home,” it is like a person pouring petrol all over his own body, setting a match to it and burning himself alive.

The reality is that we are one and when a black South African attacks an African national, he is attacking himself.

Coupled with this is the issue of suppressed and ingrained trauma, which came as a consequence of the Apartheid years and which a respected South African leader by the name of Zwelinzima Vavi, the Secretary General of the South African Federation of Trade Unions, alluded to and I mentioned in part four of this series.

The truth is that when the black South African vents such hate towards his fellow black Africans for no just cause, it is essentially a manifestation of the deep-set psychological trauma that Vavi was referring to.

It is not only uncontrollable but it is also pathological.

And coupled with poverty and the lack of any real prospect of rising to the top, it’s cause is obvious yet lost on most.

To establish that cause one has to study the history of the black South African and know what he has been through and where he is coming from.

The situation was simply shocking for the black majority population in Apartheid South Africa and many from other parts of the world have either forgotten or never knew.

What was done to them can best be compared to what was done to the Africans who were captured, transported like cattle, and sold into slavery in America and the Caribbean centuries ago, and what was done to the Herero and Nama tribes in modern-day Namibia by Imperial pre-World War 1 Germany, which literally wiped them out and ethnically cleansed them during colonial rule in the early 19th century.

For four hundred years and particularly after the Apartheid system was fully established, it was not just a question of South Africans being denied the right to lead and rule in their own country. It was far more insidious and worse than that.

The whole system was designed to dehumanise and destroy the psyche of the black South African, crush his spirit, wound his soul, rob him of his manhood, turn him into what in modern parlance is described as the proverbial “cuck” and strip him of all hope.

I am constrained to set my prejudices aside and reluctantly admit that no one put it better than the self-exiled Nigerian opposition figure, dissident and author by the name of David Hundeyin, who wrote the following on his X handle: “the apartheid system created laws restricting black people to ‘Bantu education’ with movement restrictions and racial hub quotas, forbidding them from getting middle or high income jobs, creating unbreakable multi- generational poverty for 89% of the country’s population.”

He forgot to add the fact that black people were not allowed to live in the cities but only to go and work there, after which they were compelled to return to their filthy, run-down ghettoes and townships at the close of work.

Many forget that black South Africans only won their freedom and independence 32 years ago and up until today they are still suffering from total and complete economic bondage, because the wealth of the nation is still concentrated and trapped in the hands of a tiny white minority… This is what has led to so much frustration, resentment, anger and bitterness amongst black South Africans, and sadly instead of resolving the issue by insisting on a more equitable degree of wealth sharing, they are targeting foreign black African nationals and venting their spleen on them.

Worse still, they were required to use passes as they moved around, rather like the Palestinians who enter Israel to look for work are required to do today.

This understandably resulted in protests, which led to the massacre of 69 black South Africans and 180 injured by South African security forces in a town called Sharpeville on 21st March 1960.

Blacks who did not live in the townships and serve as a cheap labour force for the cities were forced to move and exiled to their distant ‘homelands’ in the countryside, which were little better than empty and barren reservations.

One needs to stop and actually ponder on this to fully appreciate it’s implications. There was no freedom of movement or freedom of choice in the matter.

As a black South African, you were basically a slave who lived to serve the interests of the Boers and Afrikaners or you were confined and restricted to a homeland which was not only hopeless and empty but also in the middle of nowhere.

They called all this “separate development” which, when translated to Afrikaans, is “Apartheid”.

It was so bad that at some point there was an attempt by the Apartheid state to make ALL black South African children be taught in only Afrikaans, the language of the white Boers, in school.

This was the greatest humiliation and cultural imposition of all.

When you take away a man’s language and compel his children to learn and speak in only yours, you have taken away his heritage, history, essence and soul, and left him with nothing.

And that was precisely the purpose of the exercise.

It also represented the most compelling evidence of total subjugation and conquest, because it sought to strip the African bare and deny him of the memory of who he was, what language he once spoke, and where he was coming from.

Simply put, it was evil.

Understandably, this resulted in protests by the children themselves and that is what led to the massacres of no less than 700 to 1000 CHILDREN by the South African police and security forces in Soweto on 17th June 1976.

Yet it got worse.

The South African Roman Dutch Church officially regarded and described black people as being the Biblical “drawers of the water and hewers of the wood” that chapter 9 verse 21 of the Book of Joshua in the Holy Bible referred to and were therefore nothing but “accursed slaves.”

As far as the South African Roman Dutch Church was concerned, black Africans, including the Bantus of South Africa, were the descendants of Ham who had been cursed by God thousands of years ago!

It is with this gross and perverse manipulation and misinterpretation of scripture that the South African Roman Dutch Church (which was the official church of the state in Apartheid South Africa) sought to justify and rationalise the support it willingly gave to the evil of Apartheid and white minority rule.

Outside of that, sex or marriage across racial lines was a criminal offence and those who violated this were sent to jail, whilst their offspring were treated with nothing but contempt and regarded as nothing but products of “a corrupt, ungodly and illegal sexual union” and “evidence of a break-down in law and order and societal values!”

Forgive me, but is this not utter madness? Is it not unadulterated wickedness? Is it not callous? Is it not inexplicable? Is it not unbelievable?

Can Apartheid not be legitimately regarded as being spawned from the pit of hell?

Is it not a marvel that some white South Africans still yearn for those days and that a man like Errol Musk, Elon Musk’s father, can say “black people in South Africa were better off during Apartheid than they are today”!

That is the level of hatred and oppression that the Bantus were subjected to and Musk’s comments represents the level of delusion that their Afrikaner masters once suffered from and, in the case of a few of them, are still suffering from today.

How can any race be invaded, overwhelmed, stripped of all they had, including their dignity, history, language and identity, and be subjugated to this extent and come out of it unaffected and whole?

How can they be treated like that for hundreds of years by a group of callous and cruel European settlers and conquerors that literally came over and forcefully imposed their will on them and stole their land with the arrival of Jan van Riebeeck in Table Bay (Cape Town) in 1652, and not be badly traumatised till today.

Many forget that black South Africans only won their freedom and independence 32 years ago and up until today they are still suffering from total and complete economic bondage, because the wealth of the nation is still concentrated and trapped in the hands of a tiny white minority.

This is what has led to so much frustration, resentment, anger and bitterness amongst black South Africans, and sadly instead of resolving the issue by insisting on a more equitable degree of wealth sharing, they are targeting foreign black African nationals and venting their spleen on them.

The situation is so bad that its enemies and detractors have erroneously, unfairly and cruelly described South Africa as “a nation with a black body and a white head,” which I believe is not only completely false but also inappropriate and deeply insulting.

All this and you do not expect the majority of the black population in South Africa to suffer from a debilitating level of deep-set anger and trauma?

…I sincerely hope and pray that President Cyril Ramaphosa and the entire leadership of the government and ruling class in South Africa retrace their steps, do the needful, put an end to the Xenophobia and Afrophobia that is endemic in their country and accept his wise counsel before it is too late.

Frankly I am surprised that it is not even worse.

The South African people, as hostile, violent, aggressive and annoying as some of them may be, are our African brothers and sisters, and given all they have been through they do not deserve our anger and hate but rather our compassion, sympathy, love, care, support, concern and pity.

Regardless of all, we must offer them all these things, re-build the bridge and work closely with them for the sake of our collective future.

As Reverend Martin Luther King said,

“You cannot drive out hate with hate. You can only drive out hate with love.”

Permit me to conclude this six-part series with the following.

There is an entire generation of Nigerian leaders and members of the ruling class to which I belong that dedicated their youth to resisting Apartheid and white minority rule when we were in various universities in the United Kingdom, Europe and indeed all over the world.

As students, we marched in the streets, attended rallies, joined hands with members of the Anti-Nazi League, clashed violently with members of the pro-Nazi National Front, picketed sports stadiums where South African rugby teams were playing and fought hand-to-hand combat with the pro-Apartheid gangs in the campuses, schools and streets.

We debated our enemies, wrote articles, attended rallies, delivered inspiring and passionate speeches, defied the police, broke all boundaries and, with our tightly clenched fists lifted up high, sang legendary and famous revolution songs like Gil Scott-Heron’s “Johannesburg” as we were arrested, carried away and locked up for standing up against the tyranny that our African brothers were being subjected to in far away South Africa.

The distance was no barrier and we felt the pain of our brothers as if it were ours.

That was the sacrifice we made and the price we paid.

I am talking about men like my two childhood friends and brothers, Ambassador Yusuf Tuggar and Chief Jeffrey Onyeama, both of whom were appointed Foreign Ministers of Nigeria many years later.

There were of course many others like my dear sister Senator Gbemi Saraki (who was elected to the Nigerian Senate many years later and went on to be appointed as minister of Solid Minerals); my dear sister, Honourable Temi Harriman (who was elected to the Federal House of Representatives many years later); my brother Mallam Abba Kyari (who was appointed as Chief of Staff to President Muhammadu Buhari many years later); and others who are too numerous to mention.

We paid our dues and fought a good fight.

Our dream and collective objective was the establishment of a South Africa that was free, that was rid of apartheid, that enjoyed black majority rule and that was a brother to our nation, Nigeria, and indeed to the rest of Africa.

It was a deeply emotional issue for us as it was for the black South Africans themselves and the fact of the matter is that despite the fact that they bore the brunt of the pain and trauma of the subjugation and oppression that they were subjected to, they were never alone.

We stood with them every inch of the way!

We spoke for them, fought for them and prayed for them and today we have no regrets for doing what we did.

As a matter of fact, I am sure that I speak for us all when I say, despite all we see in South Africa today, if we had to do it all over again, we would do so gladly.

Our love, like all true love, is not conditional: it is what they call ‘agape love’: a Christ-like love that stands and endures despite all the faults, weaknesses and challenges of the individual or group of individuals that it is offered to.

The South Africans are not our friends, they are our brothers.

That is why we must never allow our bridge of love and brotherhood to be burnt or our sacred and historical bond to be broken.

I close this massive six-part about 15,000 word contribution with the words of President Olusegun Obasanjo, a man who I love and revere, whose government I had the privilege and honour of serving as minister of Culture and Tourism and later minister of Aviation many years ago, and one of the few elder statesman and fathers of the African continent, who was not only there from the start but who also played perhaps the most significant role of all in the fight to liberate South Africa and Zimbabwe from the oppression and evil of Apartheid and white minority rule.

A few years ago, when President Jacob Zuma was still in office in that country, alarmed and outraged by the issue of Xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa, Obasanjo said the following:

“If I were President Zuma I would put a stop to the Xenophobia with a firm hand and make an example of those behind it. If South Africa cannot accommodate other African nationals on their soil then they no longer deserve to be regarded as being a leader in Africa.”

These are firm, clear, insightful and instructive words spoken by a leader and elder who has spent the last 60 years of his life fighting for the Rainbow nation and championing not just their cause but the cause of the African continent.

When elders like Baba speak, it is important that we listen and I sincerely hope and pray that President Cyril Ramaphosa and the entire leadership of the government and ruling class in South Africa retrace their steps, do the needful, put an end to the Xenophobia and Afrophobia that is endemic in their country and accept his wise counsel before it is too late.

May God lead and guide us all, may He grant us wisdom, patience and understanding and may an unbreakable bridge of mutual respect, love and understanding be rebuilt between the Republic of South Africa and the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

Femi Fani-Kayode is a former Minister of Culture and Tourism, a former Minister of Aviation and the Ambassador-Designate of Nigeria to South Africa.

World.title: Document reveals EFCC secured court order to freeze two more Osun govt accounts
World.content:
Fuller details about the recent account freeze launched against the Osun State Government by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) have emerged, bringing to light a wider extent of an action that has already dealt a severe blow to the agency’s reputation.

Sahara Reporters has freshly reported that the EFCC targeted not just one of the state government’s accounts as previously known, but three.

These include one federal allocation account with First Bank, which was previously known to be the only state government account the EFCC had frozen. The other two, just revealed, are joint allocation accounts with Zenith Bank.

Sahara Reporters reported that the commission indeed obtained a court order to implement the account freeze as disclosed for the first time on Thursday by President Bola Tinubu.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The freeze order has drawn widespread condemnation to the EFCC and its chairman, Ola Olukoyede, as a politically motivated step.

The action came just over a week before the 15 August governorship election in Osun State, where incumbent Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party is running against Bola Oyebamiji belonging to the president’s party, the All Progressives Congress (APC).

It fed into a broader perception that federal agencies, including the Nigerian police, have been bias and selective in its enforcement actions against the Accord Party and Governor Adeleke’s second term bid in the forthcoming election.

Expressing deep embarrassment about the development on Thursday, Mr Tinubu ordered the EFCC in a statement he signed personally to immediately take steps to vacate the court order freezing the state government’s account.

Documents newly obtained by Sahara Reporters showed that the EFCC obtained a freeze order against three accounts of the state government from the Federal High Court in Abuja on 5 August (Wednesday) through an ex parte application instituted under suit number FHC/ABJ/CS/1750/2026.

The application being ex parte meant that the adverse party that would be affected by the order sought was not meant to participate in its hearing.

According to Sahara Reporters, EFCC’s lawyer, M. A. Babatunde, moved the motion ex parte, informing the court that the affected accounts were “currently being investigated in a case of Diversion of public funds and Money Laundering pending conclusion of investigation and prosecution.”

The ex parte application was supported by an affidavit sworn by EFC’s investigator Ikenna Chukwueze and an exhibit marked “EFCC 1.”

The three frozen accounts

After listening to the lawyer, Justice Mohammed Umar went on to issue the ex parte order authorising the EFCC chairman, Ola Olukoyede, “or any officer authorised by him,” to direct the managing directors of the affected banks to freeze accounts listed in the schedule to the application.

The schedule listed three accounts of the Osun State Government affected by the court order. They are:

Osun State Government Federal Allocation Account, domiciled with First Bank Plc, Account No. 2017170947;

Osun State Joint Allocation Account, domiciled with Zenith Bank Plc, Account No. 1013374191; and

Osun State Joint Allocation Account, domiciled with Zenith Bank Plc, Account No. 1014374909.

Justice Umar ordered that the freeze on the accounts should be in place till the conclusion of EFCC’s investigations.

Until Sahara Reporters’ reporting, only the First Bank account was known to be affected by the freeze order.

It is not clear yet why the anti-corruption agency has concealed the full information from the public in its communications on the matter since Wednesday when the EFCC wrote to First Bank to impose a Post-No-Debit (PND) restriction on an account operated by the Osun State Government.

The letter dated 5 July (Wednesday) did not cite any court order and only referenced just one account of the state government.

A statement from the EFCC that same day gave the impression that only one account was targeted and confirmed the restriction on the account through a PND directive to the bank.

Also, EFCC’s Director of Public Affairs, Wilson Uwujaren, appeared on Arise Television earlier on Thursday to justify the freeze of the state government’s account without a court order. However, Mr Uwujaren disclosed during the interview that the commission would follow up with a court order within 72 hours of the PND restriction, citing the EFCC’s establishment law.

The first indication of a court’s involvement in the account freeze came on Thursday from President Tinubu’s statement directing the EFCC to immediately take steps to vacate the freeze order.

Mr Tinubu, echoing public outrage about the EFCC’s action coming about 10 days before the 15 August Osun State governorship election, said he was deeply embarrassed by the freeze order.

It is not clear yet if the EFCC has applied to the court to lift the freeze orders.

‘Embarrassment’ to the president

PREMIUM TIMES reported on Wednesday that the EFCC froze an account of the Osun State Government domiciled with First Bank, after which the anti-graft agency said the action followed suspicious movement of public funds from the account amid an ongoing investigation into alleged financial misconduct involving about 11N billion in Ecology Funds, Intervention Funds and Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) allocations.

On Thursday, Mr Tinubu directed the EFCC to lift the restriction on the account, describing the timing of the action, coming about 10 days before the governorship election, as inauspicious and capable of creating the impression that a federal agency was being used to interfere with the poll.

The president said he found the EFCC’s action deeply embarrassing.

“I must state that I feel deeply embarrassed not by the EFCC’s exercise of its mandate backed by a court order, but by the timing of the agency’s action,” Mr Tinubu wrote.

“This is so because every action taken by an institution of State, especially at the Federal level, is always credited to me, as the President, even when I may not have had any prior knowledge of the action.”

He said while he intentionally refrained from directing or interfering in the operational activities of the EFCC or any other investigative or prosecutorial agency, he felt compelled to intervene in the Osun State matter.

“Osun State is only a few days away from its gubernatorial election. Therefore, nothing ought to be done to give an impression that the EFCC or indeed any other agency of the federal government is being used to interfere with the election.

“Based on the foregoing premise, I am duty-bound to issue a directive on this issue in consonance with the overriding public interest in preserving public confidence and the integrity, credibility, and fairness of our democratic process,” Mr Tinubu stated.

“Accordingly, I have directed the EFCC to immediately proceed to the court to vacate the order and discontinue whatever action it has instituted against the Osun State Government in this regard.”

The directive marks a dramatic intervention by the president in a controversy that has dominated political discourse in Osun State over the past 24 hours, after the anti-graft agency froze one of the state’s accounts over an ongoing investigation into the alleged diversion of about N11 billion in public funds.

Presidential spokesman, Mr Onanuga subsequently announced on Thursday that Mr Tinubu spoke with Mr Adeleke in a phone conversation, informing the governor that he had directed to lift the order restricting the account of the Osun State Government.

World.title: Snakebite deaths: FG gives Benue 100 vials of anti-snake venom
World.content:
By Peter Duru, Makurdi

The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare has donated 100 vials of Panaf Premium Anti-Snake Venom, ASV, valued at over N25 million, to the Benue State Government to support the treatment of snakebite victims and check recent deaths recorded across the state.

The intervention is aimed at reducing illness and deaths associated with snakebites, while easing the financial burden on victims and their families due to the high cost of anti-snake venom.

The consignment was formally presented on Friday at the headquarters of the Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services in Makurdi.

Presenting the items, the Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr Paul Ogwuche, said the donation demonstrated the proactive leadership of Governor Hyacinth Alia and the ministry’s commitment to using strategic partnerships to address critical health challenges.

Ogwuche commended Governor Alia for his sustained commitment to improving healthcare delivery and protecting the lives and wellbeing of residents, while also appreciating the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Aliu Pate, and the Federal Ministry for responding positively to the state’s request for assistance.

According to him, the Federal Government’s intervention would complement the efforts of the Alia administration to make essential healthcare services more accessible, particularly to vulnerable residents.

He said the availability of the anti-snake venom would “reduce the financial burden on affected families and improve access to prompt treatment for victims of snakebite.”

The commissioner assured that the Ministry would ensure proper documentation, storage, distribution and rational utilisation of the consignment to guarantee that the lifesaving medicine reaches patients who genuinely require it.

Receiving the donation on behalf of the ministry, the Permanent Secretary, Dr Cephas Hough, expressed appreciation to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare for the timely intervention.

Hough said the donation would strengthen Benue’s capacity to respond to snakebite cases while easing the treatment burden on affected residents.

He particularly commended Ogwuche for his proactive engagement with the Federal Ministry, which facilitated the attraction of the donation to the state, adding that the intervention underscored the importance of sustained collaboration between the Federal and State Governments in tackling critical public health challenges.

The consignment was subsequently handed over to the Director of Pharmaceutical Services, Regina Agir, for documentation, storage and warehousing in line with established pharmaceutical management procedures.

The ceremony was attended by the Permanent Secretary, Directors and other senior officials of the Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services.

World.title: Osun 2026: Strengths and weaknesses of Adeleke, Oyebamiji, Salaam as voters head to polls
World.content:
By Shina Abubakar, OSOGBO

As the Osun State electorate prepares to vote for a governor on August 15, several factors—chief among them the personalities and track records of the candidates — will play a decisive role in shaping voter choices.

Read Also: ‘I’m embarrassed by timing of EFCC action on Osun govt account – Tinubu

Although Ademola Adeleke is the incumbent, his two main challengers are far from newcomers in Osun politics. Both possess extensive political histories that cannot be easily overlooked.

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate, Najeem Salaam, served as Speaker of the State House of Assembly for eight years during the administration of former Governor Rauf Aregbesola. Meanwhile, Asiwaju Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji (popularly known as AMBO), standard-bearer for the All Progressives Congress (APC), served as the Managing Director of Osun State Investment Company Limited (OSICOL) before holding office as Commissioner for Finance under both Governors Rauf Aregbesola and Gboyega Oyetola.

Governor Ademola Adeleke (Accord)

Strengths

Before his election as governor, Adeleke served in the Senate but lacked executive public office experience, leading critics to question his administrative capacity. However, the governor has sought to silence doubters by highlighting key infrastructure milestones, including the reported construction of over 300 kilometers of roads during his first three years in office. He has also actively countered accusations of favoring his hometown of Ede over other zones across the state.

A cornerstone of Adeleke’s appeal is his strong relationship with the state workforce. His administration prioritised civil servant welfare through prompt salary payments and the liquidation of salary arrears inherited from the Aregbesola era.

Beyond policy, Adeleke benefits from considerable “street credibility” stemming from his background as an entertainer. His charismatic persona and famous public dancing continue to endear him to voters, particularly Gen Z. Additionally, the explicit endorsement of his nephew—Afrobeats superstar David Adeleke (Davido)—gives him added popularity among young electors.

Weaknesses

Despite Adeleke’s personal popularity, internal friction within his former party, the People’s Democratic Party (PDP), forced his departure to the Accord party. Moving away from an established party platform presents a structural challenge.

Furthermore, several high-profile allies—including federal lawmakers elected alongside him on the PDP ticket—did not follow him to Accord. Key political heavyweights such as former Governor Olagunsoye Oyinlola and former Secretary to the State Government (SSG) Fatai Akinbade remained in the PDP or aligned elsewhere, leaving Adeleke’s new platform without the full breadth of the old coalition.

Asiwaju Bola Oyebamiji / AMBO (APC)

Strengths

The APC candidate’s primary strength lies in his calm demeanor and disciplined professional reputation. While Oyebamiji lacked a standalone personal political machinery prior to declaring his candidacy, he now enjoys the backing of the consolidated APC structure across Osun State.

Oyebamiji also benefits from the explicit backing of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, as well as alignment from major political gladiators in the Osun East Senatorial District who have mobilized behind the “AMBO project.” The APC’s deep organizational presence across all 3,671 polling units in the state gives Oyebamiji a formidable ground game capable of matching the incumbent’s grassroots appeal.

Because Adeleke, Oyebamiji, and Salaam all hail from the Osun West Senatorial District, the zone is poised to become a tightly contested battleground.

Weaknesses

Oyebamiji’s main vulnerability stems from his tenure as Commissioner for Finance during Governor Aregbesola’s second term, when the controversial “modulated” (half) salary structure was introduced for civil servants.

Although Oyebamiji has addressed the issue publicly on multiple occasions—explaining that the policy was a negotiated response to financial constraints agreed upon with labor leaders rather than an arbitrary imposition—it remains a sensitive topic among public sector workers.

Right Honorable Najeem Salaam (ADC)

Strengths

During his eight-year tenure as Speaker of the Osun State House of Assembly, Salaam maintained legislative stability without major internal crises. He is widely respected across party lines as a consensus builder and a political gentleman.

Salam’s approachable nature and clean legislative record resonate with moderate voters who are seeking an alternative to the two dominant parties.

Weaknesses

Salaam’s chief hurdle is the limited organizational spread of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Osun State. Lacking the widespread footprint of the APC or Accord, the ADC is not viewed by the leading campaigns as an immediate threat to win outright.

However, given his personal standing in Osun West, Salaam could serve as a key spoiler—and whichever major candidate he aligns with in the final stretch could gain a crucial edge in the race for Government House.

World.title: Senegal intensifies crackdown on homosexuality, charges 71
World.content:
Senegal has charged 71 men with “unnatural acts” as it intensifies a crackdown on homosexuality, the public prosecutor’s office said late Friday.

The men were brought before a court while 28 other defendants have had charges against them dropped entirely, according to a statement.

In March, Senegal passed a new law doubling the penalties for homosexual relations, which are now punishable by five to ten years in jail.

Recent months have seen more than 100 people, including some local celebrities, arrested on suspicion of homosexual acts and in some cases of deliberately transmitting HIV.

The charges were issued following a preliminary investigation, the statement said, adding that charges of “endangering the lives of others” and “wilful transmission of HIV/AIDS” were dismissed.

Prosecutor Saliou Dicko told AFP on Saturday that a French national, an engineer in his thirties living in Dakar and detained since February for “unnatural acts”, had had the charges against him dropped.

The public prosecutor’s office has appealed the decision.

Recent months have seen several West African countries enact laws criminalising homosexuality.

AFP

World.title: Navy recovers 24,000 litres of stolen crude oil in Rivers
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The Nigerian Navy, in a sustained offensive against crude oil theft and illegal bunkering under Operation Delta Sentinel, has recovered approximately 24,000 litres of product suspected to be stolen crude oil in Bonny Local Government Area of Rivers State.

According to the Navy, “The operation was conducted by personnel of Forward Operating Base (FOB) Bonny following credible intelligence on suspected attempts by criminal elements to establish illegal connections to oil infrastructure within the Bethel Community axis.

“The operation led to the discovery of an illegal refining site, 2 pits containing approximately 24,000 litres of product suspected to be stolen crude oil, as well as extensive hoses believed to have been installed in furtherance of crude oil theft activities.

“The illegal facilities and associated materials were subsequently handled in accordance with extant regulations.

“The successful operation disrupted an emerging crude oil theft network before it could become fully operational, further denying economic saboteurs the infrastructure required to sustain illicit activities and inflict economic losses on the nation.”

Similarly, the Navy under Operation Delta Sentinel successfully intercepted approximately 17,000 litres of product suspected to be illegally refined Automotive Gas Oil (AGO) in Rivers State.

Navy Captain Abiodun Folorunsho, Director of Information, said, “The interception was made by personnel of Nigerian Navy Ship (NNS) Pathfinder during ongoing anti-crude oil theft operations within its Area of Operation.

“The operation led to the interception of a speedboat conveying the suspected illegally refined petroleum product along the Onne/Okrika waterways.

“The recovered speedboat and the suspected illegally refined AGO were handled in accordance with extant anti-crude oil theft procedures, while efforts are ongoing to identify and apprehend those connected with the illegal activity.

“The latest operational success further demonstrates the Nigerian Navy’s sustained commitment to disrupting the illicit petroleum supply chain, denying economic saboteurs freedom of action and protecting Nigeria’s critical oil and gas infrastructure from criminal exploitation.

“The Nigerian Navy remains resolute in sustaining intelligence-driven operations under Operation Delta Sentinel to combat crude oil theft, illegal oil bunkering and other forms of economic sabotage, while safeguarding Nigeria’s maritime environment and supporting national economic security.”

World.title: An appeal to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and all Nigerians: Stop the NFF elections, please! By Segun Odegbami
World.content:
Odegbami

On March 22, 1998, I was officially decorated with the honour and title of ‘Sports Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Nigeria’ in Abuja by the then Minister of Sports. It was in addition to a previous national honour of ‘Member of the Order of the Niger’, MON.

I take both honours very seriously. They are earned, the rewards for national duty through hard work, dedication, sacrifices, patriotism, discipline, and trophies.

They also come, of course, with additional demands and even more responsibility.

That’s why I try, always, to appreciate the country’s generosity by attempting to live a simple, decent life of exemplary good conduct to serve as a model for generations coming after me through the window of sports. How far I have fared with these unwritten expectations and standards I leave for Nigerians and posterity to judge.

Today, football in Nigeria is at a crossroads. The time comes to test my judgement and character, a burden that I must carry even in the evening of my life.

I find that there is really nothing for me to lose in standing by what I believe are the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth! To be silent now means to fail the government, the people and the game of football itself. So, I am raising my voice again.
