Nigerians know me for my activities and contributions in sports and in football, in particular – playing the game, administering it, organising it, promoting it, deploying it as a tool to drive education, empowerment, health, patriotism, eradication of illiteracy, diplomacy and national orientation.

It all started in 1973. As an undergraduate student I was invited to the national football team of Nigeria, the Green Eagles, from the National Sports Festival, to start a relationship that has remained unbroken to this day.

In the 53 years since then, I played for the country; rose to be Captain of the national team and also of the national contingent to the Olympic Games; administered the game as a member of the board of the Nigerian Football Association and as Chairman of the Governing Council of the National Institute of Sports; single-handedly managed two Nigerian athletes (in a sport outside of football) to win Gold and Silver medals at the Olympic Games; served in several panels, commissions and committees promoting sports and seeking solutions to challenges in Nigerian sports; established an NGO/institution that has been promoting the combination of sports and scholarship; facilitating the migration of Nigerian student/athletes to Colleges and Universities in the USA and in India; and currently serving as head of a new and special unit developing a template and policies for sports diplomacy within Nigeria’s foreign affairs.

The measure of my work in all these national assignments are an open book for all Nigerians to see and determine.

All those experiences count in the position I have now chosen to take in the unfortunate present situation the country finds itself. With all the talented footballers that the country parades all over the world, it is a sad commentary that at international level, achievements have reached a plateau, and even started to decline. This is easily measured in the successes, or lack of them, that the country’s football has achieved in recent times. Some of the results are totally unacceptable, needless to mention them here.

The reality is that football administration in the past two decades, in particular, has not matched or complimented the level of talent and possible achievements.

The growth of our football industry has been stunted by faulty decisions taken more in ignorance than by any malicious intentions since the early part of the 1990s. These have grown, sustained and become the norm in our football, a monster that now needs the creators of it to rid it of its venom. They won’t do it because they are also the beneficiaries of the faulty architecture!

Next month, an election into the board of the Nigerian Football Association will take place. I am deliberately using the word ‘association’ because that is the starting point of all the anomalies in the present administrative architecture. This takes careful understanding that I cannot explain here , but that will make sense when the matter is tabled before a civil court for interrogation, and where a subsisting judgment to amend it has been treated with levity for almost 8 years. In law, the Nigerian Football Federation does not even exist!

As for the elections the way things are now, they have been held and sewn up already, the results determined even before a vote has been cast. The persons that can contest and will, know themselves already. Those to be deprived of the opportunity to even contest have been isolated and sent on a wild goose chase, to go around Nigeria furtively searching for endorsements they will not get in a rushed and harried election. The winners of elections have already been determined by the same group of people in office now.

The elections will also be conducted away from any prying eyes to avoid any chances of transparency, and where bribery and corrupt practices can be conducted without consequence, far from the headquarters of the federation and the supervising National Sports Commission that would have ensured neutrality.

The issues are long and endless that need the supervising ministry’s intervention. The NSC cannot do anything with their hands tied by ‘fictitious’ threats by ‘FIFA’ that have no substance in any statutes anywhere in the world.

In short, history, documents, facts and figures are essential ingredients that will illuminate the clouded areas of our football structures in order for the ship of our football to be steadied for future development.

My experiences cannot be bought in the market place or discountenanced. My current works speak for themselves. My suggestions for the future should at least be given some attention.

Therefore, I am writing this publicly with some concern but a deep sense of responsibility and sincerity. Elections into the board of the NFF have become a four-yearly ritual of crisis. The process used in conducting them have always been contentious, and were always challenged as a result of perceived irregularities and manipulation.

All of these to the detriment of the country that loves its football with passion but can only look on helplessly as football continues to suffer and fails to achieve its full potentials, fails to boost the country’s economy, and fails to empower the country’s gifted youths with the best opportunities that are available all over the world.

In the next few days, I shall be taking documents that are currently used in the administration of Nigerian football to the Nigerian civil courts for interrogation and interpretation, to explain to Nigerians documented facts about the real power and roles of FIFA in our country’s internal football affairs; the status, interpretation, role and place of State Football Associations; the equity in unequal and lopsided representation by members; the place and role of government as the biggest funder of football in the country; the justification for the convoluted, politicized, expensive conduct of ordinary football elections in Nigeria, and so on!

The next few weeks will be very interesting.

I hope all Nigerians, including the members of the Nigerian Football Association will understand why these elections should be temporarily halted for Nigerian football to find its feet again!

Olusegun Odegbami, MON, OLY, MON, AFNIIA, FNIS

Sports Ambassador, Federal Republic of Nigeria; Grand Sports Ambassador of Ogun State.

World.title: Out from prison, Nigeria’s Daga bounces back
World.content:
Daga

.Scores 2 goals in 2 games after acquittal for rape

By Douglas Baye-Osagie

Three years ago, Daniel Daga was Nigeria’s next big thing. A defensive midfielder in the Sunday Oliseh mould — strong, intelligent, with delicate long-range passing and an eye for goal. At 17 he was an Enyimba Football Club mainstay, playing for Nigeria’s most successful club. He then played for the Flying Eagles at back-to-back U20 FIFA World Cups in 2023 and 2025. At 18 he made the move every Nigerian boy dreams of — Europe — signing for Norway’s Molde FK. Where talent becomes stardom. Or dies trying.

Suddenly, a few months after arriving in Europe, news of a rape allegation hit the internet. “This can’t be true,” some of us screamed.

In December 2025, Molde removed him from training and matchday activities after he was formally charged over an alleged sexual offence involving an unnamed woman. The case reportedly dated back to April 2025. It echoed what happened to another young Nigerian, Akinkunmi Amoo, who was accused and later convicted of rape in Denmark while playing for FC Copenhagen. Everyone following Daga’s career prayed for justice — we did not want to see a bright future derailed.

In March 2026, a Norwegian district court convicted Daga and sentenced him to six months in prison for a sexual act without consent. Daga maintained his innocence, with his lawyer arguing the encounter was consensual, and an appeal was filed. Molde kept him out of the squad while the legal process continued.

The case took a decisive turn in July. Norway’s Frostating Court of Appeal unanimously acquitted Daga, overturning the earlier conviction. Molde subsequently confirmed that the midfielder was again available for selection. From suspension to a fresh start.

Daga’s return has been emphatic. He marked his comeback against KFUM with an emotional goal, then scored again against Sarpsborg — a powerful reminder of his ability after an extremely challenging period. The focus is now back where he wants it: on the pitch.

When news first filtered out of Norway, the reaction back home was instant and brutal. Social media buried him. Pundits wrote him off. For a boy who was the face of Enyimba at 16, it felt like the dream was over before it truly began.

Daga was not just another export. He was the NPFL’s proof that local football could still produce world-class midfielders. Composed, strong, and tactically smart beyond his years, he captained the Flying Eagles and bossed games for Enyimba as a teenager. Europe came calling because he looked ready.

Then came the case. The details were messy, the headlines were louder, and the process was slow. Whether guilty or not, the stain stuck. Contracts were paused. Confidence dipped. For months, the player who once played like he had nothing to lose looked like a boy who had everything to lose.

But here is the truth we rarely say in football: a man does not fall forever. Sometimes the fall is what teaches you how to stand properly. Daga is out of that process now and learning to pick his steps again. That is why people are talking about a “second coming.” His return to the pitch is the best thing that happened to Nigerian football in the month of July.

To understand why this matters and gives me so much joy you have to look back. Nigerian football has seen this movie before. Talent derailed not by injury, but by off-field trouble. The first name that comes to mind is Etim Esin.

Etim “Maradona” Esin was arguably the most gifted Nigerian midfielder of the late 80s and 90s. At 18 he was in the Flying Eagles, Olympic team and Super Eagles. He was the darling of the local league before he was scouted to Belgium, with technique that made defenders look foolish. Everyone said he would be our greatest ever.

Before we could blink, he was arrested and charged in connection with a rape case involving a minor. He spent time in detention before being released. Legally, the case ended. Professionally, it never did. While he was away trying to sort himself out, Friday Ekpo and then Jay Okocha emerged.

From national team regular to forgotten man in less than two years. By the time Okocha made his Super Eagles home debut against Algeria in 1993, the fans had forgotten about Etim Esin completely. Esin later spoke about depression, financial ruin, and how one incident cut a career that should have lasted 20 years down to less than 10. He remains a cautionary tale in every Nigerian dressing room.

Rape accusations can be career-threatening and make life unbearable for a footballer. Remember the recent cases of Benjamin Mendy, the French World Cup winner, and Thomas Partey of Ghana. In July 2025, the Arsenal and Black Stars midfielder was charged with multiple counts of rape relating to alleged incidents between 2021 and 2022. He pleaded not guilty.

The impact was immediate. Arsenal let his contract run down. Sponsors went quiet. Ghana fans were split. He was even denied entry to Canada during the World Cup and missed Ghana’s first game in Toronto. Whether he is eventually cleared or convicted, Partey has already lost momentum at 32 — an age where every season counts for a midfielder.

That is the cruel part. It is not easy to maintain focus when rape charges land. The mind is not on the ball. It’s on survival, rebuilding lost relationships, and trying to hold your concentration together.

That is why the return to the pitch of Daniel Daga case feels so important. He is 20. He is not at the end. He is at the beginning. We are all happy he has been set free because his talent is what we need going forward for the Olympics team in 2028 and possibly the World Cup in 2030. If he gets this right, the Norway episode becomes a footnote. If he gets it wrong, it becomes his entire Wikipedia page.

The problem is cultural too. Young African players go to Europe with talent but without structure. No media training. No understanding that in Europe, your name is your brand, and one mistake travels around the world in 10 minutes.

For Daga, the path back is simple but hard. Good he has played 3 league games and scored in two since his return back to the pitch in July. The same work rate that made him stand out in Aba is going to help him succeed .The same humility that let a teenager lead senior men at Enyimba. Talent got him to Europe. Character will keep him there. Mendy is trying to rebuild. Partey is fighting his case. Esin never fully recovered. Daga still has time and with focus he will get to the very top.

From Cristiano Ronaldo to Celestine Babayaro to Quinton Fortune to Rio Ferdinand — superstars who faced rape allegations and fought to rebuild their careers.

So here is to the second coming of Daniel Daga. May he remember that a fall is not a finish line. And may Daga prove that a Nigerian boy can stumble in Europe, stand up, and still become the midfielder we all saw coming. The pitch is waiting.

World.title: Imo monarch’s murder: 5 suspects arrested, gang kingpin killed in shootout
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The Force headquarters disclosed on Saturday that Police operatives have recorded a breakthrough in the ongoing investigation into the murder of HRH Eze Paulinus Ekwueme, Ochia I of Ochia Kingdom, and five others in Ohaji/Egbema, Imo State.

Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Aniete Iniedu, made the disclosure, noting that two other suspects were killed during exchange of fire between the gang and policemen.

He said, “Following actionable intelligence, operatives of the Special Tactics Squad, Force Intelligence Department (STS-FID), conducted a series of operations between 2nd and 6th August, 2026, targeting members of the criminal syndicate allegedly linked to the incident.

“The operations culminated in the early hours of 6th August, 2026, when operatives located the hideout of a suspected gang kingpin, identified as Ojiogu Elumah Martin, alias ‘Acid’, in Ohaji/Egbema.

“The suspect engaged the operatives in a gun duel and sustained injuries during the encounter, which subsequently led to his death. One AK-47 rifle, three magazines and 56 rounds of 7.62mm live ammunition were recovered from the scene.

“The suspect was identified as an alleged leader of the criminal syndicate linked to the attack of 10th April, 2026, in which the monarch and five others were killed along the Asa/Awara Road, Ohaji/Egbema, while returning to Owerri.

“Four suspects had earlier been arrested in connection with the incident, while two others reportedly died during previous encounters with the Police.

“Following the latest operation, efforts have been intensified to apprehend other fleeing members of the syndicate, establish the full extent of their involvement and recover further operational intelligence and exhibits.

“The Nigeria Police Force remains committed to ensuring that all persons found to be connected with the crime are brought to justice and that every effort is made to bring the investigation to a logical conclusion.”

World.title: History Made, Future Beckons: How Oloyede’s stewardship redefined JAMB, restored public trust
World.content:
JAMB Registrar Prof Ishaq Oloyede

By Ishola Balogun

After ten eventful years at the helm of the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board

(JAMB), Professor Is-haq Olanrewaju Oloyede on Friday formally handed over the

leadership of Nigeria’s foremost admissions agency to Professor Segun Aina, bringing to a close a tenure widely associated with sweeping institutional reforms, technological innovation, financial transparency and renewed public confidence in the nation’s tertiary admissions process.

Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker

Speaking at the handover ceremony held at JAMB’s National Headquarters in Bwari, Abuja, Prof. Oloyede described the occasion as both a moment of gratitude and reflection, declaring that whatever achievements were recorded during his stewardship were products of divine grace and collective effort rather than personal accomplishment.

“It is with a profound sense of gratitude to the Almighty Allah and immense appreciation to all people of goodwill that I address this distinguished audience today,” he said.

“I return all glory to Almighty Allah, whose boundless mercy, wisdom and grace sustained me throughout these remarkable ten years. Through periods of daunting challenges, difficult policy decisions and far-reaching institutional reforms, His guidance remained my greatest source of strength. Whatever accomplishments have been recorded during this period are not mine alone; they are manifestations of His infinite favour and blessings.”

The outgoing Registrar recalled that when he assumed office on August 9, 2016, he deliberately chose the theme, “Let’s Do It Together,” believing that no institution could succeed without collaboration.

“I had no illusion right from the outset that I would depend on God’s guidance and people’s support,” he said. “Doing it together means that many colours make a rainbow and many flowers make a garden.”

A decade built on five pillars

Reflecting on his stewardship, Prof. Oloyede said his administration was anchored on five cardinal principles—staff welfare, discipline, technology, transparency and networking—which became the foundation of JAMB’s transformation.

“When I took over the mandate of leadership at JAMB, I outlined five cardinal points that my administration would be anchored on… In these five, though perfection belongs to the Almighty Allah, I can confidently say we tried our best.”

Welfare before productivity

He explained that his administration invested heavily in staff welfare, arguing that no institution could outperform the people who run it.

Among the initiatives introduced were timely promotions, improved work environments, rehabilitation and construction of offices nationwide, over N8 billion contributed to staff retirement savings, retirement benefits ranging between N3 million and N10 million, the introduction of a 13th-month salary, examination duty allowances increased from 10 to 20 per cent, free daily meals, transport support for key operational staff and medical interventions, including N12 million approved for the treatment of a staff member at the National Hospital.

Exceptional staff were rewarded with cash prizes and awards, while one zonal office and a Professional Test Centre complex were named after a deserving employee.

“We stood by our decision because without dedicated and motivated staff, we won’t achieve the JAMB that Nigeria deserves,” he declared.

Beyond staff welfare, he said candidates also benefited from reforms, including a 30 per cent reduction in the UTME application cost and comprehensive support for candidates with special needs through sponsorship, accommodation, feeding and refund of application fees.

The Board also extended institutional support through the National Tertiary Admissions Performance Merit (NATAPM) Award, disbursing approximately ¦ 750 million annually to tertiary institutions.

Discipline without compromise

While investing in welfare, Oloyede maintained that discipline remained non-negotiable.

“It is said that the first law in heaven is discipline and indiscipline is the mother of all evils.”

According to him, more than ten staff members faced prosecution over allegations of misconduct during his tenure.

He recalled the widely publicised case involving the infamous claim that a snake swallowed ¦ 36 million, describing it as one of the disciplinary measures undertaken to restore accountability.

“The sensationalised case of a snake gulping N36 million that the media feasted on was just one of the measures taken to entrench discipline,” he said, recalling that even the EFCC had remarked at the time that “an eagle shows no mercy for money-swallowing snakes.”

He added that the insistence on discipline accounted for JAMB’s consistent remittance of billions of naira in operational surpluses to the Federal Government.

Technology as the engine of reform

Perhaps the defining feature of his administration, Oloyede noted, was JAMB’s aggressive deployment of technology.

He listed the expansion of Computer-Based Testing (CBT), development of the Central Admissions Processing System (CAPS), biometric identity verification, CCTV surveillance, digital PINs and payment platforms, Remote Authoring and Moderation System (RAMS), digital institutional reforms and the Bring-Your-Device initiative as milestones achieved during the decade.

“At the heart of our operational blueprint is technology and we owe many of our far-reaching reforms to innovative technologies,” he said.

Reflecting on recent technical challenges experienced during the UTME, Oloyede admitted that no technology is infallible.

“What happened last year which made me emotional was proof that technology has its limits, just like everything human, and eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.”

Transparency restores confidence

On transparency, the outgoing Registrar said his administration deliberately opened JAMB’s operations to public scrutiny.

“Our operational and financial transactions are in the open domain and our weekly newsletter always contains details of our activities and finances.”

He described CAPS as one of the Board’s most revolutionary innovations.

“With a system like CAPS, admissions into our institutions are transparent and anyone can question why a candidate is not admitted despite meriting it.”

According to him, the notorious culture of secret or “under-the-table” admissions has largely become a thing of the past.

“My belief is that transparency transforms institutions by eliminating toxic silos.”

Partnerships That Strengthened the Institution

Prof. Oloyede credited much of JAMB’s success to strategic partnerships with government agencies, tertiary institutions, security organisations, examination bodies, the media and over 1,010 private CBT centre owners.

“We could not have achieved anything without leveraging networks and partnerships.”

He acknowledged the cooperation of the National Security Adviser, the Director-General of the Department of State Services, the National Intelligence Agency, the Nigeria Police Force, NSCDC, EFCC, ICPC, NIMC, NCC, Vice Chancellors, Rectors, Provosts, civil society organisations and professional associations within and outside Nigeria.

He also highlighted the establishment of the Nigerian Educational Assessment Academy (NEAA), created alongside 18 national agencies to train educational assessment professionals.

“TEAM means Together Everyone Achieves More,” he said. “That became our mantra.”

Gratitude to leaders, stakeholders

Throughout his address, Oloyede repeatedly acknowledged those he said made JAMB’s transformation possible.

He expressed gratitude to former President Muhammadu Buhari for appointing him, former President Olusegun Obasanjo for earlier identifying his leadership potential, and President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for retaining confidence in him.

He also thanked Minister of Education Dr. Maruf Tunji Alausa, former Minister Prof. Tahir Mamman, Minister of State for Education Prof. Suwaiba Said Ahmad, Permanent Secretary Abel Enitan and former Permanent Secretary Sonny Echono.

Several governors also received special recognition for donating land, office complexes, vehicles and Professional Test Centres across the country.

Among those acknowledged were Prof. Babagana Zulum of Borno State, whose government built and donated the North-East Mega Professional Test Centre and named it after him; Nyesom Wike for providing office facilities and land in Rivers State within 24 hours of his request; Babatunde Raji Fashola for facilitating Certificates of Occupancy for JAMB properties; Ibikunle Amosun and Dapo Abiodun for supporting the South-West Mega Professional Test Centre project; Godwin Obaseki for relocating JAMB’s Edo office to a befitting site; Rochas Okorocha for land allocation in Imo State; Babajide Sanwo-Olu for allocating lands across Lagos State; AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq and Douye Diri for assisting JAMB’s facilities in Kwara and Bayelsa States.

He also appreciated private individuals including Ahmad Raji (SAN) for donating a fully equipped Professional Test Centre in Iseyin and Dr. Wale Babalakin for repeatedly making the Bola Babalakin Hall available free of charge for JAMB’s annual policy meetings.

The outgoing Registrar equally paid tribute to past Registrars, Governing Board members, directors, staff unions, retired employees, examination bodies, tertiary institutions, civil society groups, candidates, parents, security agencies, professional organisations and members of the media.

“I seldom say it in order to keep you on your toes,” he told JAMB staff. “But I now say it loud: thank you very much.”

A legacy beyond infrastructure

Oloyede noted that beyond physical infrastructure, JAMB under his watch earned national and international recognition for accountability, technological innovation and service delivery.

He disclosed that Prof. Emeritus Peter Okebukola had documented about 200 achievements recorded during the administration, while acknowledging the contributions of numerous academics and professionals who helped shape the Board’s reforms.

“The story of JAMB is that of continuous progress,” he said, insisting that his administration merely built upon foundations laid by previous Registrars.

Passing the baton

Turning to his successor, Prof. Segun Aina, Oloyede expressed confidence that the Board’s future remains secure.

“As I hand over the leadership of this great institution, I do so with absolute confidence in its future.”

He described Aina as a younger ICT expert capable of taking JAMB to greater heights.

“I wish my successor great success and his success is the success of all of us who have been privileged to steer JAMB since its inception.”

“My belief is that the advantage and vibrancy of his younger age and his ICT expertise would propel the Board to higher heights than previously attained.”

He pledged to remain available whenever his advice might be needed while urging Nigerians to support the new Registrar.

“There is no success without a successor. They should rather support and pray for Prof. Aina’s success. It is time to face the future with renewed vigour.”

A Personal Farewell

As he prepared to leave office, the former Registrar became reflective, thanking his wife, children, grandchildren and close friends for standing by him throughout what he described as a demanding national assignment.

“It is now over,” he said quietly.

He concluded by once again committing JAMB’s future to God.

“Finally, I thank Almighty Allah for the privilege of serving Nigeria through this noble institution. May He continue to guide, protect and bless the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board in the faithful discharge of its statutory responsibilities for generations to come.”

With those words, Nigerians have witnessed one of the most consequential tenures in the history of JAMB—a decade marked by ambitious reforms, uncompromising accountability, digital transformation and an enduring insistence that institutional success is achieved not by one individual, but by collective purpose.

World.title: Bianca, Great Asset To Humanity, Says Gov Otti
World.content:
Abia State Governor, Dr. Alex Otti, has said that Nigeria’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, is a huge asset not only to the Igbo nation but also to Nigeria, and humanity.

This was contained in a birthday message the governor sent to Nigerian former Ambassador to Spain, where he also enjoined her to continue to uphold the virtues and character that have distinguished her and made her an admirable amazon.

The governor’s birthday felicitations to the minister was endorsed by his Special Adviser on Media and Publicity, Ferdinand Ekeoma. The former Beauty Queen celebrated her birthday on August 5, 2026.

Governor Otti described Ambassador Ojukwu as an amazon who has distinguished herself in many facets of human endeavour, noting she deserves to be celebrated.

He recalled that the minister supported the struggle for Abia’s redemption, starting from when he first ran for governor on the platform of All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), adding that she is “an honest, just, and courageous Nigerian who has represented womanhood diligently and positively.”

“On a day like this, I feel excited to celebrate my sister and friend, Ambassador Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, on the occasion of her birthday. She is a woman of strong will and courage. An amazon from the East who has distinguished herself in many facets and continues to prove that, with courage and character, nothing is too big for any human being to accomplish,” the governor stated.

He noted that her appointment as Nigeria’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, “her commitment and accomplishments were already outstanding and commendable.”

The governor assured Ambassador Ojukwu that he would continue to support and stand by her at all times as she strives courageously to write more success stories in her eventful life and wished her a happy birthday, while praying that she would live long in good health to celebrate many more beautiful years ahead.

World.title: Adeleke Commends Monarch Residents  On Osun-Osogbo Festival
World.content:
Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo

The world-famous Osun-Osogbo Festival was held yesterday with more than 500,000 participants from all over the world.

Osun-Osogbo Festival is celebrated in August every year at the Grove. The festival attracts thousands of Osun worshippers, spectators and tourists from across the globe.

The Osun-Osogbo Festival is a two-week celebration of culture, spirituality, and heritage held annually in Osogbo, South West Nigeria.

Speaking on this year festival, Osun State Governor, Senator Ademola Adeleke, commended Oba Jimoh Olanipekun Oyetunji, Larooye II, Ataoja of Osogbo, and all sons and daughters of Osogbo at home and in the diaspora on the celebration of the Osun-Osogbo Festival.

The governor described the annual festival as a priceless cultural and spiritual heritage that reflects the enduring bond between the people of Osogbo and the sacred River Osun, celebrating centuries of history and faith.

He noted that the festival remains one of Africa’s foremost traditional festivals and a proud symbol of Yoruba civilisation.

The governor stated that the sacred procession led by the Arugba, the royal presence of the Ataoja, the traditional rites at the Osun Sacred Grove, the prayers, chants, and cultural displays all represent our culture and preserved heritage across generations while projecting Osun State to the global stage.

Adeleke commended the monarch, Ataoja of Osogbo, the Osun Priestess (Iya Osun), the Arugba, traditional institutions, devotees, cultural custodians, and the entire people of Osogbo for sustaining a festival that has continued to attract visitors, researchers, and tourists from across the world.

“On behalf of the Government and the good people of Osun State, I heartily felicitate with Kabiyesi, His Imperial Majesty, Oba Jimoh Olanipekun Oyetunji, Larooye II, Ataoja of Osogbo, and the entire people of Osogbo on this year’s Osun-Osogbo Festival.

“As we celebrate this sacred tradition, may the blessings of Osun continue to bring peace, prosperity, and progress to our dear state.”

The governor reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to preserving Osun’s rich cultural heritage and protecting the Osun Sacred Grove as a globally treasured heritage site.

He added that the administration will continue to support initiatives that promote tourism, cultural diplomacy, and economic opportunities for the people accordingly.

World.title: Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji and Nigeria’s Historical Amnesia
World.content:
By Mobolaji Sanusi

“We live in a society of imposed forgetfulness, a society that depends on public amnesia.”

— Angela Yvonne Davis (1944 – present)

Sometime last week, news filtered in that the Sardauna of Sokoto, Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji, had passed away. He was a model bureaucrat whose three names begin with the letter ‘A’, hence his media-coined moniker during his heyday and throughout his lifetime as the man with the triple As, or simply Alhaji Alhaji. One of the ‘Alhajis’ in his name was included because, like his father, he was born on Sallah Day.

In every sense, he was royalty personified. A true scion of the Sokoto Caliphate and a proud descendant of the Islamic reformer, Uthman Dan Fodio. In an interview he granted in the late 1980s, he said the greatest inconvenience he ever suffered was having to trek home from school one day because his father did not arrive as scheduled. Despite his privileged upbringing, those who follow the socio-political and economic evolution of Nigeria cannot easily forget his hard work and governance exploits. From the 1980s to the mid-1990s, he played a prominent role in the nation’s political, economic and institutional history.

His expertise in political economy was honed at Bournemouth College of Commerce and later at the University of Reading in Berkshire, United Kingdom. He also attended the IMF Institute in Washington, D.C., and the Institute of Social Studies in The Hague, Netherlands. Unlike many blue-bloods and children of the nouveau riche today who detest hard labour but seek undeserved opportunities to become overnight multi-billionaires, Alhaji Alhaji opted to join the Nigerian Civil Service in 1964. He rose through the ranks in the Federal Ministries of Finance, Trade, and Budget and Planning to become Permanent Secretary. As Principal Assistant Secretary and later Permanent Secretary in the Federal Ministry of Trade (1975 to 1978) and subsequently as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, he acquitted himself admirably.

To further tap his wealth of experience, successive military governments appointed him to higher responsibilities. He served as Executive Secretary of the FESTAC ’77 International Secretariat, later as Minister of State for Budget and Planning in 1988, and then as Minister of Finance and Economic Development from 1990 to 1991. In 1990, he was turbaned as the Sardauna of Sokoto, succeeding Sir Ahmadu Bello. From 1992, he served as Nigeria’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, a position he held until his retirement from public service in the mid-1990s.

He served Nigeria with all his strength when he had the option of idling away in unearned opulence. In the course of his duties as a technocrat, he became a constant feature in global institutions, including the Interim Committee of the International Monetary Fund, the Advisory Committee of Experts on Third World Debt under the Non-Aligned Movement, the Commonwealth Secretary-General’s Drafting Committee on Third World Debt, the Board of Governors of the OPEC Fund in Vienna, and the African Institute for Economic Development and Planning in Dakar, Senegal, among others. He served without blemish.

Some critics might denigrate his achievements by attributing his rise to opportunism, simply because he was a northern prince from the Caliphate. What these critics cannot take away from him is his intentionality and resolute conviction to join and stay put in the civil service, despite its routine and often boring processes, at a time when more enticing options lay before him as a Sokoto prince.

The question is: how many of today’s privileged children are willing to endure the boring routine demands of the contemporary civil service? Those who attempt to join today often do so at undeservedly high grade levels and know little or nothing about service rules and procedures. They rise to the pinnacle in barely a decade, unfairly outpacing experienced, tested and brilliant officers, even when they lack the requisite knowledge, training and experience to lead. No wonder the civil service in most states is a shadow of its old self. The toils of the likes of Samuel Manuwa, Simeon Adebo, Allison Ayida, Philip Asiodu, and indeed Abubakar Alhaji have become forgotten ideals rather than standards of service.

Shockingly, despite Alhaji Alhaji’s exploits at the highest levels of governance, it is doubtful if most young Nigerians had heard his name before or after his death. That is not entirely their fault. History as a subject, for no sensible reason, was unreasonably banished from classrooms across the country for over two decades by the civilian administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration only recently reintroduced history as a subject in schools.

Alhaji Alhaji was a prince with a difference. Born into royalty and having the rare privilege of living within the precincts of Buckingham Palace as a student in the United Kingdom, he could have, upon completion of his studies, returned to start parading himself as a businessman living off his family’s vast connections and the nation’s often fleeced public coffers, as many privileged children of power do today. Instead, he embraced hard work and dedicated himself to the civil service and to national development.

The fact that his name and legacy are largely unknown to the younger generation highlights Nigeria’s more fundamental problem of historical amnesia, which goes far beyond its numerous current challenges. We are raising a generation with little or no sense of history, yet it is a cliché that a people without a sense of their history and heritage will be obliterated. It was through the deliberate demonisation and distortion of our history that Western colonialists alienated us from our deities, norms, values, beliefs, traditions and heroes. Today, they troop to our country in droves to study and appropriate their once condemned African culture and values.

It is worth recalling that many remarkable scientific contributions were made by Black men and women who were forcibly taken to America and Europe as slaves. They were made to change their names to erase all traces of their identity and origin, barred from speaking their own languages and compelled to adopt foreign ones. They were brutalised, raped and tortured. Meanwhile, what is often projected in popular Western narratives is an image of Africa as a jungle inhabited by primates.

Sadly, we have left our own educational system in shambles and take pride in sending our wards abroad to acquire Western education to the detriment of our rich cultural and resource endowments. The country is now shamefully at the mercy of Western values and standards. This generation prefers to ‘japa’ and never look back.

Under such a forgetful atmosphere, if the new generation does not know a relatively recent and notable figure like Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji, it is futile to expect them to know former institutional heavyweights like Dr. S. O. Wey, who was the indigenous Head of the Federal Civil Service from 1961 to 1966; Chief Simeon Adebo, Head of the Western Nigeria Civil Service; Chief Jerome Udoji, the famous technocrat who led the 1974 public service review commission; Alhaji Sule Katagum, pioneer Chairman of the Federal Civil Service Commission; Dr. Samuel Manuwa, the astute federal civil servant and revered medical doctor; and Mr. M. A. Ejueyitchie, who served as Head of Service and Secretary to Prime Minister Tafawa Balewa in 1960. Allison Ayida and Philip Asiodu are also outstanding Permanent Secretaries whose contributions future generations should not forget.

That is why, even as our leaders make deliberate efforts to address the nation’s socio-economic problems, a conscious effort must also be made to revive historical consciousness among young Nigerians.

Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji’s place in history is solidified by his commitment to national duty despite being a prince with numerous other options, including idling in unmerited opulence.

The fact that President Tinubu sent a high-powered delegation led by his deputy to his funeral underscored Alhaji Alhaji’s significance. In his tribute, the President described him as “an elder statesman, a first-class technocrat and one of the prominent figures in Nigeria’s democratic and parliamentary history.” What more is there to add? Nothing, as the President has said it all.

Yours sincerely believes that not only this Sokoto prince but also other tested bureaucrats who have passed on should forever be preserved in the country’s history books. Rest well in Al-Jannah Firdaus, Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji.

To Be Reasonable Is Tinubu’s Message to EFCC

Enough of this impunity, that is the message President Bola Tinubu has sent to the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, and by extension to other law enforcement agencies in the country.

The Commission obtained a court order on August 5, 2026, freezing the accounts of the Osun State Government just days before its governorship election on August 15, 2026, leaving many mouths agape.

The public considers the order, even if circumstantial, a flagrant erosion of public confidence in the democratic process. To this, President Bola Tinubu, GCFR, has said no, by directing the Commission to immediately approach the court to seek a prompt vacation of the order in the overriding public interest.

The President was right when he said he felt “deeply embarrassed, not by the EFCC’s exercise of its mandate backed by a court order, but by the timing of the agency’s action.”

On the Osun governorship election, the President is saying: let the will of the people prevail, even if the heavens fall.

World.title: Budgets Without Results: Nigeria’s Implementation Crisis
World.content:
By Ugo Inyama

Nigeria knows how to budget. We know how to announce trillions, make grand speeches and celebrate appropriation figures as though development has already happened. Every year, the numbers grow larger and the promises become bolder.

But Nigerians cannot drive on budget speeches. They cannot receive treatment in appropriation bills. Factories cannot run on promises. Farmers cannot transport produce on fiscal projections. A budget may look impressive in Abuja, but unless it translates into roads, hospitals, schools, electricity, water and economic opportunities, it remains numbers on paper.

The real test of any budget is implementation. On that score, Nigeria has serious questions to answer.

We are already in August. More than half of 2026 is gone. Yet the impact of the 2026 capital budget remains painfully difficult to see. Where are the projects? Where are the releases? Where is the implementation? Where are the results?

These are not opposition questions. They are Nigerian questions.

President Bola Tinubu signed the 2026 budget into law in April. Total expenditure stands at ₦68.32 trillion, with about ₦32.2 trillion allocated to capital expenditure. That is a mountain of money on paper. But paper does not build roads.

The warning signs were already there. In presenting the 2026 budget, the President acknowledged that by the third quarter of 2025, only about ₦3.10 trillion, roughly 17.7 per cent of the 2025 capital budget, had been released.

That should have caused national alarm. Instead, we moved on to another budget.

We were implementing 2024 projects in 2025. Then 2025 projects spilled into 2026. Now 2026 itself is racing towards its final months. Nigeria’s capital budget is beginning to resemble a family suitcase that nobody completely unpacks. We simply carry it into the next year and add more clothes.

That is not effective budgeting. It is postponement dressed in fiscal grammar.

Nigeria has developed an unhealthy obsession with the size of its budgets. Ministers celebrate allocations. Legislators announce projects secured for their constituencies. Government officials proudly tell Nigerians how many billions have been provided for roads, hospitals, agriculture, education and power.

But allocation is not achievement. Appropriation is not implementation. Announcement is not development.

If ₦100 billion is budgeted for roads but only ₦20 billion reaches the projects, Nigerians are not driving on ₦100 billion worth of roads. The pothole does not care what the National Assembly approved.

Government must stop measuring success by what it intends to spend and start telling Nigerians what it has actually delivered. How much has been released? How much has been spent? Which projects have started? Which have been completed? What percentage of the capital budget has actually been implemented?

Every ministry, department and agency should publish a simple monthly capital implementation dashboard showing what was budgeted, what was released, what was spent and what was delivered.

If a ministry received nothing, say so. If money was released but not spent, explain why. If procurement is delaying a project, identify the problem. If a contractor collected mobilisation and disappeared, name the contractor. Accountability should not require detective work.

There is another uncomfortable problem. Nigeria appears addicted to starting new projects.

Every political officeholder wants something new to commission. Another road. Another hospital. Another secretariat. Another skills centre. Another foundation stone accompanied by speeches, photographs and applause.

Meanwhile, existing projects remain unfinished. Some have survived more budget cycles than the politicians who initiated them.

Nigeria needs a simple rule: finish what you started.

An unfinished hospital treats nobody. An abandoned road carries nobody. An unequipped school teaches nobody. An incomplete irrigation project feeds nobody. There is no economic medal for accumulating abandoned projects.

If government cannot finance 10,000 projects, budget for 3,000 and complete them. A smaller realistic budget properly implemented will always serve Nigerians better than a gigantic budget that exists mainly in government documents.

Government undoubtedly faces fiscal pressures. Debt servicing is expensive. Salaries must be paid. Revenue projections sometimes fail. But that is precisely why budgeting must become more realistic. Capital expenditure cannot continually become the sacrificial lamb whenever revenue disappoints.

Roads reduce transportation costs. Reliable electricity supports industry. Hospitals protect lives. Schools develop human capital. Irrigation strengthens food security. When capital implementation suffers, tomorrow’s economy pays the price.

The National Assembly must also accept responsibility. Lawmakers cannot approve enormous budgets, add thousands of projects and then disappear from the implementation conversation. Legislative oversight should not end when the President signs the Appropriation Act. Oversight must move from allocation to outcomes.

And the clock is ticking.

January to July 2026 is gone. We are in August.

Soon, attention will turn towards another budget, another speech, another impressive figure and another promise of transformation.

Not so fast.

Before anyone brings out the calculator for 2027, Nigerians deserve a proper account of 2026. How much of the capital budget has been released? How much has been spent? Which roads have been completed? Which hospitals have been equipped? Which power projects are delivering electricity?

A budget does not become development because the President signed it or because the National Assembly passed it. It becomes development when Nigerians can see it, use it and benefit from it.

No excuses. No fiscal poetry. Just show Nigerians the projects.

A budget is a promise. Implementation is the proof.

More than half of 2026 is already gone.

Where is the proof?

*Ugo Inyama

Executive Director

African Digital Governance Centre, Manchester

Email: ugo@africandgc.org

World.title: Radda Orders Renovation of Katsina NYSC Orientation Camp
World.content:
Francis Sardauna in Katsina

Katsina State Governor, Dikko Umaru Radda, has directed the state Ministry of Works, Housing and Transport to carry out assessment of structural defects at the state’s National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) orientation camp for renovation after 25 years.

Radda, who gave the directive Friday at the swearing-in of the 2026 Batch ‘B’ Stream II corps members deployed to the state, reiterated his readiness to improve the camp’s facilities and enhance the welfare of corps members.

He said after the “comprehensive assessment” of the dilapidated camp facilities, the state government will commence what he termed holistic renovation and remodeling of the camp for improved orientation activities.

Represented by the state Head of Service, Mr Falalu Bawale, Radda said: “The Government of Katsina State has taken note of the present challenges in the orientation camp and we are committed to fixing them within a reasonable time.

“The Ministry of Works, Housing and Transport has been directed to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the structural defects of the orientation facilities for a holistic renovation and remodeling.”

Radda, however, assured corps members deployed in the state of government’s support throughout their service year and called on them to justify the confidence reposed in them.

He reminded the corps members that the service year offers a unique opportunity to contribute to nation-building while acquiring valuable experience that would prepare them for future leadership roles.

Earlier, the state NYSC Coordinator, Mr Evans Okwor, appealed to the Governor Radda-led government to intervene in the dilapidating state of facilities at the orientation camp.

According to him, the male hostel in the permanent orientation camp has not undergone any renovation since they were constructed about 25 years ago.

He explained that although the female hostel received partial renovation in 2020, the male hostel and other camp facilities require comprehensive rehabilitation and upgrading to provide a conducive environment for corps members.

He, however, commended Governor Radda’s administration for approving additional funds to improve the feeding of corps members during the orientation exercise.

He added that the NYSC would reciprocate the government’s support by deploying corps members’ skills and expertise to improve healthcare services in rural communities and provide academic support in post-primary institutions.

World.title: Lagos Risks Worse Flooding Without Strict Shoreline Regulation, SDAL Warns
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

The President of the Shoreline Developers Association of Lagos (SDAL), Mr. Lai Omotola, has warned that continued construction on wetlands and unregulated land reclamation are worsening flooding in Lagos, stressing that sustainable shoreline development is the only way to unlock the state’s vast economic potential.

Briefing journalists in Lagos following the inauguration of the association, Omotola said developers must move beyond the pursuit of profit and embrace self-regulation to protect the environment and safeguard investments.

According to him, wetlands designated by the Lagos State Government should never be developed, as such areas play critical ecological roles, including water retention and flood control.

“You cannot build on wetlands. It is a no-go area. Once government designates an area as environmentally protected, developers must respect it. If we continue building on wetlands, flooding will only get worse,” he said.

Omotola noted that the association was established to promote responsible shoreline development and engage government agencies and other stakeholders on sustainable practices.

He warned that failure to comply with environmental regulations could lead to devastating financial losses for homeowners and investors.

“It is suicidal to build a house today only to pull it down 10 years later because of flooding. Someone may invest his retirement savings in a property, only to lose everything because proper environmental assessments were ignored,” he stated.

The SDAL president also condemned indiscriminate land reclamation without the mandatory environmental and geotechnical studies, saying natural waterways have their own flow patterns that must not be obstructed.

According to him, altering water channels without proper planning often results in flooding and storm surges.

“There are critical assessments that must be carried out before any reclamation. Some people simply begin filling land without understanding how water moves. When you block natural water channels, nature will respond, and that is what leads to flooding and surges,” he explained.

Omotola argued that protecting Lagos’ shoreline would ultimately generate greater economic returns than indiscriminate development.

He pointed to high-value waterfront locations such as Banana Island, where premium properties command billions of naira, as evidence that properly planned shoreline communities attract significant investment.

Replicating such developments across other suitable waterfront locations, he stated, could unlock trillions of naira in investments, create jobs, boost tourism and stimulate commercial activities.

“Lagos has enormous shoreline assets. If we develop them responsibly, with the right infrastructure and environmental safeguards, we can attract global investors, increase tourism, create commercial hubs and generate sustainable revenue for the state,” he said.

Omotola further lamented Nigeria’s inadequate tourism and entertainment infrastructure, noting that despite the country’s thriving creative industry, it lacks world-class event facilities capable of hosting major international concerts and attracting larger numbers of visitors.

He maintained that: “Strategic investment in waterfront infrastructure would transform Lagos into a leading tourism and investment destination comparable to global cities with thriving marina developments.”

According to him, with about 40 per cent of Lagos’ landmass covered by water, the state has barely begun to harness its shoreline resources.

He urged government, investors and developers to adopt a long-term vision, insisting that responsible planning, strict implementation of environmental regulations and adequate funding would position Lagos as a global waterfront city while preserving its environment for future generations.

Omotola said the association would promote climate-compliant, technology-driven and self-regulated shoreline development while advocating the preservation of mangrove ecosystems and the restoration of Lagos’ coastal environment.

He also urged Lagos State to prepare for the expected impact of the $3.3 billion Lagos-Calabar Coastal highway, saying coordinated planning would be essential to maximise its economic potential while minimising environmental risks.

On regulatory oversight, Omotola called for stronger collaboration among federal and state agencies to eliminate overlapping responsibilities.

“The Nigerian Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA) should continue to lead shoreline development, while the Office of the Surveyor-General, environmental agencies and the Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development should perform their statutory roles in land administration,” the SDAL president stated.

World.title: Commissioner: Why C’ River Reversed LG Teachers’ Salary Adjustment
World.content:
The Cross River State Commissioner for Local Government Affairs, Chief Victor Felix Idem, has explained that the recent adjustment in the salaries of local government teachers was not a deliberate wage cut, but the reversal of an erroneous upward adjustment that had created a disparity between the earnings of local government teachers and their counterparts employed by the state.

Idem said the action was taken to correct an irregularity in the payroll system and restore uniformity in the remuneration of teachers across the two services.

Idem, who spoke on the controversy surrounding the development, said the government discovered that local government teachers were earning more than their counterparts in the state public service, despite both categories of teachers being placed on the same salary grade levels and performing similar functions.

According to him, “The local government salaries were discovered to be excessively higher” than those of their state counterparts, stressing that the disparity was not the outcome of any duly authorised government policy but arose from an erroneous adjustment in the Local Government Teachers’ Salary Structure.

The commissioner said a review of the Revised Salary Structure for Teachers (RSST) applicable to the local government service revealed that, while the basic salary and other statutory components were identical to those applicable to state-employed teachers, local government teachers were receiving additional payments.

Idem stated that the additional payments were not the product of an approved government wage policy and could therefore not be sustained once the anomaly was detected.

“That money was given illegally; there was no approval or authorization by government for them to add such money to make it more than that of the state,” he said, maintaining that the government had a responsibility to correct an irregular payment structure once discovered.

The commissioner further argued that describing the development simply as a salary reduction was unfair to the government, insisting that what had occurred was the correction of an earlier administrative error.

“Instead of the government actually asking them to refund those monies they were paid illegally, we just left it and stopped paying the money,” he explained, adding that government had opted for a less burdensome approach rather than immediately demanding repayment of the excess payments.

Idem said the decision was therefore part of a broader effort to harmonise the salary structure of teachers in the local government service with that of teachers in the State public service.

He explained that the objective was to ensure that teachers performing similar duties and occupying the same grade levels were remunerated under a consistent and equitable framework.

“The government reverting it is to ensure that there is no industrial disharmony between the state teachers and the local government teachers,” he said.

The proposed harmonisation is expected to eliminate the disparity created by the additional allowances contained in the local government teachers’ salary structure and ensure equity, consistency and uniformity across the two services.

Idem said the relevant authorities had been requested to initiate the necessary review, with the State Government Teachers’ Salary Structure made available for comparison and as a basis for aligning the two remuneration frameworks.

He disclosed that consultations had also taken place with representatives of organised labour as part of efforts to resolve the disparity and achieve an acceptable harmonisation of teachers’ salaries.

Idem said the issue had become necessary to address because maintaining two different remuneration outcomes for teachers on the same grade levels and performing similar functions could undermine fairness and create avoidable tension within the teaching service.

He maintained that the harmonisation process was not designed to deprive teachers of legitimate earnings but to correct an anomaly and establish a properly authorised salary structure that could be applied consistently across the state and local government systems.

The commissioner urged teachers, labour leaders and other stakeholders to properly understand the circumstances behind the adjustment rather than interpreting it as an arbitrary reduction in workers’ earnings.

He maintained that the government’s position was essentially about correcting an administrative anomaly and restoring the appropriate salary structure, saying the ultimate objective was to ensure that teachers across Cross River State were treated equitably under a harmonised, consistent and sustainable remuneration framework.

World.title: Tense Osun Poll: Vote Buying Worries INEC
World.content:
*CSOs flag 13 high-risk LGAs, appeal for police neutrality

*Kudos, knocks trail Tinubu’s directive to unfreeze state’s account

*Police assure Nigerians of peaceful, credible governorship election

Adedayo Akinwale, Sunday Aborisade and Linus Aleke in Abuja and Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo

Ahead of the August 15 governorship election in Osun State, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) yesterday expressed concern over the growing threat of vote buying, warning that the practice could undermine the credibility of the poll if not decisively checked by security agencies.



This comes as Civil Society Concerns on Election Security in Osun urged the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to remain neutral and professional during the state governorship election.

Also yesterday, reactions continued to trail President Bola Tinubu’s Thursday’s directive ordering the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to return to court and vacate the order freezing the Osun State Government’s bank accounts, with political parties, civil society organisations and security agencies expressing divergent views over the development.



While the Inter-Party Advisory Council (IPAC) in Osun State and the opposition Accord Party commended the President’s intervention as a demonstration of respect for democracy and the rule of law, the Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre (CISLAC) warned that the directive could undermine the operational independence of anti-corruption institutions.

The House of Representatives Minority Caucus said the directive issued by the President to the EFCC was due to massive public outcry and not by respect for the rule of law.



Also, the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu, yesterday assured Nigerians that adequate security arrangements had been put in place to ensure a peaceful, free, fair and credible governorship election.

Speaking on INEC’s level of preparedness, a senior official of the Commission who spoke to THISDAY on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to comment publicly on the election, said while the electoral body was fully prepared for the exercise, vote buying remained one of its biggest concerns given the heightened political atmosphere in the state.



The official disclosed that the commission had completed virtually all critical preparations for the election, including the deployment of election materials, training of personnel and testing of its electoral technology.

“As far as INEC is concerned, I can confidently say we are over 90 per cent prepared for the election,” the official said.

He revealed that INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, recently led a comprehensive readiness assessment in the state, which involved six National Commissioners, directors, senior officials and technical staff.



According to him, the exercise, which lasted about five days, involved a thorough review of every aspect of the commission’s preparations, including a mock accreditation exercise to test the effectiveness of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS).

The official, however, stressed that INEC alone could not guarantee a credible election, saying the success of the poll would depend on the conduct of security agencies, political parties and their supporters.



He described the political environment in Osun as “quite tense,” urging all stakeholders to exercise restraint and uphold the rules of engagement.

“Our biggest concern is vote buying, which we fear could be widespread. We want the Nigeria Police and other security agencies to remain professional, impartial and above board in enforcing the law.



“Vote buying is prohibited under the Electoral Act. It is a criminal offence and one of the greatest threats to the integrity of Nigeria’s electoral process. Anyone arrested for the offence should face the full weight of the law,” the official added.

Meanwhile, the Civil Society Concerns on Election Security in Osun has urged the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to remain neutral and professional during the state governorship election.



The group made the call yesterday, during a press conference at the Nigeria Police Force Headquarters in Abuja.

Executive Director Samson Itodo, who spoke on behalf of the group, warned that public confidence in the electoral process would depend largely on how security personnel conduct themselves before, during and after the poll.



“This is the last major election to be held ahead of the 2027 general election. Therefore, it has a lot of significance, and it’s a unique opportunity to inspire public trust, not just in the management of the election, but election security.

“The public would want to see institutions demonstrate neutrality so they can have confidence in those institutions,” Itodo stated.

He warned that the level of pre-election violence and political tension recorded in parts of Osun State could undermine public trust and confidence if not effectively addressed.



He disclosed that findings from Yiaga Africa’s election observation and risk assessment showed that 13 of Osun State’s 30 local government areas have been classified as high-risk due to recurring violent incidents and heightened political tension.

These he said included Irewole, Osogbo, Boripe, Obokun, Ife North, Ife Central, and parts of Ijesaland.

He added. “Our comprehensive assessment and monitoring process shows that there have been about 34 known fatalities across incidents recorded between 2025 and June 2026.”



In the meantime, reactions have continued to trail President Tinubu’s directive ordering the EFCC to return to court and vacate the order freezing the Osun State Government’s bank accounts ahead of the August 15 governorship election.



IPAC, in a statement issued yesterday by its Caretaker Committee Chairman, Odesola Oluseye Titus, described President Tinubu’s directive to the EFCC as a demonstration of respect for democratic principles and the rule of law.

The council said the President’s action had reinforced confidence in Nigeria’s democratic institutions and should serve as a guide for all agencies involved in the electoral process.



Commending Tinubu for directing the anti-graft agency to vacate the court order, IPAC also praised the President’s insistence on the independence and professionalism of law enforcement agencies.

Quoting Tinubu’s position that anti-corruption agencies should discharge their statutory responsibilities “independently, professionally, without fear or favour or political interference,” the council described the President as “the father of the nation.”



It urged INEC, the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigerian Army and other security agencies to emulate the President’s example by performing their constitutional responsibilities impartially.



According to IPAC, the President’s directive should guide the conduct of all agencies involved in the forthcoming governorship election, stressing that security agencies and electoral officials must act professionally to sustain public confidence in the electoral process.

The council also appealed to political actors to respect the rules of engagement and urged eligible voters to come out en masse on election day, expressing confidence that every vote would count.



However, the opposition Accord Party demanded the immediate resignation of the Chairman of the EFCC, Ola Olukoyede, insisting that he should be held accountable for approving what it described as the unconstitutional freezing of the Osun State Government’s bank accounts.



Speaking at a world press conference in Abuja, the party’s National Chairman, Chief Maxwell Mgbudem, commended President Tinubu for what he termed a timely intervention that prevented a constitutional crisis.

He, however, argued that the EFCC chairman had embarrassed the President, damaged Nigeria’s democratic image and brought the anti-corruption agency into disrepute.

Mgbudem said if Olukoyede failed to resign voluntarily, President Tinubu should remove him from office to restore public confidence in the Commission.



The Accord chairman also called for the immediate release of about 60 of the party’s members allegedly detained in Abuja, Osun and Nasarawa States, saying their continued detention could heighten political tension ahead of the election.

He further urged INEC to conduct a free, fair and credible governorship election, describing the Osun poll as a critical test for Nigeria’s democracy ahead of the 2027 general election.



In a sharp contrast, the Executive Director of CISLAC and Head of Transparency International Nigeria, Auwal Musa Rafsanjani, criticised the President’s intervention, warning that directing the EFCC to seek the lifting of the court order could weaken the operational independence of anti-corruption institutions.



Addressing journalists in Abuja, Rafsanjani argued that while governance should not be unnecessarily disrupted, presidential intervention in specific enforcement actions created a dangerous precedent.

According to him, the EFCC derives its powers from the law and should be allowed to investigate and prosecute economic crimes professionally and without political interference.

He maintained that if the Commission took an inappropriate decision, the proper avenue for redress remained the judiciary rather than executive intervention.

Rafsanjani also stressed that lifting the restriction on the state’s accounts should not signal the end of investigations into the alleged diversion of public funds, insisting that anyone found culpable should face prosecution regardless of political affiliation.

In the meantime, the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, assured Nigerians that the Nigeria Police Force had concluded comprehensive security arrangements for the August 15 governorship election.

Hosting civil society organisations in Abuja ahead of the poll, the IGP said the Police had no preferred candidate or political party and remained committed to ensuring that the lawful choice of the people prevailed.

He disclosed that adequate personnel and operational assets had been deployed across Osun State, while intelligence gathering and threat assessments had been intensified in collaboration with INEC, the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES) and other stakeholders.

Disu warned that anyone involved in vote buying, ballot box snatching, voter intimidation, thuggery or any other electoral offence would be dealt with in accordance with the law, irrespective of political affiliation.

He also urged political parties and their supporters to conduct themselves peacefully, stressing that elections should be contests of ideas rather than violence and intimidation.

The Police boss encouraged eligible voters to come out without fear to exercise their constitutional rights, assuring them that the Force would provide a secure environment throughout the electoral process.

The political atmosphere in Osun also became more charged yesterday as the All Progressives Congress (APC) asked Governor Ademola Adeleke to apologise to President Tinubu and the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, for accusing them of influencing the EFCC’s action against the state government.

The party maintained that while the President objected to the timing of the account freeze, he did not exonerate the Osun State Government from the allegations being investigated by the anti-graft agency.

The House of Representatives Minority Caucus said the directive issued by the President to the EFCC was due to massive public outcry and not by respect for the rule of law.

It added that the move exposed deep contradictions and a deliberate plot to intimidate the Osun State Government ahead of next week’s gubernatorial election.

Its Leader, Hon. Fredrick Agbedi and the Spokesman of the caucus, Hon. Afam Ogene in a statement issued yesterday, said the President’s directive exposed “a government at war with itself,”.

The caucus pointed out that while EFCC Spokesman, Mr. Wilson Uwujaren, stated on national television on Thursday that the freezing of Osun’s account was done “without a valid court order”, the President’s statement later same Thursday afternoon directed the Commission to go to court to “vacate the order.”

The caucus noted: “So, which is it? Was there a court order or not?. Is the President not aware of what his own appointees are saying and doing?

“Has the President lost control of his army of sycophants who behave like lords over the people? Or are they simply trying to hide an illegality that has already been exposed?”

The Caucus also accused the President’s senior aides of being the first to circulate and defend the EFCC’s initial press release supporting the EFCC overreach.

The Caucus described the August 5 EFCC action as the latest in what they termed a sustained campaign of intimidation against Osun by the APC-led Federal Government.

The caucus decried that for months, the federal government had illegally withheld and seized statutory allocations due to Osun Local Governments, describing it as economic strangulation aimed at crippling governance at the grassroots ahead of elections.”

It noted: “ The gestapo-style arrest and detention of the Secretary to the Osun State Government, Teslim Igbalaiye and others over flimsy accusations is a direct attack on the institution of the state government.”

Also yesterday, the World Bishops Council (Africa Chapter) and the Religious Engagement (Christianity) Committee working for Governor Adeleke’s re-election endorsed the governor for a second term, describing him as “a man of destiny” who had promoted peace and religious harmony in the state.

The groups urged voters to re-elect Adeleke and announced a seven-day fasting and prayer programme for peaceful elections and the governor’s victory.

In another development, the Imole Campaign Council dismissed an alleged oath-taking video circulating on social media and purportedly linked to Governor Adeleke, describing it as a desperate smear campaign orchestrated by the APC.

The council insisted that Adeleke neither authorised nor participated in any oath-taking exercise, maintaining that his re-election bid was anchored on his performance in office and the goodwill of the people rather than intimidation or superstition.

World.title: Cameron Waldeck-Cooks appears carefree in video before ‘murder’
World.content:
Cameron Waldeck-Cooks in a video captured before her death. Images via TikTok

Cameron Waldeck-Cooks was seen dancing with a group of pals, just days before her death, in a video posted on TikTok. The St Stithian Grade 11 learner was allegedly killed in a murder-suicide involving former matriculant Ethan Coetzee.

The teens’ bodies were discovered in a Sabi game lodge in Mpumalanga on Monday, 3 August.

Police have confirmed that an initial inquest has been upgraded to a murder charge.



CAMERON WALDECK-COOKS LAST DAYS

In a tribute posted by a pal on TikTok, Cameron Waldeck-Cooks joyfully danced alongside a group of friends

The blonde teen appeared happy and carefree, blissfully unaware of what would transpire a few days later.

“Here’s to you, my Cam”, her pal captioned the clip.

In the comments section, another friend added: “To think this was just a week ago”.

Watch the video here.

According to a statement from her family, Cameron Waldeck-Cooks would spend the weekend with another family at a lodge in Sabie on a hiking adventure.



On Monday, 3 August, her body and that of her alleged boyfriend, Ethan Coetzee, were discovered by his father

An independent forensic pathologist’s preliminary findings indicated that Cameron died as a result of strangulation and suffocation. Police have stated that Ethan, who was 19-years old, may have died by suicide.

BRIGHT FUTURE AHEAD

Both Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and Ethan Coetzee’s lives were tragically cut short in the double tragedy,

Cameron, a St. Stithians Girls College Grade 11 student, was working towards the Gold level of The President’s Award for Youth Empowerment, which is part of the Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award.

She was also in the rowing and netball clubs and was described as a “natural leader” and a “big sister”.

Meanwhile, Ethan – who matriculated in 20215 – had been part of the first team rugby club, was a national champion in the equestrian sport of Eventing, and was a respected senior student at Penryn House.

World.title: LIVE MATCH REPORT: Orlando Pirates vs Durban City
World.content:
Orlando Pirates starting line up: Chaine, Sibisi (captain), Seema, Sebelebele, Ndaba, Mbatha, Dansin, Maswanganyi, Appollis, Moremi, Mbuthuma.

Substitutes: Dladla (GK), Kgositsile, Masilela, Zulu, Mokobodi, Mthiyane, Radiopane, Lungu, Hotto.

Durban City starting line up: Asare, Msomi, Mokone, Ncanana, Shandu, Poggenpoel, Sanger, Nodada, Sifumba, Sirino, Lubumba.



Substitutes: Dreyer, Gcaba, Maseko, Mthembu, Mofokeng, Makua, Morris, Green, Domingo.

13:00: The team buses have arrived at the Orlando Amstel Arena.

14:00: Starting line ups to be confirmed

15:00: Match kick off.

MTN8 QUARTERFINAL: ORLANDO PIRATES VS DURBAN CITY

The Soweto giants enter the clash with history firmly in their sights as they chase a record-breaking fifth consecutive MTN8 title. Orlando Pirates began their remarkable run in 2022, defeating AmaZulu 1-0 in the final. Monnapule Saleng scored the decisive goal to secure the Buccaneers’ first trophy under former coach Jose Riveiro.

They successfully defended their crown in 2023, overcoming Mamelodi Sundowns on penalties after a goalless final. Goalkeeper Sipho Chaine proved to be the difference, producing three crucial saves in the shootout.



Orlando Pirates continued their dominance in 2024, defeating Stellenbosch FC 3-1 in the final to become the first club in the PSL era to win the MTN8 three seasons in succession.

The Buccaneers extended that remarkable record last season under Abdeslam Ouaddou. They defeated Stellenbosch FC 3-0 after extra time, with Tshepang Moremi scoring twice as Pirates secured their fourth consecutive crown and 14th MTN8 title overall.

DURBAN CITY EYE UPSET

Durban City head to Soweto determined to prevent another chapter being added to Pirates’ remarkable cup history. The Nedbank Cup holders have strengthened their squad under new coach Khalil Ben Youssef. They will believe they have enough quality to challenge the defending champions.

The Citizens also know they can frustrate the Buccaneers. They held Orlando Pirates to a goalless Betway Premiership draw when the sides last met.

Victory on Saturday would take Orlando Pirates one step closer to an unprecedented fifth straight MTN8 crown, while Durban City will be targeting a major quarter-final upset at the Orlando Amstel Arena.

World.title: ‘Chiefs will be eliminated by Arrows’ – Junior Khanye predicts
World.content:
Former Kaizer Chiefs winger Junior Khanye has backed Golden Arrows to knock Amakhosi out of the MTN8 in the quarter-finals.

Chiefs return to the competition after missing out on the previous two editions. They will host Arrows on Sunday afternoon, knowing that victory would take them one step closer to lifting the trophy they last won 12 years ago.
