World.title: Low Danube water reveals Wehrmacht motorbike on riverbed
World.content:
The water level in the Danube has never been this low. The low water has revealed what lay hidden on the riverbed for decades, among them a Wehrmacht motorcycle, a DKW NZ 350-1 model from the Second World War.

 

It was found in the riverbed in the heart of Hungary's capital, Budapest, at the level of the Hungarian parliament building. For staff at the local Institute and Museum of Military History it is a genuine once-in-a-century discovery. The vehicle is almost completely intact, according to the institute. It was preserved in the Danube's mud.

DKW racing motorcycles from 1939 and 1931, archive Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

The motorcycle recovered is a model that was developed specifically for wartime use and was produced from 1944 onwards. Around 12,000 units were built by the end of the war in 1945. Its predecessor, the DKW (source in German) NZ 350, reached a top speed of 105 km/h, according to the ADAC.

The motorcycle was manufactured by Auto Union AG, a car and motorcycle producer founded in 1932. Auto Union AG was created through the merger of several brands, including Audi.

By autumn 1936 the NZ range, made up of the 250 and 350 models, was ready for mass production. However, because another motorbike range was selling so well, they did not go into series production until 1938.

On earlier models from the manufacturer the frame sections were still bolted together. On the NZ range they were welded. Because this required a large amount of electricity, the work could only be carried out at night, when the power grid was not otherwise under heavy load.

German troops drive through Liège, 30 May 1940 AP

German anti-tank mines, remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells have also been found on the bed of the Danube. The Hungarian Institute of Military History says this stretch of the river may have been used as a "war rubble dump".

From March 1944 German troops besieged Budapest. Between October 1944 and February 1945 the Battle of Budapest took place between the Soviet Red Army and German and Hungarian forces. Around 30,000 German, more than 17,000 Hungarian and about 80,000 Soviet and Romanian soldiers were killed. After the surrender of the remaining German units, Budapest was liberated on 13 February 1945.

World.title: Russian attacks on Kyiv region kill three, including a child
World.content:
Three people, including a child, have died following Russian attacks on the Kyiv region overnight, according to local authorities.

 

Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said Russian forces had struck three sites in the Brovary district near the capital, killing three people and injuring three others.

"Falling debris has damaged a private residential house, outbuildings and cars. A fire also broke out on the premises of a non-residential building," he wrote in a post on Telegram.

At least four people were also injured in an attack on the city of Kyiv, per the Kyiv City Military Administration.

Firefighters have been battling flames in the city's Holosiivskyi and Obolon districts, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) reported on social media, while sharing images showing blazes ravaging what appeared to be warehouses and garages.

A Russian drone strike on the Chernihiv region in northern Ukraine also sparked a fire at a warehouse in the Pryluky district, per the DSNS. No casualties have been reported so far.

Zelenskyy in Serbia

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Serbia, where he is set to meet with Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić and Prime Minister Đuro Macut.

According to Zelenskyy, the trio are due to discuss "expanding economic ties" as well as their relationship with the European Union and security issues.

US Senate approves Russia sanctions bill

On Friday, the United States Senate passed a sweeping new round of sanctions on Russia.

The bill, which had been championed by the late Lindsey Graham, is designed to punish Moscow and countries that purchase its oil and natural gas.

Responding to the news on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "very grateful" and that the sanctions package would help "increase pressure" on Moscow and bring this "insane Russian war against our independence and our people to an end."

"Real, strong American pressure and sanctions against Russia are what will help the most," he added.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border
World.content:
A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning.

According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania. He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone.

Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine.

"We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said.

What do we know about the drone?

Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was.

However, he said that it was believed that the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced.

When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type.

"This is not a toy drone; it's a larger drone," he told journalists, according to the BTA news agency.

However, Radev also mentioned that the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size.

Drone incidents on rise in EU countries

In recent months, there have been an increasing number of incidents involving drones in Eastern European countries that are both EU and NATO members and that support Ukraine in its four-and-a-half-year war against Russia's invasion.

The origin of the drone that exploded in Bulgaria and its potential connection to Russia or Ukraine are still unclear. Radev said that teams from the Bulgarian border police and the Ministry of Defense are working to determine the origin of the drone.

Bulgaria's Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said the incident would be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council early next week.

Romania, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent drone incursions, including crashes on its territory, such as a May incident in which a drone struck an apartment building.

Earlier this week in Germany, an explosive-laden drone was defused at Leipzig Airport, in what Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called a "new level of danger."

World.title: EU holds talks with big tech over Ceuta misinformation
World.content:
EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen has called for closer monitoring of social media platforms moving forward, amid the spread of misinformation during the recent migrant influx at Spain's Ceuta.

EU Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen has called on social media giants to exercise closer monitoring of their platforms for misinformation, especially "during crisis situations."

Virkkunen was referring to last week's Ceuta border crisis, which European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities say was exacerbated by the spread of misinformation on social media, including TikTok, Telegram and Meta platforms.

Commissioner Virkkunen addressed the disinformation on social media, calling for greater EU monitoring of platforms during crisis situations.

"Platforms must act decisively in keeping the integrity of the digital space, in particular during crisis situations," she wrote on X.

"Monitoring must increase, cooperation with fact-checkers to be strengthened," Virkkunen wrote after a Friday meeting with representatives from TikTok and Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Social media increasingly central to 'political debate'

A number of the estimated 72,000 people who stormed Ceuta from Morocco said they were attracted by false promises disseminated on social media and that they were lied to about the situation.

Spain and Morocco have also exchanged blame, with authorities in Rabat blaming a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that it says was exploited by human traffickers and misrepresented on social media.

Madrid says Morocco should have done a better job at stopping the tens of thousands of migrants who crossed the border.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the end, Spanish authorities say 80 people were killed during the course of events.

Moroccan authorities reported that 11 people died on their side of the border.

Rights groups estimate the total number of dead at more than 140.

The situation in Ceuta and the circumstances surrounding it have added more fuel to Europe's ongoing political fight over issues related to immigration and security.

Did misinformation on social media cause the Ceuta crisis?

In Ceuta, migrants pointed to social media messages and videos announcing that the EU border at Ceuta was suddenly open.

Why young Moroccans risked everything to reach Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other posts informed people looking to get to the EU that accommodations would be available once they got to the Spanish territory and that they would be bused to the Spanish mainland from there.

Last week, EU member states convened an emergency meeting at which representatives mulled early-warning systems and social media monitoring as potential levers for improving the bloc's shared assessment capabilities in emerging situations.

Virkkunen said the EU would continue that discussion on Monday.

World.title: When German Catholics and Protestants share a church
World.content:
Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed in Germany. But there is a new, unique development.

From the outside, the Catholic church in Mannheim's Neuostheim district appears to be a typical 1950s church building: a relatively simple structure, nothing particularly remarkable about it. Yet St. Pius is truly unique. In this place of worship, Catholic and Protestant Christians celebrate services sharing the same space and taking turns in gathering around the same altar for Communion and the Eucharist.

"It actually began in the early 1970s," Annette Hübner, a Catholic parishioner, told DW. The 57-year-old has lived in the district with her family for more than half a century and is a member of the parish team. At the time, the parish priest of St. Pius was committed to fostering cooperation with the Protestant community and began holding ecumenical services in 1970. Then, at the end of 2009, the nearby Protestant St. Thomas Church sustained extensive water damage, and the building was found to be beyond repair.

What began as a temporary arrangement gradually evolved into a lasting solution. That lasting solution, in turn, grew into a genuine ecumenical friendship.

"It became increasingly clear that it made sense to continue working together," Hübner recalled. A banner on the facade of St. Pius proclaims: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." What may sound like a theological phrase from a Sunday sermon is part of everyday life here, on weekdays as much as on Sundays.

Annette Hübner feels that the Catholic and Protestant congretations in St.Pius are on a long journey that is well worth the effort Image: Christoph Strack/DW

Catholics and Protestants under one roof: Germany is home to 65 so-called Simultankirchen (shared churches). Their joint use was mandated by secular rulers soon after the Reformation and the resulting division of the Church. In some cases, detailed regulations even specified who was allowed to enter the church and at what times. The best-known examples are Altenberg Cathedral near Cologne and St. Peter's Protestant Cathedral in the eastern German city of Bautzen in Saxony.

In hospital and airport chapels, shared use by different Christian denominations is now almost taken for granted. A similar trend, however, is increasingly emerging in ordinary parish communities. Protestant and Catholic churches in Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia had already begun addressing the issue in 2017, during the commemorations marking the 500th anniversary of Martin Luther's Reformation.

"What If We All Moved In Together?" is the title of the Practical Guide to the Ecumenical Use of Churches and Parish Halls. The publication presents examples from the dioceses of Cologne and Aachen, as well as Essen, Münster and Paderborn.

The guide repeatedly points to the "accelerating reduction in church buildings." According to official church statistics for 2025, Germany had 24,500 Catholic and 21,100 Protestant churches, ranging from small chapels to grand cathedrals. Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed.

A new life for Germany's deconsecrated church buildings To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Attending a Protestant church was once considered 'a sin'

Examples of new shared church spaces can be found in both western and eastern Germany. In Schildow, on the northern outskirts of Berlin, only one church is expected to remain in use in the future: the larger and more prominent Protestant church. The Archdiocese of Berlin's press office describes the initiative as "an ecumenical project with exemplary character." Its statement also hints at the significance of this development: "For all the ecumenical openness that is now taken for granted," the Catholic participants still remember "earlier times when even attending a Protestant church was considered a sin."

Small congregations in the East

Catholic bishops in eastern Germany are quite accustomed to celebrating Mass in Protestant churches. For major occasions such as confirmations or parish anniversaries, the generally smaller Catholic churches are often unable to accommodate everyone. In such cases, their Protestant counterparts are often happy to provide the necessary space.

The German Bishops' Conference is also currently addressing the issue and plans to publish a practical guide on the subject. Here, too, the focus is on declining membership, church buildings that are no longer needed, financial constraints, and the potential for shared use.

St. Pius new altar was crafted from red and grey stone from the altar of two Protestant and Catholic Churches Image: Christoph Strack/DW

Two altars merged into one

But St. Pius in Mannheim is different. It is far more than a temporary arrangement born of necessity. Here, the two congregations have developed a deep and wide-ranging form of cooperation. Between 2020 and 2022, the church underwent extensive renovation and redesign. The place where the altar once stood is now occupied by the baptismal font, serving as a shared focal point for both churches. A new altar, crafted from red and grey stone, now stands in the nave.

"The red sandstone comes from the altar of the Protestant church, and the grey travertine from the altar of the Catholic church," Hübner explained. Both were crushed and cast together to form the new altar. Parts of its surface are completely smooth, while others remain rough, with visible grooves and fissures. "It was a beautiful symbol of the relationship between Protestants and Catholics. We want to come together. But there are still points of friction and unresolved questions."

Careful legal arrangements

St. Birgitta-Thomas Church in the northern German city of Kiel can likewise look back on decades of ecumenical cooperation. Since 1980, the Catholic parish of St. Birgitta and the Protestant Thomas congregation have shared both the church and the parish hall. Here, too, this "sharing" is governed by carefully defined legal arrangements.

Officially, the church belongs to the Catholic parish, while the parish hall belongs to the Protestant congregation. "But we use both parts of the complex jointly and on an equal footing," Pastor Rebekka Ulrich told DW. With a smile, she adds: "The Protestant side leased the printer, but the Catholic side uses it too."

The 36-year-old pastor sees "an incredible number of points of overlap." These include joint worship services, celebrations and ecumenical dialogue. Each year, the two denominations adopt a shared motto. A hymn of the month, selected alternately from the Protestant hymnal and the Catholic Gotteslob, is sung by the entire congregation during services.

In the ecumenical pastoral care center Emmaus in Bad Griesbach, Lower Bavaria, Protestants and Catholics share a common church space Image: Dietmar Stegmann

A shortage of clergymen and organists

The close partnership extends even to church music: both congregations share the same organist. "On Sundays, he accompanies the Catholic Mass at 9:30 a.m. and then the Protestant service at 11:00 a.m." If only everything were that simple. As Ulrich explains, the steadily declining number of Catholic priests is creating growing challenges for the Catholic side.

In Mannheim, Annette Hübner described the process as a journey that was long but, in her view, well worth the effort. The number of clergy is declining in both the Catholic and Protestant churches. At the local level, services of the Word conducted without a priest or pastor are becoming increasingly common.

Even the Eastern Christian tradition has found a place here. Since 1971, Mannheim has been home to the "Eastern Church Center Cyril and Methodius," which has been based at St. Pius from the very beginning. Once a month, a Catholic liturgy is celebrated according to the Byzantine Rite. Since the renovation, the church entrance area has included a specially designed space with icons and a symbolic iconostasis. All of this exists under a single church roof.

This article was translated from German.

The participants seemed overjoyed to leave their days of isolation Image: Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt e.V. (DLR)/dpa/picture alliance

Six men and women from six different countries on Friday ended their 100-day stay in cramped, artificially lit isolation as part of a study to prepare future space missions to the moon, Mars and beyond.

The participants, from Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Portugal, are now able to return to their daily lives — following a recovery phase — after leaving the simulation facility at the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) in the western city of Cologne.

The goal of the SOLIS100 study was conducted on behalf of the European Space Agency (ESA) and aimed to investigate the effects of long-duration space missions on health and performance.

The participants had to live from non-perishable foodstuffs and were not allowed personal contact with family or friends.



Every day, they carried out scientific work, medical data collection, a strict exercise program and station maintenance.

World.title: Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan as China braces for coming storm
World.content:
A typhoon is lashing Japan's south, causing injuries and blackouts. It is now headed for China, where ports have been closed in preparation.

Typhoon Dolphin raged over Japan's southern regions on Saturday, causing some injuries and blackouts.

Okinawa and Amami island in Kagoshima prefecture were the areas expected to be worst affected.

The storm is expected to move on to China, making landfall along its eastern and southern ‌coast between late Sunday and early Monday, with Chinese authorities shutting down ports and ferry services ahead of the storm.

What do we know about Typhoon Dolphin in Japan?

The typhoon has brought maximum sustained winds of 162 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour) and ​gusts reaching ‌216 kph

Authorities in Okinawa prefecture said 240 people had taken shelter at evacuation centers in the region on Friday

Five elderly people were reported to have suffered non-life-threatening injuries

Japan Meteorological Agency forecast strong winds, heavy rain and high waves in the Okinawa region through Sunday

The Naha Airport on Okinawa Island said it closed on Friday, and all domestic and international flights in and out of Naha, the prefectural capital, have been canceled

Power was cut to some 14,000 buildings in Okinawa

What preparations is China making for Typhoon Dolphin?

The China National Meteorological Centre Typhoon Dolphin has said Typhoon Dolphin will probably make landfall between the city of Zhoushan in Zhejiang province and the city of Fuding in Fujian province.

Zhejiang has raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level, while ceasing port operations and suspending 162 passenger ferry routes.

The storm is expected to bring rain and strong winds to eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, through August 12.

Some parts of eastern Zhejiang could be in for a deluge, forecasters say, with more than 600 mm (23.6 inches) of rain possible.

Ningbo ⁠Lishe ​International Airport in Zhejiang said it will stop its operations from 11:30 ​p.m. (1530 GMT) on Saturday and suspend all flights on Sunday.

Fishing boats in Wenling in Zhejiang province have sought shelter ahead of the storm Image: Zhou Xuejun/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

Taiwan-China tensions over typhoon restrictions

Taiwan, where 63 international flights have been cancelled, is also expected to experience heavy rain in the north over the weekend.

New political friction between Taiwan and China has also arisen after Beijing ordered that ships passing through ⁠the Taiwan Strait must heed ​its traffic control instructions amid the typhoon.

Taipei has slammed Beijing's injunctions as "ridiculous," saying that Beijing has no right to restrict access to international waters.

"The unreasonable and crude statement ‌by ​the relevant Chinese Communist departments reflects an ignorance, disregard, and trampling of international order and norms. It is utterly ridiculous!" Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said in a statement late ​on Friday.

China regards the democratically governed island as a breakaway territory of its own and also claims to own the strategic strait, a stance rejected by both Taipei and Washington.

World.title: Germany debates reintroducing mandatory civilian service
World.content:
Social organizations are skeptical about the government's ideas for a civilian service program that youths could choose as an alternative should Germany reinstate mandatory military conscription.

Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, guarantees that no person can be forced into armed military service. Should the government reinstate mandatory conscription, a civilian-service alternative would have to be established for people who invoke their right to refuse military service on moral grounds as conscientious objectors.

Germany's federal government is making arrangements for this. The Family Affairs Ministry, led by Karin Prien, of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), has confirmed that in recent months it reached out to 23 large associations and organizations to ask what capacities they had to offer if civilian service were reinstated. Of those, 22 indicated a general willingness to offer opportunities for civilian service participants.

Thorsten Frei, the parliamentary group leader of the center-right bloc of the CDU and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) in the Bundestag, told the German broadcasters RTL and ntv that it was "very clever and correct" for the Family Affairs Ministry to prepare in this way. However, Frei said, there are no new developments in the discussion surrounding the possible reinstatement of conscription.

Germany looks at conscription to boost military numbers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bundeswehr seeks soldiers

After lengthy negotiations, the coalition government of the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) agreed that military service would remain voluntary in Germany for now. Whether this remains the case will depend on how many soldiers the German armed forces, the Bundeswehr, can recruit in the coming months and years.

The goal is to increase the number of troops from 185,000 to at least 260,000 by 2030 in order to strengthen national defenses and fulfill NATO requirements. Or, as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) put it: The Bundeswehr should become the strongest conventional army in Europe.

The so-called new military service, which has been in force since the start of this year, is also expected to boost the recruitment effort. It combines improved conditions for volunteers with responsibilities applying to all 18-year-old men: They must fill out a questionnaire to answer if they would be prepared to serve in the army.

They are required to undergo medical examinations and to state whether they are interested in joining the armed forces. However, they maintain the constitutional right to refuse military service as conscientious objectors.

Bundeswehr applications increase

Even without reinstating compulsory military service, the recruitment drive is on track to reach its target for 2026, according to a June forecast by Germany's Defense Ministry. However, only about 530 young men have voluntarily signed up to the military as a direct result of the Bundeswehr questionnaire in 2026.

So, though a return to conscription is not currently expected, it remains an option for the government. Combined with civilian service, it was in place in Germany (starting in West Germany in 1956) until 2011, when it was suspended. However, it was not removed from the constitution. So, parliament can reactivate it by law if needed, for example if the country's security situation changes.

The alternative, mandatory civilian service (Zivildienst) usually involved working in a hospital or care home for several months.

This civilian service was replaced in 2011 by the Bundesfreiwilligendienst , or federal volunteer service, which is open to people of all ages and genders. Conscription only applied to men.

'Government-mandated cheap labor'

Major German welfare organizations have pledged their support should civilian service be relaunched. At the same time, they warn against false expectations. The general consensus is that civilian service is no fix for acute staff shortages in the social services sector. Instead of relying on obligation, the federal government should instead strengthen the optional engagement of young people.

"Our main wish is improved conditions for the voluntary services," Eva Maria Welskop-Deffaa, the president of the German Caritas Association , told the public broadcaster ARD. "And there is still a lot of room for improvement on that."



Imported care giver: Skilled, needed, stalled by bureaucracy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's opposition parties have also criticized a possible return to mandatory civilian service. According to the socialist Left Party, the state "should not dictate how young people spend a year of their lives," co-leader Ines Schwerdtner said. That applied to both military and civilian service. On the other side, young people should not serve as "stopgaps for a welfare state" which the government "has been systematically underfunding for years." Nursing care, emergency services and social institutions did not need "government-mandated cheap labor," Schwerdtner told the Funke media group.

In any case, the Family Affairs Ministry sees a need to revise and modernize the current civilian service law. It plans to present its proposals after Germany's summer recess.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy
World.content:
Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy. The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week.

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy?

The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy.

Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population."

Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years.

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

World.title: El interés compuesto también ayuda a comprar una casa: cómo invertir para ahorrar el dinero de la entrada
World.content:
Comprar una vivienda en España se ha convertido en una misión cada vez más complicada para muchas familias. La escasez de oferta, unida a la subida de los precios, impide a muchas personas, y especialmente a los más jóvenes, ahorrar el dinero necesario para la entrada a una casa. La mayoría de los bancos piden contar con al menos un 20% del precio del inmueble para conceder una hipoteca, al que hay que sumar impuestos y otros gastos. Para una vivienda de 300.000 euros, eso supone contar de antemano con 90.000, una cifra inalcanzable para la mayoría. Entre las opciones para reunir ese dinero, invertir puede ayudar a acelerar el proceso.

El punto de partida es conocer con qué plazo temporal se cuenta. No es lo mismo querer comprar una casa dentro de un año que dentro de diez. “Ahorrar para la entrada de una vivienda requiere de una estrategia de inversión alineada con el horizonte temporal. Cuanto más cercano sea el objetivo, más importante será priorizar la preservación de capital y reducir la volatilidad, mientras que, si el plazo es largo, tiene sentido asumir más riesgo para intentar obtener una mayor rentabilidad potencial”, explican fuentes de MyInvestor.

La primera regla que apuntan los expertos es automatizar el ahorro a través de aportaciones periódicas. La intención es construir poco a poco el ahorro y evitar que la inversión dependa de decisiones puntuales o del momento del mercado. Invertir una cantidad más o menos fija cada mes ayuda a comprar a distintos precios y reduce el riesgo de invertir todo el dinero justo antes de una caída brusca de las Bolsas. Para ello es importante hacer un presupuesto y calcular cuánto dinero se puede dedicar cada mes para hacer una aportación.

En segundo lugar, hay que elegir los productos adecuados en función del perfil de riesgo y el plazo temporal. Para plazos cortos, cuando la compra de la vivienda se prevé a uno o tres años vista, el margen es reducido. Por ello, los expertos aconsejan productos conservadores, con alta exposición a la renta fija y baja volatilidad. En este caso, el objetivo no es maximizar la rentabilidad, sino conservar el capital, evitando que una caída de mercado justo antes del momento de la desinversión para ejecutar la compra de la vivienda obligue a retrasar o renunciar a la operación. Para estas situaciones, MyInvestor cita algunos fondos como el Santalucía Pagarés BF (acumula una rentabilidad del 0,8% en 2026), el iShares Global Aggregate 1-5 Year Bond Index Fund (1,2% de rentabilidad en el año) o el Twelve Capital UCITS ICAV (3,1% en lo que va de 2026). El R-co Conviction Credit Euro es otra opción. Su rendimiento en el año es del 0,9%, pero de media desde su creación se sitúa en un 4,1% anual.

Hay que tener en cuenta que las ganancias en estos productos no serán espectaculares; es más, si no se eligen bien, su rentabilidad quedará reducida a la mínima expresión por las comisiones. En plazos cortos, el inversor debe buscar una alternativa mejor que tener el dinero parado en el banco, pero sin asumir grandes oscilaciones del mercado. Si se cuenta ya con una parte importante de la entrada y se espera comprar en poco tiempo, la prioridad es que el dinero esté disponible y no sufra pérdidas.

Horizonte temporal

Para horizontes algo más amplios, de entre tres y cinco años, el abanico de posibilidades aumenta. En estos plazos es posible asumir más riesgo mediante fondos de inversión mixtos o carteras diversificadas que combinan renta fija y renta variable. “Para objetivos a medio plazo, la estrategia puede requerir un equilibrio entre crecimiento y estabilidad. Los inversores pueden seguir necesitando cierta exposición a activos de crecimiento, como la renta variable, aunque con un mayor énfasis en la diversificación y la gestión del riesgo de caídas”, apuntan desde Vanguard. Algunas de las opciones que se encuentran en el mercado pueden ser el fondo Cobas Renta FI (ofrece una rentabilidad del 6,5% en los últimos años) o el Gamma Global FI (con una rentabilidad media cercana al 7%). Ambos cuentan con cinco estrellas de valoración en Morningstar.

Por dar una idea de cuánto dinero se puede obtener invirtiendo en este tipo de productos, un ahorrador que cuente con 10.000 euros e invierta 300 al mes durante cinco años con una rentabilidad media anual del 4% contaría al final del periodo con 32.000 euros, frente a los 28.000 que supondría no hacer nada con ese dinero. Con una rentabilidad del 6%, alcanzaría unos 34.200 euros. Y con un 8%, rondaría los 36.600 euros. En este caso, las subidas tampoco son espectaculares. Se trata de un impulso y una ayuda extra, pero invertir no hace milagros si el plazo es corto y las aportaciones son reducidas.

En los plazos superiores a cinco años, la renta variable puede ganar protagonismo. Un horizonte largo permite asumir más riesgo porque hay más tiempo para compensar las caídas que se vayan produciendo en el mercado. Y el potencial de rentabilidad también es mayor. En este caso, los expertos mencionan el fondo MyInvestor Value, con una rentabilidad anual media del 7%. También el iShares Developed World Index, que ha registrado una rentabilidad anual del 12%, o el iShares US Equity Index Fund con una rentabilidad del 13,8%. Estos últimos son fondos cotizados que replican índices, con la ventaja de sus comisiones son muy bajas.

De nuevo, por dar una idea, una inversión inicial de 10.000 euros, con aportaciones de 300 al mes y una rentabilidad anual media del 8%, el dinero acumulado al cabo de cinco años sería de unos 36.600 euros. A diez años, crecería hasta unos 75.600 euros. En ese mismo plazo de tiempo, si la aportación mensual fuera algo superior, de 500 euros, y se mantiene una rentabilidad media anual del 8%, el dinero con el que contaría al final se elevaría por encima de los 111.000 euros, suficiente para esa ansiada entrada. Hay que tener en cuenta que es necesario pasar por Hacienda, que se quedará con entre el 19% y el 30% de las plusvalías.

De todas formas, es importante tener en cuenta que se trata de un ejercicio hipotético. La rentabilidad nunca está garantizada. Las Bolsas pueden subir a doble dígito en un año favorable y caer también a doble dígito en años adversos. Por ello es importante mantener la constancia y evitar dejarse llevar por los nervios. “Las fluctuaciones de mercado son inevitables. Mantener la disciplina en lugar de reaccionar a la volatilidad de corto plazo es esencial para alcanzar los objetivos a largo plazo”, apuntan desde Vanguard.

Una carrera de fondo

Tan importante como invertir es saber desinvertir. A medida que se acerca el momento de comprar la vivienda, conviene reducir el riesgo. Quien ha acumulado durante años una cartera con alto peso en Bolsa, no debería llegar a la firma de las arras expuesto a una caída importante del mercado. Una caída del 10% o del 15% puede ser asumible cuando quedan diez años para comprar, pero no cuando la vivienda ya está elegida y el comprador necesita el dinero de forma inminente. En ese sentido, los expertos recomiendan hacer una transición desde la renta variable hacia alternativas de muy bajo riesgo, como depósitos remunerados, fondos monetarios o soluciones de ahorro conservador. El objetivo es tener el dinero listo para aportar la ansiada entrada.

Los gestores también recomiendan evitar varios errores típicos. El primero de ellos, invertir sin tener los objetivos definidos. Sin una meta concreta, resulta complicado establecer el nivel adecuado de riesgo, el horizonte temporal o los productos que más convienen. No es lo mismo querer ahorrar para una casa, para un coche o con vistas a la jubilación. Otro error es asumir un riesgo inadecuado. Los inversores con objetivos a corto plazo pueden pecar de ambiciosos y exponerse a una volatilidad peligrosa. Y al revés, los inversores a largo plazo pueden pecar de conservadores y limitar la rentabilidad que buscan. El otro error habitual es tomar decisiones basadas en emociones. Los vaivenes de la Bolsa pueden llevar a vender en el peor momento posible, amplificando pérdidas, o comprar cuando los mercados ya han subido, limitando las ganancias.

La recomendación que apuntan los gestores es comenzar cuanto antes a invertir para que alcanzar el objetivo de ahorro sea más sencillo. “Comenzar a invertir cuanto antes aumenta la probabilidad de éxito al permitir más tiempo para beneficiarse de la capitalización compuesta y reducir la necesidad de asumir riesgos excesivos más adelante. Como suele decirse, el mejor momento para empezar a invertir era ayer, el segundo mejor momento es hoy”, concluyen los expertos de Vanguard.

Para planificar el futuro a largo plazo, cada vez más entidades financieras lanzan productos de ahorro e inversión dirigidos a menores. En ese sentido, es una opción interesante para que, cuando estén en disposición de comprar una vivienda, tengan un ahorro previo. Una inversión inicial de 1.000 euros para un recién nacido, con aportaciones de 100 euros al mes y una rentabilidad estimada del 7% anual, se convertiría en unos 87.000 euros cuando cumpla los 25 años, la edad con la que muchos jóvenes se incorporan al mercado laboral. De ese dinero, 56.000 serían los intereses generados. De nuevo se trata de una simulación y ese dinero nunca está garantizado. Pero empezar a invertir antes puede marcar la diferencia.

World.title: Una sola semana de calor abrasador causó 9.600 muertes en Alemania en junio
World.content:
Las temperaturas extremas que se vivieron en Alemania a finales de junio dejaron más muertos de lo que se había estimado hasta ahora y más que en cualquier año completo desde 2016. En total, se produjeron 9.600 fallecimientos relacionados con el calor entre el 22 y el 28 de junio, según ha informado este jueves el Instituto Robert Koch (RKI).

Asimismo, según estas cifras, el número de fallecimientos relacionados con el calor este año asciende, hasta la fecha, a unos 11.900. Así pues, la mayor parte de las muertes se debe a los días de temperaturas extremas de finales de junio, en los que se superaron incluso los 40 grados en algunas zonas, algo nunca visto en el país. De este modo, este año ya han fallecido por este motivo muchas más personas que en cualquier año completo desde 2016. Hasta ahora, el 2018 había sido el de mayor número de fallecidos, con unas 8.900 víctimas estimadas a lo largo de todo el año. Hay que tener en cuenta también que la situación continúa Alemania, donde este fin de semana se esperan máximas de entre 29 y 36 grados, por lo que es probable que la cifra siga creciendo hasta el final del verano.

Los datos del RKI se basan, entre otras cosas, en el seguimiento de las cifras de fallecimientos de la Oficina Federal de Estadística (Destatis) y en la información de 52 estaciones meteorológicas del Servicio Meteorológico Alemán (DWD). Dado que el cálculo de las muertes por esta causa se basa en un modelo estadístico, existe un margen de incertidumbre, que hace que la cifra pueda ser incluso mayor de lo estimado. Por eso, el número de 5.100 muertos, de los cuales 4.310 correspondían a la última semana de junio cuando tuvo lugar la intensa ola de calor, publicado a principios de julio ha aumentado ahora más del doble. Además, para justificar estos datos considerablemente más elevados, el instituto explicó que los efectos de la ola de calor de junio no se habían hecho evidentes hasta ahora “en su totalidad”, ya que las cifras de mortalidad de los estados federados se publican con un retraso de cinco semanas y también al hecho de que “en Alemania apenas se habían registrado temperaturas de tal magnitud, o no se habían registrado en absoluto”.

“En algunos casos, como por ejemplo en el golpe de calor, la exposición provoca la muerte de forma inmediata, mientras que en la mayoría de los casos es la combinación de la exposición y enfermedades preexistentes lo que conduce a la muerte”, explicaron los expertos del RKI. “Por ello, el calor no suele figurar en el certificado de defunción como causa subyacente de la muerte. En su lugar, es necesario aplicar métodos estadísticos para estimar la magnitud de las muertes relacionadas con el calor”. Por lo tanto, se calcula comparando el número de fallecimientos en las semanas de verano con y sin olas de calor.

En Alemania, un país nada preparado para hacer frente a temperaturas extremas, este fenómeno provoca habitualmente un aumento de la mortalidad. Las olas de calor son especialmente peligrosas para las personas mayores. La mayoría de los fallecimientos del total registrado hasta el momento fueron personas de 85 años o más; unos 6.060 fallecidos. Además, casi 3.000 de los que perdieron la vida a causa del calor tenían entre 75 y 84 años, y casi 1.800, entre 65 y 74 años. En el caso de los menores de 65 años, se registraron algo más de 1.100 muertes.

Normalmente, según los científicos, el aumento de la mortalidad debido al calor se hace evidente a partir de una temperatura media semanal de 20 grados, es decir, la media de las temperaturas diurnas y nocturnas de una semana. Del 22 al 28 de junio, la temperatura media semanal en todo el país fue de 26,4 grados. En todos los estados federados se registró esa semana una temperatura media superior a los 20 grados.

De acuerdo con el DWD, el mes de junio de 2026, con una media de 19,5 grados, fue el segundo más cálido desde que se tienen registros. Solo junio de 2019 fue más cálido. Además, la noche del 27 al 28 de junio fue, según los datos actuales, la más cálida desde que se tienen registros. El servicio meteorológico registró en varias ocasiones temperaturas superiores a los 41 grados. El 27 de junio, 46 estaciones de toda Alemania superaron la barrera de los 40 grados.

El Colegio Federal de Médicos, unas 80 organizaciones sanitarias europeas más, junto con numerosas asociaciones ecologistas, exigen a Alemania y a la UE que redoblen sus esfuerzos en materia de protección. “La declaración de la emergencia climática debe traducirse en compromisos vinculantes y el calor extremo debe reconocerse como un grave peligro para la salud”, indicaron en un comunicado las entidades. Los médicos exigen, entre otras cosas, que los centros de asistencia, las guarderías y los colegios se adapten a las condiciones climáticas. La mayoría de hospitales y clínicas no cuenta con aire acondicionado, ni siquiera tienen persianas que puedan proteger las habitaciones del sol directo. Solo existen normas claras para que haya aire en los quirófanos o en el servicio de radiología, ya que los equipos, sencillamente, no soportan el calor. Tampoco las residencias de ancianos o de cuidados están preparadas y las temperaturas pueden superar los 30 grados por la noche en las habitaciones de muchas personas mayores, como sucedió recientemente.

Pero habilitar los centros hospitalarios y residencias cuesta mucho dinero y estos espacios se enfrentan desde hace años a retos financieros cada vez mayores. La reciente reforma hospitalaria plantea actualmente a los centros de salud grandes incertidumbres financieras. Las inversiones adicionales en sistemas de aire acondicionado, al margen de las unidades de cuidados intensivos —que en su mayoría ya cuentan con refrigeración— parecen utópicas en estos momentos.

En este contexto de temperaturas extremas y de sequía, que no solo aumenta el riesgo de incendios forestales, sino que también provoca nuevos mínimos históricos en ríos como el Rin y el Elba, la asociación de Fridays for Future ha convocado para este jueves por la tarde una manifestación a las puertas de la Cancillería de Berlín para reclamar un plan para estar mejor preparados ante futuros contextos similares a los recientes. “Toda Alemania sufre olas de calor sin precedentes. Cada semana aumenta el número de víctimas mortales, mientras que en España y Francia cientos de miles de personas se ven obligadas a huir de enormes incendios forestales”, escribieron en la convocatoria. Además, una amplia alianza formada por asociaciones de protección de la naturaleza, organizaciones sociales y sindicatos exigió la celebración de una cumbre nacional sobre este problema.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Football club Ajax, bank ING and eyewear chain Ace & Tate have been caught up in the data breach at logistics firm CEVA Logistics, which came to light this week when Bol and De Bijenkorf warned customers their details may have been exposed.

CEVA handles deliveries for the companies and had access to the customer data needed to fulfil orders. The firm says it cannot rule out that personal details were leaked, although the companies affected say no payment details, usernames or passwords were taken.

Whether addresses, email addresses or phone numbers were exposed remains unclear.

At ING, the breach affects customers who ordered physical products through the bank’s rewards points scheme.

Ajax has advised supporters to be extra alert to phishing messages in the coming weeks. The club and Ace & Tate have both reported the breach to privacy watchdog AP, as Bol did earlier this week.

Ace & Tate has warned customers that current orders may be delayed, although online ordering is still running. CEVA said it would respond to the breach at a later stage.

World.title: Actor Peter Faber, star of Dutch cinema’s golden age, dies at 82
World.content:
Peter Faber, one of the best-known faces of Dutch film and theatre for half a century, has died at the age of 82.

Faber was admitted to hospital in early July with breathing difficulties related to untreatable heart problems, his family told news agency ANP.

He broke through in the 1970s, widely regarded as the golden age of Dutch cinema, with roles in Keetje Tippel and Paul Verhoeven’s wartime classic Soldaat van Oranje – the film that later spawned the long-running musical which closed last month after 16 years.

He also took the title role in the 1976 film of Max Havelaar, Multatuli’s classic novel about Dutch colonial rule, and appeared alongside Sean Connery and Anthony Hopkins in Richard Attenborough’s A Bridge Too Far.

Faber began his career as a co-founder of Het Werkteater, an Amsterdam collective set up in the early 1970s to shake up Dutch theatre with performances about ordinary people and recognisable emotions. He won the Louis d’Or, the top Dutch theatre prize for a male actor, twice.

He kept working into his eighties. His final film role came in 2023 in Sweet Dreams, the Dutch entry for the 2024 Oscars, in which he appeared alongside his son Jesse.

Faber often spoke about his difficult upbringing, part of which he spent living on the streets of Amsterdam as a teenager. In 2008 he set up the Peter Faber Foundation to help young people build confidence, and to “make the switch from destructive to creative energy”. Its motto is “I can do it, I want it, I’m doing it. Now!”

A public memorial service will be held at Het Zonnehuis in Amsterdam-Noord on Monday between 10am and midday.

World.title: Cabinet rules out compensation for drought-hit businesses
World.content:
Despite the country’s continuing water shortage, entrepreneurs feeling the squeeze won’t be receiving any help from the government any time soon.

“There are arrangements in place for the event of a natural disaster, such as the flooding in Limburg in 2021, but we are not there yet,” infrastructure and water management minister Vincent Karremans said while visiting Nijmegen on Thursday.

“We don’t have the money in the account either. We can’t help it that it isn’t raining.”

Maarten Ouboter, a technician for the Amstel, Gooi and Vecht water authority, told DutchNews: “The question is: how much is a government – the public – responsible for the weather? The minister was clear: droughts can happen.”

Low water levels are hurting everyone from inland vessels that can’t sail down dwindling rivers to houseboat owners on the Rhine who have effectively been marooned. Several locks have been closed, ferries have been cancelled and the economically important Twente Canal, reported broadcaster NOS, is also inaccessible.

And while Karremans estimates that the economic damage to businesses runs “into the tens, if not hundreds of millions of euros”, he views the water shortage as an “entrepreneurial risk, after all” – not a natural disaster.

A shortage but not a crisis

For now, the country’s water level remains at 2 – a shortage but not yet a crisis. That could change if the drought continues for another few weeks. But the government maintains its priorities are preserving the country’s dikes and ensuring enough available drinking water, not propping up businesses.

“We are now at a point that the rivers flowing into our low-lying delta have never been so low in August,” said Ouboter, who focuses on the Amsterdam area. “We are comparable to 1947, but that was in November.”

Using a football analogy, he said the drought “in June was ‘second league’; in July it was ‘first league’; in August, it’s Champions League.”

Boosting water storage

Karremans said more water must be stored for the future, including in places like the IJsselmeer and the Volkerak-Zoommeer. The cabinet is currently working on the Freshwater Delta Plan to ensure rainwater captured in the spring, for example, can be used in drier months.

In Amsterdam, an innovative system of wadis – dry water ditches – catches rainwater that can be distributed later where needed and also absorbs extra rainwater to prevent flooding.

“The way we think about water has changed,” said Ton Hilhorst, the chief garden designer at Amsterdam’s Artis zoo. “Water was always seen as the enemy, but now we must keep it in the country, not pump it out.”

Weather forecasters are predicting another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with rain unlikely in the current week.

World.title: Philip Morris rebuked over AI campaign against EU tobacco rules
World.content:
The Dutch advertising standards watchdog RCC has reprimanded tobacco behemoth Philip Morris for an AI-powered ad campaign that it says violated the country’s tobacco advertising ban.

As the EU prepares its biggest tobacco tightening rules in 15 years, the public was invited to share its views via comments.

But a recent investigation by broadcaster NOS and the journalism platform Pointer found that Philip Morris used AI to generate hundreds of fake “citizen” responses opposing tougher EU rules on vapes, which along with other cigarette alternatives like e-cigarettes and heated tobacco, now account for 40% of the company’s revenue.

Here’s how the campaign worked: Philip Morris put up yellow posters carrying QR codes in tobacco shops under the slogan “Your Voice Your Choice.” Scanning the code led to a tool that asked multiple-choice questions and then an option to write a first-person text, which users could then send to the Commission.

The investigation found that some 71% of responses from the Netherlands were written by AI, the second highest after Portugal.

The RCC had several problems with the campaign, including that the text generator was paid for and owned by Philip Morris. The company defended its actions by saying it contributed to the public debate.

“The fact that the statements are framed as a call for public consultation does not detract from their commercial character,” said the watchdog.

The written responses also portray alternative tobacco products positively, which the RCC says constitutes advertising and therefore violates the tobacco advertising ban.

Doctors

In June, a group of doctors and healthcare campaign groups made a formal complaint to the RCC, saying the “misleading” campaign used an AI tool to influence European decision-making on tobacco and nicotine products.

Lawyer Laura van Gijn, who represents the doctors, told NOS that violating the tobacco advertising ban is a criminal offence. “This decision is a clear signal to the tobacco industry that digital influence campaigns do not fall outside the scope of the advertising ban, even when packaged as citizen participation. This precedent is relevant for similar campaigns elsewhere in Europe.”

World.title: No more “shame lips”: Dutch dictionary adds new word for labia
World.content:
Women’s rights groups are applauding the latest addition to the definitive Dutch dictionary Dikke Van Dale of the word labia: vulvalippen, added alongside the word schaamlippen.

While both words mean labia, the old schaamlippen translates as “shame lips”, which the organisations say is stigmatising as compared to the more neutral “vulva lips”.

“We should just mention these parts in our education with children and young people,” artist Esther van der Valk told broadcaster NOS. “People now know that this is a normal word, and with that we can break the taboo.”

Van der Valk is a member of Dolle Mina, the women’s rights group that was founded in the Netherlands in 1969 and has been advocating for the inclusion of vulvalippen in the Dutch dictionary to counter stigmatisation. They’re joined by Schaamteloos, a more recent campaign seeking to change language and attitudes regarding female anatomy.

Body positive

While schaamlippen will remain in the dictionary, the addition of vulvalippen means the word gets official Dutch language status – proof, say the activists, that the normalisation of sexuality via language can be achieved if enough people want it.

Schaamlippen is not the only word where shame is embedded in its name. There’s schaamhaar – “shame hair” – which is the name for pubic hair, schaambeen (shame bone) for pubic bone and even schaamstreek (shame area) for pubic area.

But Schaamteloos says it had to start somewhere, so it picked schaamlippen. “Everyone has pubic hair, a pubic bone, and a pubic area,” says the group, but “only half of us have labia – or ‘shame lips’ … which adds to a disproportionately large amount of trouble due to the taboo on talking about this.”

While some doctors and even the media have taken to using vulvalippen, it’s not yet part of the everyday Dutch vernacular.

That may change when the new anatomically correct word is included in the Dikke van Dale. That’s expected to happen during its next online update, likely this Autumn.

World.title: Four arrested for death threat against Breda mayor
World.content:
Police have arrested four men suspected of threatening to kill Breda mayor Paul Depla, after a photograph found on a football supporter’s phone revealed new evidence for a case that had stalled.

A banner bearing the words “Depla Dood” (Depla dead) was hung on the front of a café in the city’s Meidoornstraat on March 8, when NAC Breda played Feyenoord. Depla reported the threat to the police, but in May prosecutors said the case had halted because the suspects could not be linked to the banner.

A breakthrough came when several NAC supporters were arrested over rioting around the club’s match against Heerenveen on May 10 and their phones were seized, police said. On one of them, officers found a photograph of the banner in which four men could be identified.

The four – three from Breda, aged 16, 32 and 34, and a 24-year-old from Oosterhout – were arrested on Thursday and will be questioned. Threatening a public official carries a maximum prison sentence of four years.

It is unclear what prompted the threat, but broadcaster NOS reported it may have followed a warning from the city council to a different café, which had planned to host a pre-match party for the club’s hardcore supporters.

When the owners called the party off, the group gathered at the Meidoornstraat café instead, where the banner was hung.

Threats and intimidation against Dutch public officials are a growing concern. Some 45% of local and regional political office holders, including mayors, told a 2024 home affairs ministry survey they had faced aggression in the preceding year.

World.title: Warm, dry weekend ahead as drought shows no sign of ending
World.content:
The Netherlands is set for another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with barely a drop of rain likely for the coming week, according to forecasters.

Friday will be calm and dry with temperatures of 21 to 25°, with morning cloud in the north east giving way to sunshine. Saturday will be sunny and slightly warmer, at 25 to 28°, before temperatures climb to around 30° inland on Sunday.

A brief cooler spell will push maximums down to around 25° on Tuesday, but forecasters expect the warmth to return later in the week – without any significant rain.

The dry spell means no let-up for the ongoing drought, which has pushed the Rhine to record low levels and prompted water use restrictions in several regions.

World.title: Childcare benefits falling short for most parents: CBS
World.content:
Almost two-thirds of parents who claim childcare benefits pay more than the government’s maximum hourly rate, leaving them with hundreds of euros in costs the benefit does not cover, according to national statistics agency CBS.

Parents claiming the benefit spent an average of €10,510 on childcare in 2025, of which 68% was covered, up from 65% in 2024. The benefit was raised in both years as a step towards the government plan for near-free childcare.

But childcare providers are free to set their own fees, and the benefit only applies to costs up to a ceiling fixed by the government each year. In 2025, 63% of parents paid more than the maximum rate for at least one child.

On average, parents paid €3,340 towards childcare themselves last year – €2,860 in regular contributions, plus an extra €480 to cover fees above the official maximum.

The share of parents paying over the ceiling varies widely. In Nunspeet, Bloemendaal, Houten and Midden-Delfland, almost 90% pay more than the maximum rate, compared with just 8% on the island of Ameland. The proportion is highest in the provinces of Utrecht and Noord-Holland and lowest in Friesland and Groningen.

Households in the lowest income group paid an average of €1,190 towards childcare, or 11% of the total cost, while the highest earners paid €5,950, just over half the bill.

In total, 719,000 parents claimed the benefit last year for nearly 1.1 million children. More children attended nurseries and after-school clubs, while the number looked after by registered childminders (gastouders) fell by 10,000 to around 95,000.

The cabinet plans to make childcare almost free for working parents from 2029, covering 96% of costs regardless of income – a scheme that has been repeatedly delayed.

World.title: Candidate to lead Polish state history institute rejected in rare clash between houses of parliament
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The nominee, Mateusz Szpytma, has served as deputy head of the IPN since 2016, including when it was under the leadership of Karol Nawrocki, who last year was elected president of Poland with the support of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Szpytma’s candidacy has been opposed by most of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, who argue he helped politicise the IPN under the former PiS government. However, some more conservative elements of the coalition joined the opposition in supporting Szpytma, giving him a majority in the Sejm but not the Senate. Senatorowie nie wyrazili zgody na powołanie Mateusza Szpytmy na Prezesa Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej – Komisji Ścigania Zbrodni przeciwko Narodowi Polskiemu — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) August 6, 2026 The IPN is a body tasked with researching, documenting and educating about Poland’s tumultuous and tragic 20th-century history. It also has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when the country was under Nazi and communist rule. The institute was led by Nawrocki from 2021 until August last year, when he became president of Poland. Since then, the IPN has been without a permanent head. Last October, the IPN’s council nominated Karol Polejowski, another of the institute’s deputy heads, to be its new president. But he was rejected by the Sejm, which, along with the Senate, must approve the choice. In April, the council instead recommended Szpytma, whose candidacy was approved by the Sejm last month. He received support mainly from opposition parties, including PiS and the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, in a rare split within the ruling coalition, one of its junior members, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), also backed Szpytma, as did some MPs from the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050). That was enough to give him a majority. By contrast, the main ruling party, Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), and The Left (Lewica) opposed his nomination, citing a letter signed earlier this year by 170 academics, who described Szpytma as “one of the faces of IPN’s politicisation” under the former PiS government. However, PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who also serves as Poland’s defence minister and deputy prime minister rejected that characterisation and said that PSL had backed Szpytma because of his work commemorating historical figures from the agrarian movement in which PSL is rooted. In a rare split in the ruling coalition, MPs from two parties, PSL and Poland 2050, voted with the opposition in the Sejm for a new head of the Institute of National Remembrance. However, PM Donald Tusk says their choice will be rejected by the Senate https://t.co/0CGmbsNp4F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 However, it was widely expected that Szpytma’s candidacy would be blocked by the upper-house Senate, where even the PSL and opposition combined do not have a majority in the 100-seat chamber. That was confirmed in a vote on Thursday, when 50 senators were opposed to Szyptma and only 38 were in favour, with one abstention. “We voted against further politicisation” of IPN and “against tolerating financial irregularities”, wrote the speaker of the Senate, Małgorzata Kidawa-Błonska of KO. The latter comment was likely a reference to a report by the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) last year which found that the IPN had, between 2022 and 2025, failed to properly manage tens of millions of zloty in spending, including various violations of regulations on the use of public funds. Szpytma told journalists that he was not surprised by the result of the vote, saying he believes his connection to Nawrocki, who is an ardent opponent of the current government and has vetoed a record number of laws, is the reason why he lost. Nie zgodziliśmy się w Senacie, by człowiek Karola Nawrockiego został prezesem IPN. Zagłosowaliśmy przeciw dalszemu upolitycznianiu Instytutu. Przeciw tolerowaniu nieprawidłowości finansowych. Pan Szpytma nie wprowadziłby żadnych zmian w funkcjonowaniu IPN. — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) August 6, 2026 The IPN plays an important role in Polish public life, including in commemorating, investigating and prosecuting crimes that took place during the Nazi-German and Soviet occupations of Poland in World War Two, as well as during the decades of communist rule afterwards. Under Nawrocki’s leadership, the IPN accelerated the process of demolishing remaining Soviet monuments in Poland, often prompting criticism from Russia. It has also been closely involved in the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during World War Two. During PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023, the IPN was accused of becoming increasingly politicised, using its activities to support the historical narratived promoted by the government. In 2021, Israel protested after a former far-right activist was appointed to head one of the IPN’s local branches. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement.
