World.title: US Senate backs huge tariffs on Russian energy buyers – Hungary could be in the firing line
World.content:
The US Senate has overwhelmingly approved a major new Russia sanctions package that could impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries buying Russian oil and natural gas, potentially putting Hungary in the firing line.

The bill, named in honour of the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, passed by an 86-11 vote on Friday. According to CNN, it would introduce mandatory sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian oligarchs and state-owned companies, as well as foreign businesses supporting Russia’s defence industry.

However, one of the most significant elements of the legislation is the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from some of the largest buyers of Russian energy.

Hungary could be among the countries affected

The legislation targets the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas. China and India are expected to be the most significant countries affected, but Hungary could also find itself on the list.

Hungary remains heavily dependent on Russian energy. According to European Commission data, Russian gas accounted for around 74 per cent of Hungary’s gas imports in 2025. The country’s dependence on Russian oil is even greater, with Russian crude reportedly accounting for more than 90 per cent of Hungary’s total oil imports last year.

The proposed legislation could therefore create a significant problem for Budapest. There is, however, an important potential exemption concerning natural gas. Countries importing less than 15 per cent of Russia’s total gas exports could avoid the additional tariffs if they are also taking significant steps to reduce their dependence on Russian gas.

This distinction is important for Hungary. Although Russian gas makes up a large share of Hungary’s own imports, Hungary’s total purchases represent only a fraction of Russia’s overall gas exports. The country could therefore potentially meet the first condition for an exemption. The second condition could prove more difficult.

Budapest would need to show it is reducing Russian energy dependence

The European Commission has acknowledged that Hungary has signed long-term gas supply agreements with American and European companies. Once deliveries begin, these contracts could cover around 12 per cent of Hungary’s annual gas consumption.

Nevertheless, Brussels has assessed Hungary’s overall progress in reducing its dependence on Russian energy as limited. That could become crucial if the US legislation is ultimately adopted in its current form.

Washington would have to decide whether Hungary’s efforts to diversify its gas supplies are sufficient to qualify for the exemption. In other words, simply arguing that Hungary does not import 15 per cent of Russia’s total gas exports may not be enough.

The situation is potentially more serious when it comes to oil. Unlike natural gas, the proposed legislation does not provide a similar 15 per cent exemption for Russian crude oil. Hungary imported roughly 5–5.5 million tonnes of Russian crude in 2025, equivalent to approximately 100,000–110,000 barrels a day.

Although the temporary shutdown of the Druzhba oil pipeline has forced Hungary to seek alternative supplies this year, Russian crude remains by far the dominant source of oil for the country.

Have you read this? PM Magyar: After Ukraine war, EU will return to Russian gas

Trump could still grant exemptions

There are several factors that could soften the impact of the legislation. The proposed tariffs would initially target countries that knowingly continue making new purchases of Russian oil or gas from the 30th day after the legislation takes effect.

The US President would also retain the power to grant exemptions to individual countries, provided the administration explains why doing so would be in the interests of the United States. This could become particularly relevant in Hungary’s case.

The former Hungarian government has previously claimed that Budapest secured a full and open-ended exemption from US sanctions affecting Russian energy delivered through the TurkStream gas pipeline and the Druzhba oil pipeline.

However, it’s unclear whether that earlier arrangement would automatically protect Hungary from the new tariff mechanism. The proposed legislation could create a separate legal framework specifically targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy.

A very different bill from the original proposal

The measure has changed substantially during more than a year of negotiations. The original version unveiled in 2025 was considerably tougher and reportedly envisaged minimum tariffs of 500 per cent, with far fewer exemptions. The latest version reduces the potential tariff to 100 per cent and gives the US Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, a key role in determining the final tariff rate.

The bill also gives the Trump administration considerable discretion over whether and how aggressively to implement the measures. Some senators had raised concerns that the legislation could hand the US administration excessive power to impose tariffs. An amendment seeking changes to the tariff provisions was ultimately rejected.

Zelenskyy watched the Senate vote

The timing of the vote carried particular significance. Graham had spent more than a year working on the sanctions package and announced in Kyiv, just one day before his death, that an agreement had finally been reached with the White House and his Senate allies.

Following his death, colleagues described the legislation as one of his most important political achievements. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended Graham’s funeral in Washington and subsequently met senators at the Capitol. He also watched the procedural vote from the Senate gallery.

Zelenskyy has argued that stronger sanctions against Russia could both restrict Moscow’s ability to finance its war and send an important message to Ukraine and Europe.

Zelensky and Trump in the White House on 28 July 2026. Photo: Anadolu Agency

Never miss a headline: join our newly-launched Messenger group!

The bill still needs House approval

Despite the Senate vote, the new sanctions are not yet law. The legislation must still pass the US House of Representatives before it can reach the President. The House is currently on its summer recess and is not expected to return until September.

This gives Hungary and other potentially affected countries additional time to lobby Washington and seek changes or exemptions. For Budapest, however, the Senate vote is already a warning sign: if the legislation becomes law in anything close to its current form, Hungary’s continued reliance on Russian oil and gas could expose it to significant new US trade pressure.

World.title: 18-year-old Hungarian man suspected of killing Austrian man in anti-gay attack
World.content:
An 18-year-old Hungarian man is suspected of killing a 29-year-old Austrian man in Lower Austria, with investigators examining the possibility that the attack was motivated by the victim’s sexual orientation.

The victim was found dead early on Thursday in a house in Langenzersdorf, north of Vienna. The Hungarian suspect was arrested at the scene and reportedly gave a full confession on Friday. According to Austrian newspaper Krone Zeitung’s report, the two men had met online and arranged to meet at a house in Langenzersdorf while its owners were away.

Police investigate possible hate crime

The Korneuburg Public Prosecutor’s Office has confirmed that the case is being investigated as a possible hate crime. Spokesperson Gudrun Bischof told Austrian media that investigators believe the victim’s perceived sexual orientation may have been a motive for the killing.

The suspect reportedly lured the 29-year-old man to the house, which he was looking after in the absence of the owners. According to reports, the victim suffered severe injuries to his face and died at the scene.

Krone reported that the suspect practised taekwondo and allegedly used his martial arts skills during the crime. No weapon has been found, according to the report. Police were called to the property after an emergency alert. When officers arrived, the older man was lying on the floor with severe facial injuries and could no longer be saved.

The 18-year-old was arrested without resistance.

Links to ‘paedophile hunter’ groups

Austrian media have reported that the Hungarian suspect was allegedly associated with so-called “paedophile hunter” circles.

These groups claim to target paedophiles, but authorities have previously linked some of them to attacks on gay men based on the false equation of homosexuality with paedophilia.

According to reports, members of such groups have used social media to identify and lure men they believe to be gay before confronting, humiliating, assaulting or robbing them.

Austria has previously investigated similar attacks

The case comes amid wider scrutiny in Austria of groups accused of carrying out attacks under the guise of “paedophile hunting”.

A series of raids launched at the request of prosecutors in Graz last year across seven Austrian provinces resulted in numerous arrests. Those targeted included people suspected of hate crimes and individuals allegedly involved in attacks against members of the LGBTQ+ community.

Investigators in those cases reportedly uncovered allegations of victims being robbed, humiliated and physically assaulted, in some cases seriously.

According to HVG, following the death in Langenzersdorf, Austrian LGBTQ+ rights organisation HOSI Wien, the Social Democratic Party (SPÖ) and the Greens have called for the country’s national action plan against hate crime to be fully implemented as soon as possible.

The case is being investigated as a suspected murder and possible hate crime.

World.title: New Hungarian foreign-policy priorities set out for relations with Putin’s Russia, MAGA world, EU, V4, NATO and Balkans
World.content:
What is underway at the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs may prove to be more than a simple change of leadership: it could amount to a restructuring that reaches to the institution’s foundations.

The institute has been transferred from the Prime Minister’s Office back to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Its new director-general is Botond Feledy, while András Rácz has been appointed his deputy, responsible for research and academic affairs.

Botond Feledy (l) and András Rácz (r) Photo: Prtscr/Youtube

Both researchers have been outspoken critics of the Orbán governments in recent years, condemning their confrontational approach towards the EU and conspicuously close ties with Russia. In an interview, they have now outlined the priorities they believe should guide Hungary’s foreign policy — and the role they envisage for a revitalised Institute of International Affairs.

A complete break with Orbán’s foreign policy

Feledy told InfoRádió that the institute was being rebuilt “from the ground up”. The aim is to create a background institution that does more than communicate political decisions after they have been taken. Instead, it would support the Foreign Ministry with analysis and expertise before decisions are made, bringing perspectives into the process that are less prominent within the ministry’s own structure.

In an interview with 444, also published yesterday, the pair said they were planning a complete break with the American- and MAGA-focused foreign policy direction associated with Balázs Orbán, the Prime Minister’s political director. Rather than operating along ideological lines, the new leadership wants the institute to focus on preparing decisions and to draw a clear distinction between professional analysis and political propaganda.

Orbán and Trump in the White House. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

The changes could also involve staff. Feledy said some employees would remain at the institute, while others would be asked to leave. The organisational structure would not simply be imposed from above, however: the new system would be developed together with the institute’s staff.

The leadership also intends to retain the institute’s status as a non-profit private limited company, arguing that this could provide greater flexibility when testing new technologies, including the use of artificial intelligence in public administration.

The EU may once again become a central concern

One of the most significant shifts in foreign policy is likely to concern Hungary’s relationship with the European Union. Feledy said that the institute had accumulated little expertise on EU affairs in recent years, and that this would have to change.

Hungary is a member of both the EU and NATO, he noted, meaning that advancing the country’s interests within the Union is not an ideological question but a fundamental national interest. Some 80 per cent of Hungary’s trade is conducted in that direction, he said.

The institute therefore plans to build new research capacity, primarily in EU affairs. Greater attention could also be paid to issues that have received less prominence in Hungary’s foreign-policy debate, including digital sovereignty, cyber and economic security, the protection of critical infrastructure, migration and the geopolitical consequences of climate change. Water management could also become a priority, given both the climate crisis and the current water-related emergency.

At the same time, the institute would retain its traditional strengths, including research into the Balkans and the post-Soviet space. It also plans to develop new expertise on China and East Asia.

Rebuilding relations in central Europe — particularly with Poland, Austria, the Czech Republic and Slovakia — could likewise receive greater emphasis.

Hungary’s foreign policy strategy may also be renewed. The current strategy, drawn up in 2011, would be replaced by a new document, in the preparation of which the institute would play a role. The leaders said civil-society organisations and other professional bodies would also be involved.

No break with Russia, but servility is over — and Ukraine must be rebuilt

In the case of Russia, the proposed shift would involve a change in the style of the relationship rather than a complete foreign-policy reversal.

Rácz said there was no short-term alternative to maintaining pragmatic relations, primarily because of Hungary’s energy dependence. But he argued that there was no need to maintain such a close and “servile” relationship with the Russian leadership as that demonstrated by the ties between former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó and Sergei Lavrov in recent years.

Szijjártó and Putin. Photo: Facebook/Szijjártó

The researcher added that the relationship between Szijjártó and Lavrov, Russia’s foreign minister, had been even closer than the Hungarian public currently realised.

Have you read this one? Did Minister Szijjártó brief Lavrov during EU talks and offer to forward documents? Leaked recordings here!

The approach to Ukraine is more cautious. The new leadership does not expect a rapid breakthrough, but Rácz said that “something has already begun”.

On minority rights, the priority should be the implementation of existing agreements rather than the conclusion of new ones. They also said that the concessions secured in this area had been achieved not by the Orbán governments but through pressure from the EU.

The change, therefore, would not take the form of a single dramatic foreign policy U-turn. Instead, it points to more professional and less ideological decision-making focused on the EU, stronger regional ties and a more pragmatic approach to relations with Russia and Ukraine.

The reformed Institute of International Affairs could become one of the main centres of expertise behind that new foreign policy direction.

World.title: Sziget Festival to kick off on Sunday – everything you need to know
World.content:
Alongside its stages showcasing global superstars, Sziget Festival is placing renewed emphasis this year on cultural diversity and visitors’ comfort. Revamped festival districts, distinctive new and returning artistic productions, new food and drink venues, communal spaces and comfort-enhancing improvements will all await festival-goers. The festival will begin with two special days before its official opening, before once again operating for five days as a diverse city waiting to be explored – one in which culture, entertainment and shared experiences all take centre stage.

Sziget Festival: warming up with two special days

Sziget will launch this year with two special days before its official opening. On 9 August, the Minus One Day will host Bródy Songs Day, when more than 50 Hungarian performers – including Gábor Presser, Zsuzsa Koncz, Charlie, András Lovasi, Azahriah, Beton.Hofi, Dzsúdló, Bagossy Brothers Company, Carson Coma and Wellhello – will come together to celebrate the six-decade career of János Bródy. The evening will be a musical celebration spanning generations, culminating in a performance by Bródy himself.

The unique, unrepeatable six-hour programme is expected to draw older visitors to the festival as well. With them in mind, the organisers will provide minibus transport from the entrance to the Main Stage, while 5,000 cardboard chairs will also be available for the occasion at a cost price of HUF 600 each.

The Zero Day on 10 August will bridge Sziget’s past and present. This year, the organisers are inviting former ‘Sziget-goers’ back to the festival so that they can experience its atmosphere once again – this time, perhaps, with their children. Artists closely associated with Sziget’s history, including Faithless, Morcheeba and Goran Bregović, will return to the Main Stage. The evening will continue at the Revolut Stage, where György Korda and Klári Balázs will return to a Sziget stage after a long absence with a one-off show featuring a live band and dancers.

Afterwards, a nostalgia party led by Péter Janklovics, aka Pietro Fabuloso, will continue until dawn, recreating the atmosphere of the legendary Dance Song Festival tent. The two special opening days will both honour iconic figures from Hungarian popular music and underline one of Sziget’s central messages this year: the festival experience can be passed down from one generation to the next.

A city waiting to be explored

In 2026, Sziget will once again operate as a diverse city waiting to be discovered. Across the festival site, 12 districts – each with its own character, programme and atmosphere – will follow one another. Each could stand alone as a festival experience, yet they are organically connected, forming a series of easily accessible worlds that together create the complex, varied experience that is Sziget.

In the northern part of the festival, Wonderland will once again be a realm of creativity, self-expression and boundary-pushing experiences. It is where art, culture and unusual communal spaces meet, hosting the ArtGarden, Delko Checkout, the Museum of Applied Arts, the Kino Bizarre cinema with its distinctive cinematic world, the Light Stage, which invites exploration during the day, and the much-anticipated return of the iconic Luminárium. Wonderland will also remain home to one of the festival’s most distinctive meeting places, Magic Mirror / Magic Runway – a celebration of freedom, self-expression and diversity.

The heart of Sziget’s electronic music universe will be Delta District, where Arzenál x Turbina: Der Klub, BOLT Night Stage and Yettel Colosseum will offer all-night programmes across three venues with very different characters. The line-up includes internationally renowned names such as Peggy Gou, Sara Landry, Argy, Sub Focus, Richie Hawtin, Anfisa Letyago, Indira Paganotto, Dixon, Yousuke Yukimatsu, WhoMadeWho and Joris Voorn.

Numerous activities

Sziget is also offering discounted night-time admission this year. The Night Ticket by Revolut is aimed at those arriving only for the late-night programme. It allows entry to the festival site from 11 PM and remains valid until 8 AM the following morning. Night tickets for the festival days between 11 and 15 August are priced uniformly at HUF 29,900 and can be purchased through the official Sziget website.

Fans of hip-hop and rap will have their own district in dropYard, which will function not merely as a music venue but as a complete cultural space. The Graffiti Wall, Halfpipe and Skate Art programmes, The Cypher by Friss and the VISA Live x dropYard stage will together bring audiences closer to the genre’s musical, visual and street-culture worlds.

The Blue Zone will once again serve as Sziget’s centre for wellbeing and safety. Between concerts, festival-goers will be able to rest, take part in free health screenings, request a massage and seek support from mental-health professionals. The zone is designed to promote recovery, health and a safe festival experience. It will also host Kultúrapont, where visitors can enjoy acoustic concerts and slam poetry performances.

Epicentre and districts

Sziget’s epicentre will once again be Fő tér, where the festival’s biggest concerts and most spectacular programmes will take place. It is home to the Main Stage, which in 2026 will again host the festival’s biggest artists, including Skrillex, Bring Me The Horizon, Florence + The Machine, Twenty One Pilots, SOMBR, Zara Larsson, Lewis Capaldi, Skepta and Jorja Smith. Two Hungarian acts will also appear on the Main Stage this year: Sisi and Carson Coma. The Coca-Cola Stage will also be located around Fő tér, alongside the Grand Street Theatre, which will offer a spectacular experience every evening after the concerts.

The musical adventure continues beyond the main square. In the SZOHO district, The Buzz delivered by DHL will take centre stage, showcasing international acts who are already stars in their home countries but are still waiting to be discovered in Hungary. It will once again be one of Sziget’s most important destinations for musical discovery, giving promising artists from around the world – many on the cusp of international careers – the chance to introduce themselves. Visitors will have the opportunity to encounter the defining names of the coming years before they become household favourites.

Further music stages and entertainment venues will line Grand Avenue. These include Bacardi Stage, offering energetic programmes and tribute acts; the atmospheric Piros Pezsgő Piano Bar; and the Revolut Stage, which will host large-scale productions and international stars such as Natasha Bedingfield, Underworld, BUNT, Dijon and Ashnikko.

At the Budapest Park venue, leading figures from Hungary’s popular music scene will meet the festival audience at the Budapest Park Stage by Johnnie Walker. The programme will also offer a journey through Sziget’s history, with legendary bands such as Kispál és a Borz and Tankcsapda returning to the festival. Tankcsapda will perform songs from its era-defining album A legjobb méreg. They will be joined by Majka, Pál Utcai Fiúk, Quimby, Bëlga, Beton.Hofi, Pogány Induló, Co Lee, Mehringer and Manuel, among others.

The centre of Sziget’s artistic programme in 2026 will be the new Jardin des Arts, where the various strands of contemporary performance will converge. Visitors will be able to see the distinctive circus productions of Cirque du Sziget, the spectacular audiovisual performances at Le DÔME, the large-scale circus and theatre productions at Le Grand Theatre, and the immersive experiences of Mobilis, which actively involve the audience.

The district will also be home to The Joker, one of Sziget’s more playful and entertaining venues. Moving into a new building in 2026, it will offer board games during the day, followed by stand-up comedy and magic shows in the evening.

The We are Family district is designed for festival-goers arriving with children. From family camping and childcare facilities to a playground, everything is intended to ensure that parents and children alike feel comfortable at Sziget. Vándor Vurstli, which offers entertainment for every member of the family, will once again take visitors on a journey through time. Its world evokes the atmosphere of a 20th-century fairground, with games, performers and unusual productions providing carefree entertainment.

Visitors looking for nostalgia, playfulness and a little innocent escapism will find target games, magicians, puppet theatre, fortune-tellers, jugglers and a mini Ferris wheel. Vándor Vurstli is one of Sziget’s most colourful attractions – a place where the imagination can run free and everyone can rediscover the joy of childhood curiosity.

In the southern part of the festival site, Impact Village will serve as a hub for community initiatives, social responsibility and active participation. It will include Bartók-negyed, Civil Sziget, EU Meeting Point, Green Sziget Center, Sziget Changemakers, Szitizen Center, Wedding Garden and XS Land, which offers accessible experiences designed to promote awareness of disability and inclusion.

At Sziget’s southernmost point, the focus will turn to exercise and active recreation. In addition to sports pitches, the Field of Sports will feature a running club, the Hottie Pilates Tent and the Padel Zone / Workout Zone for those wishing to enrich their festival experience with sport, movement and relaxation alongside the concerts and cultural programmes.

Major comfort improvements

To tackle the increased risk of dust caused by the dry conditions, the organisers installed a temporary irrigation network at their own expense several weeks ago, in response to the earlier heatwave. Main routes without a permanent hard surface, as well as the audience areas in front of the stages, have been covered with ground protection, while several large continuous areas have been fitted with temporary flooring.

The routes will be watered continuously, and substantially more dust-binding material will be used this year than in previous years. In a record for Sziget, a total of 89,600 square metres – almost nine hectares – of ground protection has been laid, connected to the paved roads of Hajógyári Island. This is nearly 20,000 square metres, or almost two hectares, more than in 2025, making it the largest ground-protection project in the festival’s history.

One of the most important elements of the development is an increase of more than 5,000 square metres in the ground-protected area around the Main Stage. A second protected route will also be created alongside the Revolut venue, following the line of the flag road, further improving ease of movement around the site.

Sziget is also taking extensive measures to deal with the summer heat. Around 2,500 square metres of air-conditioned indoor space will be available for visitors seeking relief. The cooled venues include Magic Mirror, Joker, La Dôme, Luminárium, Sziget Ville Camping Wellness and the Skyboxes in the VIP area.

The amount of shaded space will also increase significantly. This year, festival-goers will have access to 14,000 square metres of shaded areas – around 3,000 square metres more than in 2025. The festival’s largest covered venue will remain Revolut, whose almost 6,000-square-metre space is one of Sziget’s principal communal areas.

In addition, more than ten hectares of tree-covered, shaded audience space will be available. As part of the heat-protection measures, the number of misting arches will be increased. Several areas were also closed during the construction period to preserve green spaces, which help cool the festival site naturally.

An extensive drinking-water network will ensure that visitors can stay hydrated. The site will have six drinking fountains, ten single-tap drinking points, three nine-tap drinking points and seven three-tap drinking points. Subject to the results of water-quality tests, drinking water will also be available in all toilet facilities.

Sziget 2026: food and drink elevated

Sziget will welcome visitors in 2026 with a revamped food and drink concept. Across the festival site, a broad selection of Hungarian and international flavours will be available, from street-food favourites to restaurant-style dishes. Alongside Thai, Italian, Japanese, Mexican, Greek and French cuisine, Hungarian food will play a prominent role.

Food courts will remain an important part of the offering, while vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, lactose-free and other special-diet options will receive more attention than ever before. The Budget-Friendly programme will also continue, with most food outlets offering at least one one-pot dish priced below HUF 3,500.

Festival-goers should also note that all drinks will be available at a ten per cent discount until 6pm on festival days. New this year is Food Paradise, combining premium gastronomy with daytime programmes and communal experiences. The Piros Pezsgő Piano Bar will bring together sparkling drinks, Hungarian wines, local flavours and live piano music.

For the first time, Sziget will also host a Farmers’ Market, showcasing a carefully selected range of products from local growers and craftspeople. As part of the revamped VIP experience, guests will be served by leading gastronomic partners including Costes, Digó Nápolyi Pizza, Buja Disznók, 101 Bisztró and TOKIO.

New solutions will also make eating at the festival more convenient. A QR-code ordering system will debut in the Food Paradise area, allowing visitors to order food more quickly and easily.

ALDI will once again provide festival-goers with shopping facilities on the Sziget site. At the pop-up shop, Szitizens will be able to buy freshly baked bread, fruit, vegetables, chilled products and non-food items at the usual shop prices. In the ALDI Grill Zone, staff will cook the grill products purchased in the shop free of charge.

Visitors will be able to choose from 25 dishes, including sausages, marinated meats, fish, vegetarian products and vegan options. ALDI will offer Sziget’s most budget-friendly meal options: a breakfast can be put together from HUF 207, vegan grill products start at HUF 469, and grilled sausages at HUF 1,159. The Grill Zone will have almost twice the capacity of last year, operating 24 grills and seating up to 100 guests at a time.

Sziget will again place a strong emphasis on sustainable catering. Partners will operate under stricter environmental requirements, with waste reduction, responsible sourcing and energy-efficient operations all receiving particular attention. Cooperation with the Hungarian Food Bank Association will help reduce food waste.

Visitors will also find comfortable, shaded communal areas and a wide choice of drinks, while the DRINKiQ programme will once again promote responsible alcohol consumption.

The Green Sziget Center will remain one of the festival’s main hubs for sustainability and environmental awareness. New this year is a farmers’ market offering local, seasonal fruit and vegetables, processed products and healthy snacks. The programme will include educational events on climate change and biodiversity, while the popular Nature Walk guided tour will continue to introduce visitors to Sziget’s distinctive natural environment.

The festival is also strengthening its sustainability efforts. The tent-deposit scheme has significantly reduced the number of tents left behind, while donated tents and camping equipment will once again be passed on to the Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta. Comprehensive waste-management improvements will also be introduced, with greater emphasis on prevention, recycling and the active involvement of partners.

In the spirit of sustainable transport, adventurous visitors will be able to arrive at Sziget this year on guided bicycle tours from Vienna and Bratislava.

Power and water concerns at Sziget Festival? Founder reveals what’s really going on

Prepared for extreme conditions

Following yesterday’s announcement that the country’s energy security is not at risk and that no further voluntary reductions in consumption will be required, the festival’s electricity supply can be adequately provided by the grid. Nevertheless, Sziget can switch to its reserve generators at any time should a power shortage or system failure occur.

Water supplies in the capital are also sufficient. The festival’s average daily water consumption is expected to be around 1,000 cubic metres, supplied through the public utility network and supplemented by buffer capacity. In preparation for any disruption to the network, a total reserve of 800,000 litres of water will be available, with a further 10,000 litres of drinking water held on site.

Medical cover at the festival will be provided by the National Ambulance Service through an on-site treatment centre, supported by several hundred medical assistants and security staff. A pharmacy will also operate on the site around the clock.

MÁV railway group preparing with extra services for the Sziget Festival – details

Sziget’s safe operation will be co-ordinated by the so-called Operational Control Centre, which monitors events at the festival in real time and takes immediate action if necessary. The centre’s work involves, among others, the National Ambulance Service, the Disaster Management Directorate, the police, the National Meteorological Service and In-Kal Security.

According to preliminary figures, the festival’s maximum daily attendance this year is expected to be between 70,000 and 75,000 people – well below the officially authorised capacity of 95,000. Overcrowding is therefore not expected.

Those who would prefer quiet relaxation to all-night partying will not need to leave the festival site. Several venues have been created specifically to support rest, recovery and the preservation or restoration of physical and mental balance.

The organisers’ stated aim was to make this year’s festival visibly more comfortable. Alongside cultural diversity, they believe this is another area in which Sziget can significantly outperform its international competitors.

World.title: Why is it a problem if Péter Magyar decides who can lead Hungary’s public media?
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s intervention in two public media appointments has caused debate over the independence of Hungary’s state broadcaster.

The independence of Hungary’s public media has been one of the country’s most sensitive political issues ever since the democratic transition of 1989–90. Following the change of government in 2026, it appeared almost inevitable that the operation of the Media Service Support and Asset Management Fund (MTVA) and the wider public service media would undergo far-reaching reforms.

One of Péter Magyar’s flagship campaign promises was to bring the era of political propaganda to an end and establish a genuinely independent public broadcaster.

A cleaner public media – but at what cost?

Events over the past few days, however, have opened an entirely new chapter in that debate. The controversy began when MTVA announced the appointment of Gábor Hajdú—who had previously worked for Hír TV and Echo TV—as the new editor-in-chief of M1 News. At the same time, Miklós Borsa, a former presenter of the broadcaster’s flagship news programme, was set to return to the screen.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar clearly had a different view. Remaining true to his increasingly familiar style of direct political communication, he commented on a news article covering the appointments with just 4 words (which were two words in Hungarian):

“I don’t think so…”

The following day, MTVA announced that both appointments had been withdrawn. The speed of the reversal immediately reignited a fundamental constitutional question: should a prime minister—whether formally or informally—be able to influence who occupies senior positions within the country’s public broadcaster?

The criticism once aimed at Fidesz

The episode is particularly striking because one of the strongest criticisms levelled against Fidesz for years was precisely its alleged political control over Hungary’s public media.

Opposition politicians and independent observers frequently argued that anyone who had watched the so-called “state television” during the previous sixteen years could hardly fail to notice its editorial bias.

Yet even Viktor Orbán generally avoided creating the impression that editorial decisions were being made directly from the Prime Minister’s Office. The latest developments appear considerably more explicit: a brief public comment by the sitting prime minister was followed almost immediately by the withdrawal of two high-profile appointments.

Whether this sequence reflects direct political intervention or merely coincidental timing is open to interpretation. Nevertheless, the public perception it creates is difficult to ignore.

Echoes of the Judit Polgár nomination

Many commentators have therefore drawn parallels with another recent controversy: the nomination of Judit Polgár for the presidency. The issue then was not primarily the nominee herself. Hungary’s greatest-ever chess player would likely have been an acceptable choice for many voters.

Rather, critics argued that the government had abandoned its own promise of broad public consultation and instead acted unilaterally, much as previous governments had done when filling the country’s highest constitutional offices.

A similar criticism now emerges in the case of MTVA. For many, the problem is not necessarily that the two withdrawn media executives had previously worked within what critics describe as the former government’s media machinery. Supporters of the current administration argue that figures associated with political propaganda have no place in a renewed public broadcaster.

Instead, the concern centres on the process itself. If the prime minister can effectively overturn appointments through a public social media comment, questions inevitably arise about where institutional autonomy begins, and political authority ends.

A question that goes beyond Péter Magyar

The debate extends far beyond the current prime minister, Péter Magyar. If it becomes accepted practice that a head of government may informally reverse senior appointments with a single public remark, the same precedent would inevitably be available to every future administration, regardless of political affiliation.

That is precisely why democratic institutions are designed to function according to transparent rules rather than the preferences of individual office-holders. Supporters of Péter Magyar naturally offer a different interpretation.

In their view, this was not political interference but a necessary correction. They argue that leaving individuals who had played leading roles in what they regard as the previous government’s propaganda system would have fundamentally undermined the credibility of efforts to rebuild public service broadcasting.

From this perspective, the intervention was intended to restore institutional independence rather than weaken it.

Good decisions also require the right process

That argument, however, addresses only part of the issue. In a constitutional democracy, legitimacy depends not only on whether the final decision is correct but also on whether it is reached through a fair and transparent procedure.

If senior appointments are made through an established professional process only to be withdrawn immediately after a prime minister’s public intervention, many observers will inevitably conclude that political will ultimately overrides institutional decision-making. Ironically, this is exactly the type of governance that Fidesz’s opponents criticised for years.

The independence of public media is not strengthened simply because a different political force now exercises influence over it. It becomes stronger only when no governing party is able to shape its day-to-day operation according to immediate political interests.

If Péter Magyar genuinely intends to open a new chapter for Hungarian public broadcasting, the long-term objective should be to ensure that senior appointments are made through transparent, institutional procedures that remain as independent from political actors as possible.

Such an approach would not only reinforce confidence in the public media today. It would also establish a democratic standard that every future Hungarian government would be expected to follow.

World.title: Romanian shipyard delivers hull of largest cable-laying ship in Japan
World.content:
The VARD shipyard in Tulcea, eastern Romania, has completed the construction of the hull of “Discovery,” the largest vessel intended for the installation of submarine cables and the first such project delivered by the VARD group for the Japanese market.

The ship, valued at over USD 200 million, will have an important role in the development of infrastructure for offshore wind energy and the transport of electric energy through submarine cables.

The construction of the vessel’s hull was carried out in Romania, at the VARD shipyards in Tulcea and Brăila, and after launching, it was towed to the VARD Langsten shipyard in Norway, where the specialized equipment was installed, and the final tests were carried out before delivery. The vessel was officially handed over to the Japanese company Toyo Construction at the end of June and is currently heading to Japan, where it will be based in the port of Ishikari Bay.

“Discovery” was designed to meet the specific conditions in Japan, where the water depth increases rapidly near the coast. The vessel can operate both in shallow waters and offshore, where future floating wind farms will be installed.

The vessel is approximately 151 meters long, 28 meters wide, and can transport up to 9,000 tons of submarine cables, distributed in two carousels with capacities of 4,000 and 5,000 tons.

On board, the ship has a main crane with a lifting capacity of 400 tons and an auxiliary crane of 100 tons. The vessel is also equipped with a dynamic positioning system, a heliport and equipment for the operation of remotely operated underwater vehicles.

In addition to the installation of submarine cables, “Discovery” can also be used for offshore construction works, including the installation of foundations for wind turbines and anchoring operations for floating turbines.

The vessel is equipped with a hybrid propulsion system, in which diesel engines are used to produce electric energy, while propulsion is provided by electric motors. The system includes batteries and the possibility of shore power supply during stationing, in order to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. Up to 90 crew members and technicians can work on board.

The Japanese government has set the rapid expansion of offshore wind energy capacities as an objective in the coming period, and this vessel will be used for the installation of the submarine electric cables necessary to connect the new farms to the energy grid.

For VARD, the project marks the first delivery to the Japanese market in the segment of specialized vessels for the offshore wind industry. In recent years, the VARD Tulcea shipyard has specialized in the construction of the hulls of some of the most complex vessels intended for the offshore industry, including vessels for the installation of submarine cables and for the development of offshore wind energy projects.

Several of the most advanced vessels of this type currently used worldwide were built in Romania and subsequently equipped at the VARD group’s shipyards in Norway.

World.title: Romania’s eMAG to come under sole control of Naspers after EU approval
World.content:
The European Commission has approved, under the EU Merger Regulation, the acquisition of sole control over Dante International of Romania by South African investment fund Naspers Limited.

"The Commission concluded that the notified operation does not raise competition concerns, as the companies are not active on the same markets or on markets that are in a vertical relationship, and the impact on the market structure is limited. The transaction was examined under the simplified merger control procedure," the EC stated in a press release.

Last month, businessman Iulian Stanciu announced the sale of his stake in the eMAG Group to global consumer internet and technology investment group Prosus, 17 years after taking over the company and 14 years after signing the partnership with Naspers, the owner of Prosus.

After the sale, eMAG will continue its development and extensive investment plans, with RON 1.2 billion budgeted in this fiscal year alone for technology, logistics and financial services, with the support of Prosus and an experienced management team, company representatives stated. They also noted the regional growth potential of e-commerce, which remains significant, with growth rates of up to three times in the coming years, compared to the current penetration rate of 11-12% of total retail.

"The investments will be directed predominantly toward logistics and delivery infrastructure, AI and financial services, consolidating the foundation for a strong digital economy in the region. I want to thank Iulian for his dedication, vision, and for keeping us focused on the customer and on continuous personal development," said at that time Tudor Manea, CEO of eMAG Group, cited by News.ro.

At group level, eMAG recorded in fiscal year 2025 a turnover of RON 11.4 billion (USD 2.64 billion), up 11% compared with the previous financial year. The eMAG Group portfolio includes the eMAG brand, the Fashion Days online store, Romania’s 100% online hypermarket Freshful, the IT and electronics specialist store PC Garage, the Romanian national and international express courier company Sameday, the Depanero repair workshop, the most relevant recommerce platform in South-Eastern Europe Flip, as well as the financial services company HeyBlu.

World.title: Eurostat: Romania allocated only EUR 18.8 per inhabitant to R&D in 2025, lower than in 2015
World.content:
European governments allocated an estimated EUR 130.2 billion, or 0.69% of their combined GDP, to research and development in 2025, according to a Eurostat analysis published on Friday, August 7.

The sum represents an increase of 2.4% compared to 2024 (EUR 127.14 billion) and an increase of 60.5% compared to 2015 (EUR 81.13 billion).

In 2025, on average, government budget allocations for research and development at EU level amounted to EUR 288.9 per inhabitant, an increase of 57.7% compared to 2015 (EUR 183.2 per inhabitant). Luxembourg (EUR 917.2 per inhabitant) recorded the highest budget allocations for research and development per capita among the EU member countries. It was followed by Denmark (EUR 627.1) and Germany (EUR 553.5).

At the opposite end, the lowest values were recorded in Romania (EUR 18.8), Hungary (EUR 57.4) and Malta (EUR 73.7). Moreover, compared to 2015, Romania (-9.6%) was the only EU country that recorded a decrease in budget allocations for research and development expressed in euros per inhabitant, from EUR 20.8 in 2015 to EUR 18.8 in 2025.

The other EU countries recorded increases ranging from +14.7% in Sweden (from EUR 363.4 per inhabitant in 2015 to EUR 416.7 in 2025) to +495.5% in Bulgaria (from EUR 15.5 to EUR 92.3).

As regards the distribution according to socio-economic objectives, 37.3% of the amount was allocated to the general advancement of knowledge, financed mainly through a global public grant known as public general university funds, used by public higher education institutions to support their activities. In addition, 18.4% of R&D funds were allocated to the general advancement of knowledge from sources other than the general university funds, 9.5% to industrial production and technology, 6.7% to health, and 5.8% to defense.

World.title: EIB lends EUR 100 million to BRD Sogelease to increase financing for businesses in Romania
World.content:
The European Investment Bank (EIB) is lending EUR 100 million to the leasing subsidiary of BRD Groupe Société Générale to expand financing for businesses in Romania.

The goal is to facilitate financing for Romanian SMEs and Mid-Caps, which face greater hurdles in accessing long-term funding than their counterparts in many other European Union countries, EIB said.

The operation will enable BRD Sogelease to provide funding to Romanian companies seeking business expansion, productivity improvements and sustainable development.

Of the total loan, 15% is earmarked for green projects such as energy efficiency, renewable energy and sustainable transport.

Around 80% of the EIB loan is projected to be deployed in less-developed areas known in the EU as “cohesion regions.”

The new operation builds on previous EIB loans to BRD Sogelease IFN that total EUR 305 million over the past decade.

“In today’s rapidly changing economy, access to finance is a key enabler of competitiveness,” said EIB Vice-President Ioannis Tsakiris. “By partnering with BRD Sogelease, we are mobilizing investment where it matters most: among Romanian entrepreneurs. This financing will help businesses become more resilient, more innovative and better prepared for the opportunities of tomorrow.”

“Our long-standing partnership with the European Investment Bank reflects a shared commitment to supporting the growth and resilience of the Romanian economy. This new financing facility will enable us to provide SMEs and Mid-Caps with enhanced access to long-term funding on attractive terms, helping them invest in expansion, innovation, productivity and sustainable development,” said BRD Sogelease GM Gabriel Mihai.

BRD Sogelease IFN SA is the leasing subsidiary of BRD Groupe Société Générale, one of the leading banks in Romania with total assets of RON 96.3 billion as of June 2026. Established in 2001, BRD Sogelease IFN provides financial lease and other asset-based financial solutions to over 10,000 SME and Small-Cap clients in Romania.

World.title: Platform for foreign workers coming to Romania up and running, authorities say
World.content:
Romania’s Interior Ministry announced on Thursday, August 6, that the platform WorkinRomania.gov.ro is now up and running, simplifying the process of hiring foreign workers.

The platform aims to make it easier for immigrant workers to enter the domestic labor market. Among its benefits is the facilitation of the relationship between the employer and the future employee.

The platform helps both Romanian employers looking for a workforce and aids the state in managing more efficiently the employment of new workers coming from other states. “Less bureaucracy, shorter deadlines and the possibility to track each application in real time,” the Ministry noted, cited by Agerpres.

The services of this platform include: permanent access to one’s own electronic file; the possibility to track each stage of the procedure; automatic notifications regarding requests for additional documents or the adopted solutions; reduction of waiting times; increased transparency of the entire administrative process. The platform also connects future employees with the Trade Register, the Employee Records Register, as well as with IT systems for the checks provided by law.

The platform also centralizes the actions of several Romanian state institutions.

The General Inspectorate for Immigration within the Ministry of Internal Affairs handles the procedures within its competence regarding the regime of foreigners and the right of residence for employment purposes; it analyzes and resolves applications regarding the granting and extension of residence

The right of residence for employment purposes, issues the specific documents and participates in the electronic exchange of data necessary for substantiating administrative decisions.

The National Agency for Employment operationally administers the module intended for the registration and authorization of employers and agencies for the placement of foreigners and configures the workflows related to these procedures;

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, through the national visa system and the eViza platform, participates in the workflows regarding the granting of long-stay visas for employment;

The National Agency for Fiscal Administration provides the information necessary for the fiscal checks provided by law;

The Ministry of Education and Research, through the National Center for the Recognition and Equivalence of Diplomas, contributes to the verification of qualifications and diplomas, in the cases provided by legislation.

The platform offers useful information for employers, placement agencies and foreign workers, available also in English. Interested persons can find on WorkinRomania.gov.ro all the information they need for creating and validating an account on the platform, the registration and authorization conditions, the necessary documents and the method of using the electronic services available on the platform.

At the same time, users have a support chat service, available both in text and voice format, which provides assistance and guidance in the use of electronic services, in Romanian and other languages.

In terms of security, the program is included in the Ministry’s Services Hub, specially designed to keep personal data safe at the level of each county.

Although Romania set an official quota of around 90,000 newly admitted foreign workers for 2026, employer demand significantly exceeds that ceiling. In some years, requests have reportedly been more than double the approved quota. Still, filling vacancies is only part of the challenge. A large share of newly arrived workers subsequently seek opportunities in other EU member states, where wages, working conditions, and social benefits are often more attractive.

World.title: Thriller starring Nicolas Cage to open this year's horror and fantastic film fest in Biertan
World.content:
The Full Moon Horror and Fantastic Film Festival, presented by the Transilvania International Film Festival, returns to Biertan for its 11th edition, bringing three days and three nights of premieres, cult films and open-air screenings.

The festival opens with the Romanian premiere of The Carpenter’s Son, starring Nicolas Cage. Another highlight of this year’s edition will be the cine-concert Trenul Fantomă, featuring live music by Dubase, preceded by an acoustic performance by Ana Coman and her guitar as part of Full Moon Unplugged.

At Bastion Open Air, the programme kicks off on Friday, August 14, with Nightborn, the new film by Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, known to horror audiences for Hatching. Selected for the competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the film follows a couple who move into an isolated house in the Finnish woods, where the arrival of their first child awakens a disturbing presence. The evening continues with The Rocky Horror Picture Show, the horror musical that has become one of cinema’s great cult phenomena. The story behind the film will also be explored from behind the scenes in the documentary Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror, screening on Saturday at Cinema Ion Hobana.

On Saturday, Bastion Open Air will screen Her Private Hell, the new film by director Nicolas Winding Refn, as well as the original Dutch version of the thriller The Vanishing. The programme also includes the 1993 American remake, also directed by George Sluizer, giving audiences an opportunity to compare the two versions.

On Sunday, Carrie returns to the Bastion screen. Directed by Brian De Palma and based on Stephen King’s novel, the classic marks 50 years since its release.

On Friday, August 14, Méliès Open Air will host the Romanian premiere of The Carpenter’s Son. Directed by Lotfy Nathan, the supernatural thriller stars Nicolas Cage as Joseph, alongside FKA twigs as Mary and Noah Jupe as their teenage son.

On Saturday, August 15, audiences are invited to the cine-concert Trenul Fantomă. Made in 1933 by Jean Mihail, the first Romanian-language talking film tells the story of travelers forced to spend the night at a railway station believed to be haunted. The film will be screened with live music performed by Dubase.

The Méliès programme concludes on Sunday, August 16, with The Virgin of the Quarry Lake, directed by Laura Casabé. Inspired by the prose of writer Mariana Enríquez, the film blends adolescence, jealousy and black magic against the backdrop of Argentina’s 2001 crisis.

The selection continues at Cinema Karloff and Cinema Ion Hobana, with titles including The Turkish Coffee Table, Gaua, Species, Roqia, Veins, The Uncertainty Principle, Feels Like Home, Anemoneciacs and Transylvania Tapes.

The program also includes Romanian short films, the documentary Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror, and repeat screenings of The Carpenter’s Son, Nightborn and Her Private Hell.

The festival takes place between August 14 and August 16.

World.title: Romania’s Banca Transilvania extends EUR 71.4 mln loan for Entek Elektrik PV park
World.content:
The largest bank in Romania, Banca Transilvania, announced that it will finance the development of the Eco Sun Niculești photovoltaic park, Entek Elektrik’s first investment in local green energy production, with EUR 71.4 million.

It is one of the largest bilateral financings granted to a photovoltaic project under development in the country. Once completed, the park, located in Dâmbovița County, will have an installed capacity of approximately 205 MW. The total value of the project is estimated at EUR 100 million.

“Projects of this scale contribute to strengthening energy independence and modernizing the Romanian economy. We are pleased to support Entek Elektrik’s first investment in renewable energy production in Romania and to continue the solid partnership that we have built together,” said Cosmin Călin, Deputy General Manager Large Corporate, Banca Transilvania.

The investment in the Eco Sun Niculești project is made through Entek Elektrik Üretimi A.Ş., the renewable energy company of the Koç Group, and its main shareholder is Türkiye Petrol Refinerileri A.Ş. (Tüpraş), the largest industrial company in Turkey and the seventh largest refinery operator in Europe.

In Turkey, Entek owns an energy capacity portfolio of 550 MW. The company aims to further expand its renewable energy portfolio and seeks to become one of the leading green energy producers in Turkey.

World.title: Albanian Court Puts Turkish Activist in Custody After Extradition Demand
World.content:
Protesters rally with pictures of victims of the 2013 Gezi Park protests in Istanbul, April 2022. Photo: EPA-EFE/SEDAT SUNA.

The Tirana Court on Friday ordered a custody remand for Julide Yazici, who is wanted for extradition by Turkey to serve a prison sentence for aiding a terrorist organisation – charges that she claims are motivated by her political activism.

Yazici was arrested on August 4 at Tirana Airport while travelling from France to Albania after it was discovered that she was wanted for extradition to Turkey.

The judge granted the prosecution’s custody request despite Yazici’s lawyer’s arguments that his client “holds political asylum status in France and poses no danger”, and could be placed under house arrest instead.

The lawyer, Artan Shllaku, said that the decision will be appealed.

Shllaku added that Yazici, who teaches at an elementary school in France, had visited Albania a year earlier to see relatives and had encountered no issues.

Yazici is wanted by Turkish authorities to serve the remainder of a four-year prison sentence – three years, five months and 22 days – for providing logistical support to and participating in a terrorist organisation.

According to a decision by the French National Court of Asylum dated November 2020, a document obtained by BIRN, Yazici was involved in political activism in Turkey and participated in the Gezi Park mass protests in 2013 against the administration led by Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

She actively supported the former People’s Democratic Party, HDP, a left-wing political group that supported Turkey’s Kurdish minority, and which later became the DEM Party.

The French court decision granting asylum to Yazici stated that she was arrested in January 2016 “for having allowed a young woman she did not know, who had been introduced to her by a friend, to stay in her student room”.

The French court decision in the document that Yazici had “a well-founded fear … of being persecuted if she returns to her country due to her political activism”.

Yazici is not the first Turkish national to be arrested in Albania for extradition in controversial circumstances in recent years. Teachers and others linked to the movement previously led by the now-deceased cleric Fethullah Gulen, which is classified as a terrorist organisation by the authorities under Erdogan, have also been detained and then deported in line with Ankara’s demands.

World.title: Secrecy Surrounds Croatia’s Arrest of Alleged Serbian State-Linked Hacker
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH.

The Croatian and Serbian authorities are remaining tight-lipped over the arrest last week of a Serbian businessman named as Georgije V., 33, on suspicion of hacking into the computer systems of various Croatian state institutions and public agencies.

The Serbian man is reportedly suspected of hacking into the Croatian Interior Ministry, the Central Register of Pension-Insured Persons, the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, the Croatian Regulatory Agency for Network Activities, the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute, the Croatian Tax Administration and the Croatian Automobile Club.

Tomo Medved, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, was asked about the case on Friday but declined to provide details.

“I would like to commend the entire security and intelligence system for its responsible and vigilant monitoring and protection of the interests of the Republic of Croatia. Given the ongoing proceedings, I cannot comment further than that,” Medved told journalists.

Croatian daily Jutarnji list has reported that the arrest took place on July 28, when Georgije V. was on holiday in Croatia. He had arrived with his wife, two children and mother at a tourist resort on the Adriatic coast a few days earlier.

Following his arrest, police searched his electronic devices, vehicle and accommodation under court orders. They seized items and digital data allegedly linking him to criminal acts, including two mobile phones and a laptop containing a large amount of data.

The court ordered one month of pre-trial detention, despite the man offering 20,000 euros in bail money and his family home in Novi Sad as collateral.

Croatia’s Chief State Attorney, Ivan Turudic, initially sparked public interest on Monday when he made a comment about a case related to national security. It was then reported by Jutarnji list that Turudic was referring to the arrest of an alleged hacker linked to Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA.

It is not known whether the suspect’s alleged access to the computer systems of various institutions and agencies endangered Croatia’s national security in any way, or what he did with any data he may have obtained.

Nera Gajdarov Beg, the suspect’s lawyer, told Jutarnji list that the court’s custody order is being contested.

“An appeal has been filed against the decision to order pretrial detention because we believe that not all legal requirements for such a decision have been met. At this point, I cannot provide details of the defence because the proceedings are in the investigation phase, which is secret,” Gajdarov Beg said.

The Serbian authorities have not commented on the arrest so far. However, Serbian media have reported that Georgije V. is the owner of an active Novi Sad-based company specialising in computer programming and cybersecurity.

World.title: Croatian Serb Leader Deplores Hate Speech at Operation Storm Commemoration
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Milorad Pupovac, president of the Independent Democratic Serb Party, SDSS, and MP, on Friday said that slogans and chants heard on the streets of Knin on August 5, the day marking the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, represented a “serious attack on constitutional values and democracy”.

Pupovac, leader of the main party representing Serbs in Croatia, argued that “hatred and incitement to crime are incompatible with true patriotism”.

At a press conference, he showed a compilation of recordings from Knin, the town that was the headquarters of a rebel Serbian statelet crushed by the Croatian Army’s Operation Storm in 1995.

They included sports fans and army veterans singing songs glorifying the Ustasha – the army of the Independent State of Croatia, NDH, a World War II fascist puppet state operating under the patronage of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

The recordings also showed people chanting: “We Croats do not drink wine, only the blood of Chetniks [Serbian nationalists] from Knin”; “The battle is fought, it is fought, the Ustasha flag is flying”, as well as insults directed at St Sava, the patron saint of the Serbian Orthodox Church.

“Those who have been trying to pass this off as an act of patriotism for years are actually seriously violating the true values of patriotism. In peacetime, the greatest patriotic virtue is constitutional patriotism,” Pupovac said.

He added that such behaviour was a “vicious attack on democracy”.

The SNV cited articles of the Croatian Constitution that it believes were violated by the shouting of the Ustasha salute “For the Homeland, Ready” and other glorifications of the NDH. The violations came after, not during, the official anniversary celebrations, it said.

Every year, Knin hosts a commemoration of Operation Storm, which liberated about 18 per cent of Croatia’s territory from rebel Serb forces and was followed by the flight of around 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. Some of them later returned.

SDSS leader Pupovac also criticised the Croatian judicial authorities, questioning why the State Attorney’s Office often does not react to hate speech and incitement to violence, appealing for an end to what he called a policy of appeasement.

He warned that failure to condemn such phenomena represents a direct threat to the Serb community in Croatia, and to all citizens who advocate for a state governed by the rule of law.

World.title: Week in Review: The Electoral Merry-Go-Round
World.content:
Last week, a no-confidence motion in the Serbian government was held in the country’s parliament. A boisterous discussion ensued between ruling and opposition MPs, but the motion failed – as expected.

Its real significance was not so much the outcome as the fact that the holding the vote, tabled at the beginning of the year, cleared an important obstacle to calling early parliamentary elections.

President Aleksandar Vucic has fuelled speculation that polls are imminent. Our analysis takes a look a look at what will determine when they happen – and whether they will happen at all.

World.title: One Year in the Palace: How Nawrocki Made the Polish Presidency His Own
World.content:
Nawrocki vetoes again and again

At home, he has repeatedly used his veto to frustrate the government. In his first year, Nawrocki vetoed 41 bills, more than any other Polish president since the fall of Communism. Among the most consequential were legislation linked to Poland’s access to nearly 44 billion euros under the EU’s SAFE defence program, bills concerning the justice system and public finances, two laws expanding rights for unmarried couples and, three times, legislation regulating the crypto-assets market.

The conflict, however, extends beyond legislation. Forty four ambassadorial nominations remain unsigned amid a long-running dispute between the palace and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski. Poland still has no fully accredited ambassador in Washington, one of its most important diplomatic postings; Bogdan Klich continues to run the embassy as chargé d’affaires.

But Nawrocki has also been unusually active in proposing legislation of his own. In a year, he submitted 22 bills; if he continues at this pace, he is on course to breaking another record by the end of his term. His predecessor Andrzej Duda by comparison submitted 32 during the entire first five years of his presidency.

“I want, in fact, to change the model of the presidency,” Nawrocki told the crowd on Thursday. “The president is not only there to review the law and deal with bills that come from parliament. The president is also there to come forward with legislative initiatives and carry your voice and your demands.”

That ambition goes beyond the number of bills. Poland is a parliamentary democracy in which the government runs most day-to-day policy, while the president has important but more limited powers, including the veto and a role in foreign and defence affairs. Nawrocki has repeatedly floated constitutional change and has been pushing the Presidential Palace towards something closer to a parallel centre of power. His ministers regularly speak on the same issues as their government counterparts, while the 17 presidential councils that aid him, involving around 700 people, are working on a broader development strategy that Nawrocki says he will unveil within months.

“I deeply believe that the presidential development strategy… will become, in the next parliamentary elections, a point of reference for all those who aspire to govern Poland,” he said.

Tusk has accused Nawrocki of trying to change Poland’s political system in practice without changing the constitution. Government spokesman Adam Szlapka described the first year of the presidency as a “bad time”, accusing Nawrocki of thinking primarily in political terms and obstructing government policy.

So far, however, the confrontation has not hurt the president much. Nawrocki remains Poland’s most trusted politician: an IBRiS poll published in late July found that 51.3 per cent of respondents trusted him.

Foreign policy has been another central part of his presidency. Nawrocki has worked hard to cultivate ties with Donald Trump and the US, while taking an increasingly confrontational line towards Ukraine over the historical legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for massacres of Polish citizens during World War II.

On Thursday, he again tried to hold both positions at once. It was in Poland’s strategic interest, he said, for Ukrainian soldiers to keep Russia as far from Poland as possible. But it was also in Poland’s interest that “Banderite flags” should not fly in Warsaw, referring to the common term used for fighters of the UPA. “You can help and you can demand.”

World.title: Democracy Digest: Study Finds Slovakia Has Europe’s Weakest Spy Agency
World.content:
Police investigate Czech MP over car crash; countdown to municipal elections; Havel human rights award to be preserved

Czech police this week launched an investigation into MP and government commissioner for the Green Deal Filip Turek on suspicion of bodily harm through negligence over a car crash last month, which saw the honorary president of the Motorist Party – a ruling coalition junior partner – collide with an ambulance at a busy thoroughfare in Prague’s city centre. Caught on CCTV, the traffic accident led to the ambulance’s driver being injured and incapacitated for several days, sparking calls from opposition parties as well as President Petr Pavel for Turek to step down from both his parliamentary and government positions – although experts remain divided on who precisely was to blame for the collision. Turek has since temporarily vacated his position as the government’s plenipotentiary for climate change and the Green Deal pending the results of the investigation and vowed not to use his parliamentary immunity should the police file criminal charges against him. “I think the investigation will go well for me because I kind of know the regulations,” he told TV Nova, also suggesting the injured ambulance driver was “talked into” staying under hospital care longer than necessary for the optics.

This week was the deadline for political parties, movements and coalitions to officially register for the upcoming municipal elections, scheduled to be held across Czechia on October 9-10. Candidacies will now be reviewed by state electoral authorities by August 22. In the capital Prague, two dozen political groupings will take part in the race to win the big and hotly contested prize, a couple more than four years ago, on top of electoral fights for the city’s 57 local districts. In addition to electing their political representatives in the Czech Republic’s more than 6,000 towns, cities and municipalities, voters will also vote for a third of the Senate’s seats. About 155 candidates have registered to run for this year’s partial Senate race, less than the last ballot, mainly a result of pre-election agreements and joint candidates put forward by opposition parties.

Dagmar Havlova, the widow of the former dissident and president, along with the Vize 97 foundation confirmed this week that the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize will be preserved and continue to be awarded every year. This follows a previous announcement by the Vaclav Havel Library – which has faced an exodus of staff, sponsors and funding in recent months – that it would no longer participate in the annual award ceremony after Havlova withdrew her consent for the NGO to use the former playwright’s name. Coming with a cheque of 60,000 euros, the award was established shortly after Havel’s death in 2011 to recognise outstanding achievements in the field of human rights and has been awarded by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe since 2013 together with the Vaclav Havel Library and the Charter 77 Foundation. Past laureates include Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, Russian journalist Vladimir Kara-Murza and Belarusian activist Maria Kalesnikava.

World.title: Lands in Limbo: Danube ‘Microstates’ Dream Big Despite Lack of Recognition
World.content:
From the village of Batina in Croatia's far northeast, the only land route leads to the Free Republic of Liberland, a self-proclaimed microstate on the banks of the Danube River.

A bicycle is the only practical means of transport. The journey begins on an asphalt road before continuing onto gravel and then a dirt track, until the road disappears altogether.

The final kilometre must be covered on foot, across the dried-up bed of a Danube backwater. In summer, it feels more like walking across desert sand before reaching the dense forest that forms the "centre" of Liberland.

World.title: Letter from Brussels: Ceuta Migrant Panic Casts Shadow Over EU’s Summer
World.content:
The weeks that bridge July and August are a period when the EU buildings around Schuman here in Brussels grow quiet, and correspondents’ group chats go mute.

But this year the last week of July was far from quiet. While EU spokespersons were cycling through out-of-office messages and the unlucky ones were covering for absent colleagues, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - the largest single-day surge in irregular arrivals ever recorded on EU territory.

Dozens died. Within two days, the story had stopped being about victims. It had become a story about Europe’s political nerves.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Dead Sea On a Dalmatian Island Paradise
World.content:
August the 8th, 2026 – There’s a so-called Croatian dead sea, tucked away on a southern Dalmatian island paradise, just a stone’s throw away from the hustle and bustle of Dubrovnik.

Hidden away on an island in the very far south of Croatia lies an unusual lake that shares its name with the saltiest sea in the world. In summer it is a popular swimming spot. Just a few hundred metres from the famous Dubrovnik lies the island of Lokrum. Putni kofer writes that this beautiful little island of small size and great diversity is a must-visit destination for a trip from the Mediterranean pearl and offers peace and beauty that can rarely be experienced elsewhere. But did you know that Lokrum also hides the Croatian Dead Sea? That is exactly what an unusual lake is called that has become one of its most popular swimming spots in the summer months.

The Croatian Dead Sea – 30 metres wide and 10 metres deep

The island of Lokrum itself is believed to have got its name from the abundance of sour wild orange trees that once grew on it, derived from the Latin word for sour fruit, acrumen. Its highest peak, Glavica, is 96 metres high, and on the southern part of the island there is also a small lake. That is precisely the Croatian Dead Sea!

It is 30 metres wide and, at its deepest point, ten metres deep. Its southwestern shore is not kind to visitors, but the northeastern one is. That is why the Croatian Dead Sea has become one of the favourite swimming spots on the island, especially for families with small children.

This natural wonder is actually a saltwater lake connected to the Adriatic Sea by a narrow channel. The enclosed natural cove is ideal for swimming because there are never any waves in it, and the water is shallow and warmer than that on the open sea. In summer the lake on the island of Lokrum is full of bathers and tourists, so it is best to visit it out of season or in the early morning hours. Nearby there is also a natural stone arch that locals call “Buža”, a favourite backdrop for photographs among tourists. The Croatian Dead Sea was of interest to numerous researchers and travel writers who, as early as the 19th century, analysed and described the chemical composition of its seawater. Today this lake is part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, and its condition is regularly monitored.

the island of plants…

Over many millions of years, the rocks have been extremely tectonically disturbed, as evidenced by the systems of cracks and faults that are gradually widened by karstification and the erosive action of the sea. Thus a former erosional depression in the relief, today known as the Lokrum swimming area, was filled with the sea in the youngest geological period, the Quaternary. You can very easily reach the island by regular boat lines from Dubrovnik. This pearl of the southern Adriatic was first protected as early as 1963, and since 1976 it has had the status of a special forest vegetation reserve. Hundreds of plant species grow on it, including 70 species of eucalyptus.

Besides the botanical garden and the beaches, the biggest attractions are also the abandoned Benedictine monastery and the castle on the southern part of the island. You can simply walk across Lokrum, but if you really want to enjoy it and explore it in more detail, we definitely recommend setting aside a whole day.
